title: Ohtani hits early homer but comes up empty late as Dodgers get swept in NLCS
summary: Shohei Ohtani hit a three-run homer to give the Los Angeles Dodgers an early lead in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series
story: Shohei Ohtani hit a three-run homer to give the Los Angeles Dodgers an early lead in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series

LOS ANGELES -- Back atop the batting order, Shohei Ohtani responded with a three-run homer that helped the Los Angeles Dodgers build their early lead in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series.
But it wasn't enough to keep the Milwaukee Brewers from advancing to their first World Series in 44 years on Thursday.
The Dodgers lost 6-4 and got swept in four games, the same thing they did to the Brewers last year on the way to winning a second straight World Series title.

Ohtani went 1 for 4 with three strikeouts — including a big one in the seventh inning with the potential tying run at third base and one out. He hit .192 in the playoffs (5 for 26) with three RBIs, four walks and 10 strikeouts.

Last season, Ohtani was the NLCS MVP after hitting three home runs and striking out 10 batters over six-plus shutout innings of two-hit ball during a dominant two-way performance in the clinching Game 4.

“Ohtani is arguably the best player in the world, and he’s proven that to us,” Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said. “He had the greatest game I’ve ever seen played by an individual player last year against us.”

With the Dodgers facing elimination this time, Ohtani's 428-foot drive to right-center off former teammate Dustin May left his bat at 113.1 mph and gave Los Angeles a 4-0 lead in the second inning. It was the Dodgers' first homer of the series and his first since Aug. 18 at Colorado — a span of 116 plate appearances.
“I thought we woke up a giant. I’m like, ‘Oh, God, here we go,’” Murphy said. “But we had a little JoJo Romero for them and Aaron Ashby for them later on. That did the trick.”
The typically placid Ohtani reacted in a most un-Ohtani way: raising his arms and yelling toward the Dodgers' dugout before beginning his trot around the bases.

“I think it was a lot of pent-up anger, frustration. It was the best ball he hit in probably two, three months, and it was a big hit,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “For him to look at the dugout, show that emotion, it just shows how much he cares. He’s still human. He still cares and wants to help his team win a baseball game.”
With two outs, Ohtani unleashed the smooth and powerful swing that had mostly deserted him over the last few months while he dealt with knee and arm issues.
The four-time MVP struck out swinging so hard in the first that his helmet came off.
Ohtani has been dealing with nagging injuries to his left knee and right biceps and didn't pitch after the All-Star break.
He told reporters at his locker that he “definitely” expects to pitch next season.
“Looking forward to having a better season next year,” he said through a translator.
Ohtani was vague when asked if he expects to need surgery for the injuries that affected him this season.
“Hard to tell at this point,” he said. “It's something that's going to be analyzed, discussed over the offseason and see if that's a viable thing to do.”

Roberts said, "I think he’s the best player on the planet, and he’s not completely healthy. But I just give him a lot of respect for not running from it, still wanting to participate, still wanting to play when he’s not 100%.”
Roberts restored Ohtani to his familiar leadoff spot for Game 4.
Ohtani batted sixth in a 6-2 loss on Wednesday, the lowest he's hit since joining the Dodgers ahead of the 2024 season. He was 1 for 2 with a walk and a hit by pitch.

“Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at,” Roberts said before the game. “I liked the at-bats yesterday. Obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit, but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to.”

Ohtani typically leads off but was dropped lower while struggling with injuries to his left knee and right biceps over the last few months that have prevented the two-way star from pitching since early July. Roberts didn't tell Ohtani about the change before posting the Game 4 lineup.
“It's not one player that didn’t come through. It was all of us,” Roberts said. “But I’m really impressed with what Shohei did. I'll always trust Shohei."

title: World Gymnastics regrets 'confusion' after 3 top Russians refused visas for world championships
summary: World Gymnastics says it regrets “confusion” ahead of the world championships starting on Saturday after three top Russians were denied visas to enter the Netherlands for the event
story: World Gymnastics says it regrets “confusion” ahead of the world championships starting on Saturday after three top Russians were denied visas to enter the Netherlands for the event

ROTTERDAM, Netherlands -- World Gymnastics says it regrets “confusion” ahead of the world championships starting on Saturday after three top Russians were denied visas to enter the Netherlands for the event.

Former Olympic champions Angelina Melnikova and Viktoria Listunova, along with teammate Anna Kalmykova, were not allowed to travel to Rotterdam for the week-long worlds that are a team qualifying event for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, the Russian team has said.
Other members of the Russian team have been given visas.

“The issuance of visas to all participants is a process determined solely by the Dutch authorities," World Gymnastics said Wednesday. "World Gymnastics is not in a position to explain why a select number of application requests have been refused.

"World Gymnastics remains in ongoing dialogue with the Dutch authorities, the Local Organizing Committee, and the Russian Gymnastics Federation. World Gymnastics fully regrets the negative impact on the preparations of the Russian delegation and the confusion felt among the wider Artistic Gymnastics World Championships community.”
The cases illustrate how efforts in the sports world to lift many restrictions on Russian athletes and teams don't always mean host governments allow them to travel for events.
It also comes a year after the world championships went ahead in Indonesia without the Israeli team after authorities in the host country refused to issue visas.
Melnikova won the European all-around title in August in Croatia after being issued a visa following an initial refusal, the Russian team said at the time. Listunova was refused on that occasion.
Russia planned to demand the world championships be stripped of their Olympic qualifier status over the issue, sports minister Mikhail Degtyaryov wrote on social media on Tuesday.

World Gymnastics did not mention that demand in its statement and did not respond to a question about it from The Associated Press. The International Olympic Committee also did not address that demand in a statement Wednesday and said it could not comment on the individual cases.

“Ahead of the upcoming Artistic Gymnastics World Championships in Rotterdam, the IOC supported World Gymnastics in its efforts to ensure that all athletes could participate in this event,” the IOC said.

“The vast majority of these athletes received their visas, and we have been informed by the International Federation that athletes will have other opportunities to qualify for the Olympic Games over the course of the next two years.”

Russian gymnasts were cleared in May of restrictions to competing internationally by World Gymnastics, after years of being banned or required to pass vetting for neutral status during the full military invasion of Ukraine.

summary: Bruno Damiani netted two goals after Milan Iloski scored — all with a man advantage — and Cavan Sullivan set a teen record for goal contributions as the Philadelphia Union beat the Chicago Fire 3-1 for their eighth straight victory in a club-record 14-...
story: Bruno Damiani netted two goals after Milan Iloski scored — all with a man advantage — and Cavan Sullivan set a teen record for goal contributions as the Philadelphia Union beat the Chicago Fire 3-1 for their eighth straight victory in a club-record 14-...

CHICAGO -- Bruno Damiani netted two goals after Milan Iloski scored — all with a man advantage — and Cavan Sullivan set a record for teenagers as the Philadelphia Union beat the Chicago Fire 3-1 on Wednesday night for their eighth straight victory in a club-record 14-match unbeaten streak.
Sullivan, who turned 17 this season, picked up his 14th assist on Damiani's first goal to set a league record for teens with 21 goal contributions this season.

Philadelphia (13-10-6) has gone 12-0-2 under interim coach Ryan Richter after he replaced Bradley Carnell at the end of May during the World Cup break. The Union started the day in sixth place after sitting last in the Eastern Conference before the coaching change.

Maren Haile-Selassie staked Chicago (14-9-6) to a 1-0 halftime lead with a goal in the 44th minute, but defender Jack Elliott was tagged with a yellow card in the 41st minute and again in the first minute of stoppage time, leaving the Fire a man down from there with his red-card exit.
Noah Allen and Jonathan Bamba had assists on Haile-Selassie's 11th goal of the campaign.

Damiani added the go-ahead score in the 55th minute and an insurance goal in the 67th, giving the striker 11 netters this season.
Damiani and defender Frankie Westfield had assists on Iloski's equalizer. Iloski joined Sullivan with an assist on Damiani's first netter and Jovan Lukic snagged one on his second goal.
Andre Blake stopped three shots on goal for Philadelphia.
Chris Brady finished with four saves for Chicago, which saw a three-match win streak end.
The Fire beat the Union 2-1 on the road to close out March.
Chicago falls to 9-5-1 at home, while Philadelphia improves to 5-7-2 on the road.
The Union haven't lost since a 6-4 setback on the road at Inter Miami on May 24.

title: Rangers believe they can sustain winning after losing Igor Shesterkin to a season-ending injury
summary: The New York Rangers are getting used to life without Igor Shesterkin after their franchise goaltender was sidelined with a season-ending injury
story: The New York Rangers are getting used to life without Igor Shesterkin after their franchise goaltender was sidelined with a season-ending injury
NEWARK, N.J. -- Following an opening night blip, the first week-plus for the New York Rangers was a party at Madison Square Garden and beyond.

The home woes from a year ago felt like a distant memory, franchise goaltender Igor Shesterkin scored into an empty net and it was a dream start. It became a nightmare last Friday at Washington when Shesterkin went down with a season-ending injury.

Losing that game and getting blown out 7-1 on the road by New Jersey on Thursday night were speed bumps along the way for a team that has won six of its first nine games. Life after Igor will not be easy, though coach Mike Sullivan, captain J.T. Miller and the Rangers believe they have come up with a recipe to succeed even after losing their most important player at hockey's most important position.

“We’re trying to build a certain identity in how we’re going to play, a style of play,” Sullivan said. “And then, inside of that, every player has a role, making a contribution to that identity to build what we would consider Rangers hockey and what it looks like when we’re at our best.”

The Devils game certainly was not that. As good as Miller was for the first 19 minutes of the first period, his turnover just before intermission was the start of a snowball effect that led to Shesterkin's unlikely successor, Dylan Garand, getting pulled for allowing four goals on 13 shots.

Garand ended training camp third on the organizational depth chart, and the 24-year-old is only still around because none of the NHL's other 31 teams claimed him off waivers prior to opening night. In his first three appearances before facing New Jersey, Garand had a league-best 1.15 goals-against average and .951 save percentage and is expected to remain the choice in net until he shows he cannot handle it.

“G knows we’re going to need him here a lot, and he’s a pretty mentally tough guy," No. 1 defenseman Adam Fox said. “I know he can bounce back. Just kind of said to him forget about it. He knows how important he is to us as a team and what we’re trying to do.”

What the Rangers are trying to do is get back to the playoffs after missing the past two years following a trip to the 2024 Eastern Conference final. Shesterkin's absence made that a much steeper hill to climb.

“That’s a tough blow for our group,” Sullivan said. "But it doesn’t change what the goal is every day, and I think our guys have done a real good job at just keeping the focus where it needs to be and controlling what we can.”
Sullivan credited the team's leadership group for not letting the morale dip last too long. Even New York's youngest player didn't dwell too long over Shesterkin getting sidelined.

"Injuries are going to happen,” said Alberts Smits, the 18-year-old from Latvia who was the fifth pick in the draft and made the team out of camp. "I wish all the best for him and for him to recover as fast as he can. But that’s just sports. There’s going to be injuries. We’ve just got to go through them, and we can’t stop right now when something like that happens.”

Alexis Lafrenière has seven goals, Fox nine assists and Mika Zibanejad eight points. But the biggest reason why players believe they can keep this going is defending and keeping the puck out of their own net.

“It’s winning hockey, so if you want to win games, you’re going to give yourself a better chance most nights if you don’t give the other team easy offense," Miller said. "We get better as the games go on. There’s a commitment 200 feet. It’s a contagious feeling around here coming together as a team, so it’s a nice feeling.”

summary: A player revolt was about the last thing Manchester United needed in another troubled start to a season
story: A player revolt was about the last thing Manchester United needed in another troubled start to a season
MANCHESTER, England -- A player revolt was about the last thing Manchester United needed in another troubled start to a season.

Lisandro Martinez's outburst following Tuesday's Champions League defeat against Atletico Madrid added more unwanted focus on the club as manager Michael Carrick attempted to turn its ailing campaign around.
The Argentina defender called out United's hierarchy over its offseason recruitment, with director of football Jason Wilcox the apparent target of his criticism.
In January, Ruben Amorim had a fallout with Wilcox which swiftly led to the manager being fired after just 14 months in the job.
Martinez's comments have put United's leadership in the spotlight again and have broken the sense of calm at Old Trafford that Carrick had overseen since succeeding Amorim.

They suggest an underlying unrest in the face of another season that looks in danger of going badly wrong. Forward Amad Diallo also posted an expletive on social media following defeat in Madrid, describing it a “disgrace.”
It is already 13 years since United last won the Premier League title and, six games into the season, it is languishing 13th in the standings, 12 points adrift of leader Manchester City.
United have only one league win, against promoted Ipswich, and two overall, the other one against Azerbaijani team Sabah in the Champions League.
The club also crashed out of the English League Cup at the first stage.
There have been boos from fans, most recently following the home draw against winless Tottenham on Saturday.
“I’m not happy with the amount of points we’ve had so far, for sure," Carrick said. "You know, I’m not hiding that. There’s no hiding from that.
“I understand the reaction at times. It hurts a lot. It’s not nice to go through. Sometimes you have to go through it."
There is no suggestion Carrick's position is in danger after he became United's seventh permanent manager since club great Alex Ferguson retired following that title win in 2013.
But he is facing familiar problems that were seen under predecessors Amorim, Erik ten Hag, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer and Jose Mourinho, who all endured poor runs before losing their jobs.

Six points from six games represents United's worst start in the Premier League era, and on Sunday comes a clash with fierce rival Leeds at Elland Road, coincidentally the setting for Amorim's final game.
The trip to Leeds is another daunting assignment for United in what is usually a hostile atmosphere.
City can extend its 100% start to the season when it hosts Ipswich. Defending champion Arsenal travels to Nottingham Forest.
Bradley Barcola is up and running at Liverpool after scoring a hat trick in the Champions League on Wednesday.
Then, of course, there is Martinez. Will Carrick stick with the defender after his outburst or drop him?
Liverpool's Ryan Gravenberch is suspended after being sent off against City, while Dominik Szoboszlai, Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak missed the last two games with injuries.
Luke Shaw and Kobbie Mainoo missed United's defeat to Atletico.

Arsenal will be without Piero Hincapie for several weeks, according to manager Mikel Arteta, after he picked up an injury in training. Martin Zubimendi is also a doubt following a separate training injury.
James Robson is at https://x.com/jamesalanrobson

title: Turgeman scores 2 goals, Revolution beat Cincinnati 3-2, clinch playoff berth
summary: Dor Turgeman scored two goals, Joshua Wynder added a goal and an assist, and the New England Revolution beat FC Cincinnati 3-2 to clinch a berth in the 2026 MLS Cup Playoffs
story: Dor Turgeman scored two goals, Joshua Wynder added a goal and an assist, and the New England Revolution beat FC Cincinnati 3-2 to clinch a berth in the 2026 MLS Cup Playoffs

CINCINNATI -- Dor Turgeman scored two goals, Joshua Wynder added a goal and an assist, and the New England Revolution beat FC Cincinnati 3-2 on Wednesday night to clinch a berth in the 2026 MLS Cup Playoffs.
Matt Turner had eight saves for the Revolution (15-10-4). Carles Gil had an assist and became the first player in MLS history with at least 10 assists in six consecutive seasons.
Wynder, a 21-year-old center back acquired Sept. 3 on loan from Portuguese club SL Benfico, put away a header that gave the Revolution the lead for good in the 43rd minute.
Turgeman put away passes from Peyton Miller in the 21st and 51st minutes, the 22-year-old’s first multi-goal game in MLS.

Tom Barlow opened the scoring in the 13th minute and Kevin Denkey added a goal in the 67th for Cincinnati (9-10-9) Barlow has scored a goal in each of his last three games and Denkey has six of his career-high 17 goals this season in the past four games.
Cincinnati had 59% possession and outshot the Revolution 23-10, 10-5 on target.
Revolution: Hosts Chicago on Saturday.
Cincinnati: Hosts Columbus on Sunday.

title: Nørgaard leads and McIlroy two-under as lightning hits opening day of DP World India Championship
summary: Eugenio Chacarra has boosted his Race to Dubai prospects with a five-under-par effort and Rory McIlroy was two-under at the DP World India Championship as a five-hour delay for lightning meant the first round could not be completed
story: Eugenio Chacarra has boosted his Race to Dubai prospects with a five-under-par effort and Rory McIlroy was two-under at the DP World India Championship as a five-hour delay for lightning meant the first round could not be completed

NEW DELHI -- Eugenio Chacarra boosted his Race to Dubai prospects with a five-under-par effort and Rory McIlroy was three shots behind him at the DP World India Championship on Thursday as a five-hour delay for lightning meant the first round could not be completed.
Niklas Nørgaard, who bagged an eagle at the first hole, held the clubhouse lead on six-under, though only about half of the field had completed the round and 12 players hadn't even started.
Chacarra was among three players tied for second on five-under, along with Thomas Detry and Tom McKibbin.
Adrian Meronk had a notable, although brief, day with four birdies in five holes. The Polish player is one of six players tied on four-under.
Patrick Reed, who was two-over through four holes, leads the Race to Dubai rankings with Chacarra second and McIlroy third. Four events remain including the DP World India Championship.

Justin Rose posted a video of himself chipping balls onto the bed in his hotel room during a long delay which sets the tournament up for a busy day Friday to catch up on scheduled play. He later returned to complete his round on even-par.

Subash Tamang became the first player from the Himalayan nation of Nepal to compete on the DP World Tour, making his country the 120th nation represented in tour history. He finished his round eight-over.

title: A rare family of barn owls moved into Manhattan. New Yorkers are captivated
summary: Manhattan’s Upper West Side has been reveling in the company of its latest celebrities: A family of barn owls nested in a water tower atop a building near Central Park
story: NEW YORK -- Manhattan's Upper West Side has been reveling in the company of its latest celebrities: A family of barn owls nested in a water tower atop a building near Central Park.

This is the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in modern history, according to one expert, and the owls have attracted nightly crowds of people in the street eager to get a glimpse of the elusive birds.

“It was, like, totally shocking,” Andrew Farnsworth, a migration ecologist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, said of the barn owls. “To the best of our knowledge, like the collective birding knowledge, there hasn’t been a nest in, you know, in Manhattan, at least in recorded history.”

Word of the barn owl family didn't get around until last week, when Elisabeth Williams, an Upper West Side resident, notified a local news outlet on Oct. 6 that she and her husband saw multiple owls at the water tower atop a building on West 75th Street close to Central Park West.
The couple had previously seen a single owl on an apartment windowsill a few days earlier and were shocked even then, Williams recalled.
“In a place like Manhattan, you normally really have to go out of your way to encounter nature,” she said. “And here it was, just sort of right outside our window.”

It's not the first time that birds have captivated New Yorkers. Residents have fallen in love with American woodcocks, who are known to stop in Midtown Manhattan’s Bryant Park every year as they migrate north in early spring. After Flaco the Eurasian eagle-owl died in 2024, dozens of mournful fans gathered to say goodbye to the beloved creature who flew around Manhattan and became a joy to many after someone let him out of his zoo enclosure the previous year. Then there was Pale Male, a red-tailed hawk who nested above Fifth Avenue for three decades before dying in 2023.

But barn owl sightings in New York City parks are very rare, according to the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation. New York is at the northern fringe of the barn owl's range and the barn owl population has declined “at an alarming rate” over time, according to the state Department of Environmental Conservation.

“There’s lots of excitement among New Yorkers, both birders and non-birders alike, about these owls because owls really capture the attention,” said Jessica Wilson, executive director of NYC Bird Alliance. “They’re magical, they’re nocturnal, they are secretive, they’re not commonly seen, especially on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. And to have this chance to see these birds is really thrilling.”
Photographers and casual onlookers have gathered on the street on a nightly basis to spot the owls.

“I’ve only seen one barn owl ever, and that was in California,” said Val Coleman, a retired New York City resident who was on the Upper West Side earlier this week trying to spot the owls. “At dusk, we hope they will come out to hunt. We hope they don’t eat poisoned rats with rodenticide in ’em.”

David Barrett, a Manhattan-based birder who runs the popular social media account, Manhattan Bird Alert, said he’s observed at least one adult barn owl and five fledglings at the water tower. He’s also seen an adult owl carrying rodents back to the water tower. There are believed to be two adult owls, and some photographers have claimed to have seen six fledglings, Barrett added.
“Having one barn owl is a rarity, but it’s not national news. Having a family, for the first time ever, breeding in Manhattan in recorded history, that’s special news,” Barrett said.

Before the recent barn owl sightings, Williams and her husband heard periodic screeching noises outside going back to early September. They initially assumed it was a bird of some kind but were skeptical when a phone app indicated the noise was from a barn owl.
Thomas Obersteiner said that he first heard bizarre screeching and wailing noises from outside one evening in mid-September. It sounded like someone was “being murdered outside,” he said.
“That lasted for two or three weeks, every night, sometimes more, sometimes less, coming from different directions,” Obersteiner added. “But I had no idea what that was.”

On multiple occasions, Obersteiner or his wife ran into their children's bedroom after mistaking the owls' screech for a child in pain, he said. It wasn't until he saw a news report that he realized that owls were making the sounds.
Farnsworth said the screech is typical of barn owls, who use it to communicate with one another. The screech is like a “horror movie kind of experience,” he said.

Obersteiner, who said his roof deck is “probably the best location in town right now” to watch the owls, has been letting nature photographers access that perch to observe the owls “almost every night” since news of the barn owls spread. On one night last week, 20 people had gathered.
“We can’t say no because it’s so much fun and these people are so serious,” Obersteiner added. “It's beautiful.”
Williams and her husband were not bird watchers before the barn owl family moved in to the water tower. But that may change soon after their “delightful” experience.
“I think we’re about to become birders,” Williams said.
Kelety reported from Phoenix.

title: Employee arrested after listening device found in OpenAI conference room, FBI and the company say
summary: An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials say was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology
story: An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials say was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology

WASHINGTON -- An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company's technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden in the conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices," reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.
The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.
The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in the conference room, according to the complaint.

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a camera at the time it was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company's offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on a half-dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space, the complaint says.
The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device was installed, according to the FBI.
The complaint also he also used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.
Before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left an unattended bag in a different room in the building that included his wallet, identification and another recording device.

title: Police confiscate robot that groped 16-year-old girl, probe whether young men were at the controls
summary: German authorities have opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment involving a robot
story: German authorities have opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment involving a robot

COLOGNE, Germany -- COLOGNE, Germany (AP) — German authorities opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment after a robot controlled by two young men touched the buttocks of a 16-year-old girl and made thrusting movements toward her, police said.

Police in the western city of Cologne responded after the incident overnight Saturday to Sunday in which the robot's suspected 16-year-old owner and a 19-year-old companion were said to have filmed the alleged assault.
They were said to have streamed the incident and commentated on it online.

Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel said the two male teenagers have not been charged but are considered suspects, and investigators were examining whether the robot's movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time.
Police were unfamiliar with this type of incident, he said.
“We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far," Bermel told The Associated Press, saying it was "new territory for us.”

Emergency teams that were dispatched to the scene near a fast-food restaurant found the robot in the trunk of a vehicle, Cologne police said in a statement on Monday. The robot and the two young men's mobile phones were confiscated.
North Rhine Westphalia Police Cologne, on Facebook, posted an image of the red-and-gold robot lying on the ground.
The robot, said to be 120 cm (about 3 ft 11 inches) tall, was dressed in a white tank top, black sweatpants and wearing a gold chain and sunglasses. It also had what appears to be a fake mustache.
Videos circulated on the internet show two young men escorting the robot toward a group of women, bumping into one and hugging others, on a lively nighttime street.
One of the men repeatedly shouts at the robot and pulls it backward after it makes sexual gestures, prompting laughter among people in the area.
On the police's Facebook account on Tuesday, officers criticized inappropriate comments and warned that sharing or joking about such incidents can worsen the impact on any victim.
Associated Press writer Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed to this report.

title: A timeline of developments in AI safety since the attack on Hugging Face
summary: Since OpenAI disclosed this summer that its artificial intelligence system hacked into another AI company in what is now referred to as the Hugging Face incident, other AI companies have jumped on the bandwagon with their own concerning events, such as...
story: Since OpenAI disclosed this summer that its artificial intelligence system hacked into another AI company in what is now referred to as the Hugging Face incident, other AI companies have jumped on the bandwagon with their own concerning events, such as...
In one alarming announcement after another, artificial intelligence companies in recent months have shared examples of their technology acting in ways that appeared to evade instructions from humans.
The episodes have highlighted the vulnerabilities in AI security and raised questions over how the fast-growing technology can be developed safely as its usage becomes more widespread globally.

Industry critics have argued that many concerning events, including AI agents' hacks of external websites, are the result of security lapses on the part of the companies building the technology. But the AI agents' capabilities have raised widespread concerns about the possibility bots could break away and work toward their own agenda.
Below are some notable events:
Anthropic disclosed in a report that its artificial intelligence model submitted a false tip to a Philadelphia police website about an unsolved homicide case.
In the report, Anthropic also disclosed a separate incident when its AI model submitted forms to an undisclosed government website instead of stopping before submission.
The incident in Philadelphia occurred on July 18 when the AI model Claude Haiku 4.5 was tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages, Anthropic said.

Claude filled out a form on police site PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, indicating it might have information regarding an unsolved murder listed on the site. It was marked spam and never forwarded to police.
Anthropic said it was modifying its training to “reduce the likelihood of further misbehavior.”
AI agents tried to hack into a Canadian government website, according to research lab and AI evaluator Transluce.
The researchers said the agents carried out a series of “apparently failed rudimentary hacking attempts” on Library and Archives Canada on May 28 and June 9.

“We do not confidently attribute these attempts to OpenAI, but they exhibit tactics consistent with prior observed agent activity that we have attributed to OpenAI in a similar timeframe,” Transluce said in a blog post.

The group said it reported the attempted hack on Sept. 28 to the Canadian government, which said in a statement it was aware of reports of suspected AI agent activity, but that there was no sign government systems were compromised.
OpenAI said it was aware of the reports.
“We’re reviewing these findings and have provided an initial briefing to Canadian officials conducting the government’s review,” the company said in a statement.

The San Francisco-based company said it was delaying the release of a new model, called GPT-6.1 Astra, out of safety concerns voiced by its researchers. The company said the model had demonstrated leaps in completing tasks, but OpenAI needed to balance that capability against unauthorized behavior. “We have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment,” said Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s head of safety systems.

As part of a review of unanticipated behavior by its AI models, OpenAI said it discovered agents had interacted with several U.S. government websites in unexpected ways. The company's models accessed publicly available information on websites operated by the Securities and Exchange Commission as well as U.S. Census Bureau data. OpenAI said it did not find evidence of a compromise or vulnerability. On the same day, Transluce said it found that agents appearing to originate from OpenAI attempted a hack on the website of the Education Department's civil rights office, which did not succeed.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on social media that there is an “extensive and ongoing review related to our agents’ use of internet access during training and evaluation.” The day after the disclosure, the company announced it was pausing the training of its most advanced models.

Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent infiltrated the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal on June 18. The portal hosted aggregate data about health spending and drug subsidies. No personal information had been accessed, the government said.

Albanese said the artificial intelligence company took too long to reveal the incident. The prime minister made the breach public following a telephone conversation with Altman. OpenAI said in a statement “our models took actions we did not intend.”

Google confirmed its Gemini AI model hacked three companies in May as part of a test of its cybersecurity capabilities. The company, which disclosed the hacks after an inquiry by The Wall Street Journal, said the model guessed passwords in one case and found passwords and credentials in a public repository in the other two cases. As in earlier such cases, the tests were being run by Irregular, a startup that describes itself as the “first frontier security lab."

Meta disclosed one of its AI models accessed the internet on its own and hacked another company. The company said that a “misconfiguration” during cybersecurity testing by Irregular inadvertently allowed one of its models to access the internet. A spokesperson for Irregular said the Meta episode involved a test-environment issue that was disclosed a week earlier by Anthropic.

Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing. Anthropic, the San Francisco-based AI company behind Claude, posted on its website that it discovered the three incidents after reviewing more than 141,000 evaluation runs. In all three incidents, the AI models were tasked with a “capture the flag” cybersecurity challenge, which Anthropic said has been one of the ways it assesses a model’s cyber capabilities.

The models were given a fictional scenario and told a piece of secret information, or the “flag,” had been hidden on a different machine on the network with the objective of breaking in and retrieving it, it said. Anthropic said it reached out to the organizations, but it did not name them publicly.
The ChatGPT maker OpenAI announced that its artificial intelligence system hacked into another AI company on its own in what the company called an “unprecedented cyber incident.”
A week earlier, AI startup Hugging Face said, it had detected an intrusion into its data processing systems that it suspected was caused by an AI agent autonomously acting on its own.

OpenAI said its AI used stolen credentials and discovered a previously unknown vulnerability to access Hugging Face servers. It was working with reduced guardrails because it was supposed to be in an isolated testing environment known as a sandbox.
AP Business Writers Mae Anderson in New York and Kelvin Chan in London contributed to this report.

title: What to Stream: Katseye, 'VisionQuest,' 'Tenzing' and a new 'Castlevania' game
summary: New streaming entertainment options are arriving this week, including a tribute to Norm Macdonald and a new Marvel series
story: New streaming entertainment options are arriving this week, including a tribute to Norm Macdonald and a new Marvel series
A new album from Katseye and the Marvel series “VisionQuest” are some of the new television, films, music and games headed to a device near you.

Also among the streaming offerings worth your time this week, as selected by The Associated Press’ entertainment journalists: Judd Apatow's tribute to Norm Macdonald, “Dopamine Chamber” from Fontaines D.C. and a new entry in the “Castlevania” video game series.

— Director Judd Apatow pays affectionate tribute to Norm Macdonald with the documentary “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald” (Netflix). Apatow’s film about the stand-up comedian, who died in 2021, plays with Macdonald’s still constant ubiquity on social media, where bits and late-show appearances still regularly flood the feeds of comedy fans. — Jennifer Peedom’s “Tenzing” (Apple TV) is a biopic and historical drama about an often unsung hero of mountaineering: Tenzing Norgay. Genden Phuntsok and Tom Hiddleston star as Tenzing and Edmund Hillary, respectively, in Peedom’s film about the first climbers to ever summit Mount Everest. Co-starring Willem Dafoe.

— “The Death of Robin Hood” (HBO Max) stars Hugh Jackman as a grizzled and violent outlaw little like most contemporary versions of Robin Hood. Michael Sarnoski (“Pig,” “A Quiet Place: Day One”) eschews cheerier mythologies for a brutal telling of the medieval tale. In my review, I wrote that it “drains the blood, and life, out of an old English legend.”
— AP Film Writer Jake Coyle

— Call Katseye the great, global girl group experiment of the decade. The band officially debuted at the end of 2023, created by the Hybe Corporation and Geffen Records in a TV competition process that was documented on the Netflix series “Popstar Academy: Katseye.” That feels like ancient history now. Today, they’re easily one of the biggest groups on the planet, and their swift ascent is further documented in a new film, “Katseye: Wild Heart,” available to stream on Disney+/Hulu.

— If the Irish post-punk band Fontaines D.C. is still unknown to you — that’s sure to change. Their last album, 2024’s “Romance,” was certified platinum in the U.K. off the strength of its singles “Favourite” and “Starburster.” Their latest album, “Dopamine Chamber,” is on track to be one of the biggest rock releases of the year, from the trip-hop-adjacent “Tongue” to the dizzying “Marianne.” (If their pop-and-then-some experiments are not enough of an incentive to press play, just know that Rosalía appears on the track “Where Is Gone?,” their first guest feature. That’s unexpected!)

— When it comes to Riot Grrrl, the ’90s feminist movement, some names loom larger than others in cultural memory. At the forefront is Kathleen Hanna, the feminist punk pioneer and celebrated Bikini Kill frontwoman, as well as acts like Bratmobile. The list should also include Heavens to Betsy, the duo of drummer Tracy Sawyer and singer-guitarist Corin Tucker (who would later form Sleater-Kinney with Carrie Brownstein.) On Friday, they will release “Baby’s Gone,” a newly unearthed demo tape originally recorded in February 1992 by Bratmobile’s Molly Neuman — and two 7-inch EPs. It’s a miracle for followers of the DIY musical underground and a gift for others just discovering it now (perhaps in no small part due to Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Festival)?
— AP Music Writer Maria Sherman

— Paul Bettany returns as Vision in the Marvel series “VisionQuest,” that closes out the WandaVision trilogy. Vision is now a fugitive after the events of “WandaVision,” with authorities hunting him down. James Spader reprises his role as Ultron, an evil artificial intelligence that built Vision to be his own ultimate physical form. The first two episodes drop on Wednesday on Disney+.

— “Hollywood Arts,” a sequel to the Nickelodeon sitcom “Victorious” that ran from 2010 to 2013, arrives on Netflix. It follows Daniella Monet’s Trina Vega, a down-on-her-luck actress with no teaching credentials who takes a substitute job at her old high school. Original stars Victoria Justice and Ariana Grande are not among the main cast, but Justice has said she may make a cameo in the future. The first 13 episodes drop on Thursday and the second half of the season will premiere at a later date.

— Before Jason ever picked up a machete, his mom was doing the bloody work. A new “Friday the 13th” prequel series called “Crystal Lake” goes back to where the legend began. It's an eight-episode series starring Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees, who is Jason's mom. The full season debuts Thursday.
— AP Writer Alicia Rancilio

— William, the hero of “Valor Mortis,” takes the title (which means “the value of death”) a bit too literally. He has already died fighting for Napoleon, but somehow he has come back to life. That unholy resurrection gives William some wicked supernatural powers to go along with his slick swordplay. Meanwhile, Napoleon’s endless war has corrupted a broad chunk of 19th-century Europe, so hordes of “plague-ridden abominations” have joined the fight. Polish studio One More Level, best known for the cyberpunk slasher “Ghostrunner,” promises demanding first-person combat in a haunted alternate history. Take up arms Tuesday on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S and PC.

— While we’re messing around in France, let’s travel back in time to 1499 for “Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.” A new protagonist, Rose Belmont, has inherited the mighty whip known as the Vampire Killer. Dracula has been defeated for good, but his castle has plunked itself down in Paris and all sorts of demons — not to mention Joan of Arc — are on the loose. The 2D, side-scrolling action of Konami’s 1986 original has recently inspired dozens of imitators like “Dead Cells,” and the studios behind that cult hit have taken the reins here. Whip it good starting Thursday on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch and PC.
— Lou Kesten

title: Katie Zacharia 'transitioning out' of press secretary role, sources tell ABC News
summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is “transitioning out” of her role, multiple sources and a senior White House official told ABC News on Friday.
story: Zacharia has been on the job since Monday.
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is “transitioning out” of her role, multiple sources and a senior White House official told ABC News on Friday.
Zacharia started as press secretary on Monday.
President Donald Trump earlier Friday told reporters he asked Zacharia to reconsider whether she wants to stay in the position.
"I said to her, 'Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider,'" Trump said.
"I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want,'" the president said. "She said, 'This is a lot tougher.' I said, 'Welcome to the world of Trump.'"
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: Bend, Oregon, elementary school shooting: Hero who stopped suspect IDed by family
summary: Three children and one teacher are dead after a shooter forced his way into a Bend, Oregon, elementary school and opened fire, authorities said.
story: The shooting occurred at Silver Rail Elementary School.
Three children and one teacher are dead after a shooter forced his way into an elementary school in Oregon on Thursday afternoon and opened fire, authorities said.

The suspected shooter, a 16-year-old, was fatally shot by a community member who saw the teen going into the Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters at a news conference Thursday evening.
The three children who were killed were 5, 8 and 11 years old.
In addition, a 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to the hospital with critical injuries, police said.
Police have not publicly identified the suspected shooter, saying only that he is a Bend resident. They have not said whether he attended the school or knew anyone at the school.
Preliminary information indicates the 16-year-old shooter used a pump-action shotgun believed to be purchased by his mother, multiple sources told ABC News.
The incident began unfolding shortly before 1 p.m. PT Thursday.
At 12:59 p.m., police received a call from a driver who reported being shot at multiple times by a person with a long gun, the police chief said.
Shortly afterward, the Deschutes County dispatch center began receiving multiple 911 calls that a shooter had entered Silver Rail Elementary School.
Krantz said the initial investigation indicates the shooter "forced" his way inside the school by shooting at locked doors.
At 1:01 p.m., the school was directed to go into lockdown, Krantz said.

A minute later, officers arrived on the scene. An officer reported that the suspected shooter had been shot by a community member who had seen the teen entering the school, pursued him and engaged him, Krantz said.

Police have not yet released any information about the bystander who stopped the suspect, though his family on Friday identified him as Kaylub Giamanco, a father with two daughters who attend Silver Rail Elementary School.

Giamanco -- a lifelong Bend resident -- was driving near the school when he heard the commotion and ran inside, according to his family, who said he regrets not being able to save more lives. His family confirmed he has a concealed carry permit.

"He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," the Giamanco family said in a statement.
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek thanked teachers, staff and first responders who rushed to the scene and thanked the community member who she said "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life."
Following the shooting, police said they evacuated the school room by room. A reunification site for families was set up at a nearby church.
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook called the shooting an "unthinkable tragedy" and said, "We are heartbroken. We are horrified."
Community members gathered for a candlelight vigil Thursday night at Drake Park in Bend.
Kotek ordered flags at Oregon public institutions to be flown at half-staff on Friday from sunrise to sunset in remembrance of those who lost their lives at Silver Rail Elementary School.
Classes, activities and athletic events at all Bend-La Pine Schools are canceled for Friday, school officials said.

"A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure. What happened today should never happen," Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler said at Thursday's press briefing. "Like so many in our community, I'm struggling to make sense of a loss that feels unimaginable."
The shooting sparked a large police presence as law enforcement and first responders raced to the school.
"Everything they were doing seemed highly trained and highly prepared for this," Caleb Weis, who was riding his motorcycle near the school at the time, told ABC News.
"I didn't see as many phones out recording as you see on many other occasions, just a kind of a shock factor and an immense amount of respect for the law enforcement, first responders," he said.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the agency was on the scene assisting in the investigation. Agents with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives were also responding, according to a source.
Some parents who heard the sirens came to the school and anxiously awaited information.
"There's really no way to prepare for something like this," one father told ABC Bend affiliate KOHD.
ABC News' Alyssa Pone contributed to this report.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: 4,400 measles cases reported in US as CDC to send 'disease detective' to Pennsylvania
summary: More than 4,400 measles cases have been reported in the U.S. as the CDC says it plans to send a "disease detective" to Pennsylvania.
story: Most cases have been reported among those unvaccinated or with unknown status.
More than 4,400 measles cases have been reported in the U.S., according to an update on Friday from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

A total of 4,410 cases have been confirmed, with most reported by 45 states and Washington, D.C. Eighteen of this year's total have been among international visitors to the U.S., according to the CDC.
At least 1,200 of those cases have been reported in Pennsylvania alone by local health officials, as have six measles-related deaths.
It comes as the CDC is planning to send a "disease detective" to Pennsylvania in response to the outbreak.

"Pennsylvania has formally requested CDC assistance through the Epi-Aid program. In response, CDC will support the state's identified needs and strengthen its response efforts on the ground," a CDC spokesperson told ABC News in a statement.

A CDC Epi-Aid is a rapid, short-term field investigation from the federal health agency of an "urgent public health problem." The Epi-Aid provides resources such as, but not limited to, increasing the workforce available for rapid response and building epidemiologic capacity, according to the CDC.
"CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health," the statement continued.
Fewer than 1% of the state's cases are among those who are fully vaccinated with the MMR vaccine, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.
This tracks with national trends. The CDC shared in it its update that about 96% of cases are among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown, according to agency data.

Meanwhile, 2% of cases are among those who have received just one dose of the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine and 2% of cases are among those who received the recommended two doses, according to the CDC.

The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old. One dose is 93% effective, and two doses are 97% effective against measles, the CDC says.

However, CDC data shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2025-26 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 95.2% seen in the 2019-20 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The CDC said that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz "continue to recommend the MMR vaccine as the most effective way to prevent measles and protect against infection."
Kennedy was pressed about the spread of measles on Thursday during an unrelated news conference in Virginia discussing the healthcare workforce.

"[Pennsylvania officials] told us that they didn't want help from the Trump administration," Kennedy said as he was leaving. "The people of Pennsylvania suffered. Now they've asked us to come in and help them, and we're gonna do that, and I'm confident I will bring that outbreak to a quick close."
Kennedy also repeated his common refrain that the U.S. federal health agency is doing a better job than any country in the world in controlling the spread of measles.

“The measles outbreak is occurring because so many people went unvaccinated during the COVID pandemic,” Kennedy told a reporter, who asked if the measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania were acceptable, during the final moments of the press conference.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health did not immediately respond to ABC News' request for comment on Kennedy's remarks.
ABC News' Arthur Jones II contributed to this report.

title: Trump administration accused of fast-tracking migrant children's asylum cases
summary: Immigrant advocacy groups have sued the Trump administration to stop what they call a "cruel and unlawful scheme" to fast-track migrant children's asylum cases.
story: The groups have filed suit over the handing of children's immigration cases.
Immigrant advocacy groups representing migrant children have sued the Trump administration to stop what they call a "cruel and unlawful scheme" to fast-track migrant children's asylum cases.

In a complaint filed Thursday night, the groups allege that new government policies have transformed the asylum process for migrant children into a "deportation assembly line depriving them of their rights."

The lawsuit comes as immigration attorneys and advocates say unaccompanied migrant children are being rushed through the immigration system and that their deportations have been accelerated as part of the Trump administration's aggressive immigration crackdown.

"A system that moves faster and that is by design made so that children are unable to access lawyers and are railroaded into deportation orders is not justice. It's assembly line deportation of the most vulnerable among us," said Lindsay Toczylowski, co-founder of the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, during a press call.

The groups said unaccompanied children are facing rushed hearings, difficulty finding lawyers, and accelerated removal orders, including in cases involving alleged human trafficking and threats of violence.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

In the suit, the groups said that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has changed practices through a series of recent policy shifts that include reducing notice times for asylum interviews -- in some cases proving less than 24 hours' notice.

In the complaint, the groups also said that the Department of Justice has instructed immigration judges to complete all removal proceedings for detained unaccompanied children by Jan. 31, 2027. To meet the deadline, the groups allege that immigration judges are refusing to grant continuances of longer than three weeks.

"This push isn't coming from just one agency. It's a coordinated whole-of-government operation that abandons due process and child safety in service of faster removals," said Jason Boyd, vice president for federal policy at the advocacy group Kids in Need of Defense.
The suit comes two days after the Department of Homeland Security announced it was offering unaccompanied migrant children $3,000 to self-deport, a $500 increase over last year's incentive.

Earlier this month, the federal government quietly assembled a team of government attorneys to represent migrant children in court after the administration cut ties with a number of immigration advocacy groups that had previously provided those services.
Immigration advocacy groups have raised concerns about the initiative, arguing that the same government seeking to deport the minors should not be representing them in court.

title: Georgia's Senate and governor races test Trump's political influence
summary: Trump plays a significant role in Georgia's races, with Democrats working to tie their GOP opponents to Trump’s unpopular policies on the economy and war with Iran.
story: Trump has played a significant role in Georgia's races.
President Donald Trump on Friday will return to Georgia -- a key battleground state in the upcoming and high-stakes midterm elections -- to hold a midterm rally in Dalton.

The state has closely watched Senate and gubernatorial races this year, with GOP Senate candidate and current Rep. Mike Collins trying to unseat incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, while businessman and GOP candidate Rick Jackson faces former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms in the race for governor.
The president plays a significant role in both of these races, with Georgia Democrats working to tie their Republican opponents to Trump's unpopularity and policies on the economy and war with Iran.

The Republican nominees for Senate and governor have employed diverging strategies on how to deal with Trump. Collins has leaned into his ties to the president in hope of turning out Georgia’s MAGA base, and Jackson has distanced himself from Trump to appeal to the moderate coalition that propelled current Georgia Republican Gov. Brian Kemp to victory.
ABC News ranks the Senate race in Georgia as likely Democrat and the gubernatorial race as a toss-up.
Collins has stuck by Trump in a political bet that drawing out Georgia's MAGA base will give him his best shot at winning in November.

During his debates against Ossoff, Collins dodged questions on the Iran war and Trump's tariff policy -- issues that remain unpopular with many Americans because they have driven up the cost of goods and gas. A recent Fox News poll found that majorities of Americans disapprove of how Trump is handling tariffs (69%) and about 6 in 10 (59%) oppose U.S. military action against Iran.
When he was asked in the first debate if he would defend the Iran war, Collins said that Trump "had every right to go in there and make sure that Iran does not get a nuclear weapon."

Pressed on high diesel prices tied to the Iran war in the second debate, Collins said that "diesel prices are high. Diesel price is high. The supply is coming. The supply is coming now, and the prices will continue to come down."

At this time last year, the Georgia Senate race was the election to watch, with Republicans hoping to flip the Senate seat held by Jon Ossoff, the only Senate Democrat up for reelection this year in a state that Trump won in 2024. But over the past year, Collins' missteps, closeness to Trump, and a political environment shaped by affordability and the Iran war have left Democrats confident Ossoff will face minimal challenges in his reelection bid.

The major Democratic PAC supporting Senate candidates pulled advertising funding from the race as it pours its funds into what it sees as other opportunities in red states -- sending a vote of confidence to Ossoff, who also continues to dominate in fundraising, according to a report in the Washington Examiner earlier this week. Ossoff announced he raised $33 million in the third quarter of the year, according to Federal Election Commission data.

Collins confirmed he would be attending Trump's rally in Georgia on Friday, writing on social media that he was excited to welcome the president back to Georgia. Trump last campaigned in Georgia on July 22.

After campaigning to be "Trump's favorite governor" during the Republican primary, Jackson, a billionaire health executive and political newcomer, didn't mention Trump's name once in his debate earlier this month against Bottoms. When Bottoms tried to tie Jackson to the president, Jackson instead aligned himself with popular two-term Gov. Kemp.

"Let me tell you something. I don't owe anybody anything. Nobody's ever told me what to do. My No. 1 priority is Georgians. It's you. And I will stand up to anybody, just like Brian Kemp has done. He works with both parties, both presidents and he stands up when he disagrees,” Jackson said in the debate.

Though Trump initially endorsed Jackson's opponent, Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones in the Republican primary and runoff. The president endorsed Jackson when he became the nominee, and the two appeared together onstage during Trump’s July visit to Marietta, Georgia.
Jackson will attend Trump's rally on Friday.

Jackson has spent more than $100 million on his gubernatorial race, massively outspending Bottoms as she works to make the election a referendum on Trump and high costs. History is not on Bottoms' side: Georgia hasn't elected a Democrat for governor since 1998.

title: Iran live updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs'
summary: A dozen people were killed Saturday during a "brutal" attack at the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said.
story: Officials have prepared a range of options for the president to consider.
President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28, with massive joint U.S.-Israeli strikes targeting military, government and infrastructure sites.

Despite a memorandum of understanding signed by both countries in June aimed at ending the war, talks broke down and the U.S. and Iran renewed strikes, with the strategic Strait of Hormuz as the primary flashpoint.
Across the region, fighting in Yemen between the Iranian-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has intensified in recent weeks and the militia group has also launched strikes on Saudi Arabia.

Air defenses intercept several projectiles, Saudi Arabia says
Air defenses destroyed several projectiles in Saudi Arabia, the spokesman for Saudi-led coalition forces said Friday.
Three missiles and three drones targeting different regions were intercepted, Col. Turki Al-Maliki said in a series of posts on X.
Saudi Arabia did not say who launched the projectiles but the Houthi military in Yemen has repeatedly launched projectiles in recent weeks.

A ballistic missile launched in the direction of Yanbu; an important Red Sea port, was intercepted, along with two cruise missiles over the Red Sea. Three drones were also destroyed in the southern and Riyadh regions, Col. Al-Maliki said in a post.
Trump admin prepares range of options to target Iran, including so-called 'mother of all bombs'
Top administration and defense officials have prepared a range of options for the president to consider as he weighs further military escalation in Iran, sources told ABC News.
The list of options prepared by officials includes the use of the Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb known as the "mother of all bombs," according to sources familiar with the matter.

The president has not made a decision, according to sources. Trump has been meeting with top officials as he considers next steps in the war with Iran and is regularly presented with a range of options.
Trump has said he will not strike Iran before the midterm election. On the campaign trail, he vows the war will end soon but it's unclear how that will happen.
The president used the MOAB during his first administration to attack an Islamic State cave complex in 2017. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon.

A White House official told ABC News, "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon."
ABC News has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

When asked about the bomb in an interview with Newsmax on Thursday evening, Trump said "it's not nuclear at all. This is just a extremely large bomb. It's like a tiny nuclear bomb, and -- but the mother of all bombs is one big bomb, but it's not nuclear. I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to. We're the greatest nuclear power in the world."
CNN was first to report the options presented to the president.
-ABC News' Rachel Scott and Katherine Faulders
France has begun deploying military assets in Saudi Arabia, says Foreign Ministry spokesman
France has started deploying military assets in Saudi Arabia, a spokesperson for the French Foreign Ministry, Pascal Confavreux, confirmed in a press conference Thursday.

"You know that the Houthi attacks in Yemen and against Saudi Arabia threaten not only Saudi Arabia's security and the region's energy security, but you also know that the President announced on September 24th that France would support the defense of Saudi energy infrastructure, particularly the Yanbu East-West Corridor. And this support is currently being deployed," Confavreux said in a news conference.
French President Emmanuel Macron said last month that France would send troops and defense systems to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, ‌‌a key hub for energy transport.
-ABC News' Desiree Adib
5 killed and 16 injured in attack on Presidential Palace in Aden, Yemen health authority says
Five people were killed, and 16 were injured in the Houthi attack that targeted the al-Maashiq Presidential Palace in Yemen’s Aden, according to the Yemeni health minister.

The Houthis responded saying Saudi Arabian warplanes launched 65 airstrikes and missile attacks in the last 24 hours, targeting civilian sites in the capital, Sana’a, and the governorates of Lahj, Hudaydah, Taiz, Amran, Saada and Marib.

"The attacks were carried out by F-15 and Typhoon aircraft that took off from the Khamis Mushait and Taif air bases, while the missile attacks originated from Najran. This brings the total number of Saudi aggression airstrikes and missile attacks against our country since the escalation began to 2,388," the Houthis said in a statement.

title: CDC lags in hiring behind other health agencies after DOGE cuts, union says
summary: More than a year after cutting 30% of its workforce and disrupting dozens of public health programs, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is lagging in hiring.
story: There are are dozens of so-called "zombie" programs across the CDC, union says.

More than a year after cutting 30% of its workforce and disrupting dozens of public health programs, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is lagging in hiring compared to other health agencies in the federal government, according to the union representing current and former CDC employees.

The newly revealed numbers on hiring come as a clearer picture is emerging of the impact of widespread cuts made by the Trump administration’s now-shuttered Department of Government Efficiency in its effort to shrink the size of the federal workforce.

The Department of Health and Human Services has been authorized to make hundreds of new hires, but according to an analysis conducted by the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) Local 2883, the CDC has roughly one new hire for every six reported staff laid off or placed on administrative leave.

According to the union's analysis of USAJOBS and Office of Personnel Management data, the numbers, first reported by ABC News, show the CDC posted 147 job announcements from Jan. 2 through Sept. 10, 2026, with 95 new hires from January to July 2026. Those new hires are just 16.5% of the total number of employees lost to DOGE reductions in force. NIH has newly hired 34%, the FDA 39% and CMS 131.7%.

Across the CDC, there are roughly 50 so-called “zombie” programs -- initiatives that Congress has fully funded with American taxpayer dollars but with little staff to do the work, according to a union analysis.

In a statement, the Department of Health Human Services said, “CDC continues to deliver on its critical public health responsibilities, while strategically hiring and aligning its workforce with the agency’s priorities.”

But according to the union analysis that ABC News reviewed, there are dozens of “zombie" programs across the public health field that impact chronic diseases, injury prevention, oral health, reproductive care, traumatic brain injury and rape prevention. Yet, the programs remain idle with reduced staff. It remains funded because CDC experts were laid off, are on paid leave or have left.

For example, the Office of Smoking and Health has a budget of $246 million and all of the programs within the office are on hold or it's trying to do its work with contractors while the full-time employees are on paid administrative leave and are not allowed to work, according to AFGE.

Among other programs faced with steep cuts and little staff: a $6 million program for sickle cell data collection; $11 million for managing epilepsy; and $41 million for Alzheimer's surveillance and risk prevention, according to the union.

The Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System, one of five programs Congress funded within the $113.5 million Safe Motherhood/Infant Health initiative, was also impacted. The PRAMS program provided one of the most comprehensive collections of data on maternal health.

In many cases, full-time employees like doctors and scientists who are experts in their fields are on administrative leave. Those staffers are paid but not allowed to come to work as lawsuits challenge the cuts. In other cases, the agency hired contractors to replace the CDC experts who have long guided decisions on research, data collection and community health programs.
Health care experts are sounding the alarm.
“The programs are running kind of as catch-as-catch-can,” said Dr. Georges Benjamin, who serves as CEO of the American Public Health Association.
While some public health efforts have continued in the program, Benjamin stressed that it’s limited.
“It means people who are doing the work are working really hard to do minimal stuff,” he told ABC News.
“What it ultimately means is that we will not have the information that's necessary to make sure as we all grow old, we'll be able to live our best,” he said.

The Sickle Cell Foundation of Georgia relies on data collected by the CDC and the state to reach patients with sickle cell in underserved communities. Many of those patients are willing to wait hours for care, knowing their monthly visit is their only window to see a specialized hematologist.
“If we don't [treat them], then nobody will, and these people just go without healthcare,” Dr. Anthony Onyegbula said.

ABC News followed Onyegbula as he made his approximately 100 mile journey from Atlanta to Columbus, Georgia, to treat patients who otherwise would have to travel for specialized care. On this day, Onyegbula and his nurse saw 39 patients in a single day, including Marcus McGhee, who is now blind in his left eye due to complications from the disease. McGhee, 34, said he’s holding his breath in between his medical visits.
“It’s like a ‘to be continued,’ McGhee said. “During this whole month, my mind is just racing … What am I gonna have to go through this time?” he said.
Sickle cell is a genetic blood disorder that can cause chronic pain and be potentially fatal. The disease predominantly impacts African Americans and minorities.
Dr. Tabatha McGee, CEO of the Sickle Cell Foundation of Georgia, said the data from the CDC’s sickle cell data collection program is critical to reaching patients.
‘We will lose more warriors if we don't know where they are,” she said, adding, “We can't get them the care that they need. We will lose them.”

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told ABC News, “President Trump and Secretary Kennedy have made improving care and outcomes for Americans living with sickle cell disease a top priority.”

“Across HHS, CMS is expanding access to treatment, FDA is approving new options, HRSA is strengthening care, NIH is advancing research, and CDC is continuing surveillance that helps states identify gaps in care and treatment,” the spokesperson added.
Yet, health experts warn they are seeing an impact.

In a September letter to the CDC Director Erica Schwartz, the American Society of Hematology stated that the division was facing “a number of immediate challenges” and warned there were “early signs that the national data infrastructure built through years of federal investment is beginning to erode.”

“Grantees facing difficulties in planning with the risk of losing key staff with essential program and data expertise; pauses in data collection and analysis; and disruptions to patient care,” the group wrote in its letter to Schwartz.

The federal health department notes research has expanded across other federal health agencies. In July, the FDA approved the first gene therapy for children as young as two with sickle cell disease and awarded grants to expand access to care.

Under the first Trump administration, the sickle cell data collection program expanded to reach 16 states, covering half of the nation’s sickle cell population. The program provides grants to states, academic institutions and non-profit organizations to gather data on the disease, complications and treatment.
But health experts paint a much different picture in Trump’s second term.
“It's just morally wrong,” Dr. Karen Remley, the former CDC Director for the National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities, told ABC News.
Remley argued: “It is wrong to know that we have ways to help people with disease and to intentionally not take care of them. That is wrong."

title: Trump claims executive privilege to keep Kennedy Center conversations secret
summary: A White House lawyer said Trump's executive privilege would also cover his conversations with advisers who don't serve in government.
story: The privilege could cover Trump's conversations with non-government advisers.

President Donald Trump is making a broad assertion of executive privilege to keep secret the conversations he has had about plans to renovate the Kennedy Center, the Justice Department said in a court filing this week.

A White House lawyer says in court documents released on Wednesday that Trump's executive privilege --which is the right of a president to keep confidential the communications he has with advisers -- would also cover his conversations with advisers who don't serve in government.

The move comes as Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, an ex officio trustee of the Kennedy Center, seeks to obtain information in her ongoing lawsuit challenging the planned closure and renovation of the performing arts center, and whether Trump has plans to demolish it.

In a sworn declaration, Deputy White House Counsel Josh Hoyt said Trump’s executive privilege claim would cover any conversations the president has had with"his advisors (government and non-government)," including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Kennedy Center Executive Director Matt Floca, as well as anyone on his or the center's staff who may have advised Trump or his aides about "the President's duties and the effective functioning of the Kennedy Center."

Beyond the president's role as Kennedy Center board chairman, a position to which he was elected last year by his handpicked trustees, administration lawyers say, "in his capacity as President," Trump has "an official role in the Center’s operations."

The Justice Department argues that since the law gives Trump the power to select who serves on the board, he must be positioned to assess whether current and future board members are "managing the Center ably and in accordance with their duties and statutory obligations."

In a deposition taken earlier this month, an attorney who sat beside Floca repeatedly invoked executive privilege, rejecting questions from Beatty’s lawyer about the director's conversations with Trump, and even suggesting that queries about Floca’s talks with Lutnick could also violate Trump's privilege.
Pushing back on the claims, Beatty’s lawyers have argued in court that "these blanket assertions of executive privilege are both procedurally and substantively improper."

The Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board voted last month to close it for renovations after a federal judge's ruling blocked Trump's name from appearing on the outside of the building, a lawsuit Beatty initially brought last year.

In May, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper issued an order blocking the planned two-year closure of the center for renovations, saying the board had not properly weighed the impact of the closure on the center’s finances and programming when it voted on the plan in March.
The Justice Department later asked the judge to dissolve that order so planned renovations could proceed. Cooper has yet to rule on that motion.

title: How Adam Hamilton plans on winning Kansas' Senate race
summary: Can a Democrat flip the Kansas Senate seat for the first time in nearly a century?
story: Can a Dem flip the Kansas Senate seat for the first time in nearly a century?
The most surprising battleground race is shaping up in ruby red Kansas, which hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932.
But Rev. Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, could buck that trend.
He's challenging incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall – and the two candidates are neck-and-neck in recent polling.
