title: Russell Brand goes on trial to face rape and sexual assault charges
summary: British actor Russell Brand​ has appeared in a London court for the start of his trial on rape and sexual assault charges.
story: London — British comedian and actor Russell Brand appeared in a London court on Monday for the start of his trial on rape and sexual assault charges.
The hearing at Southwark Crown Court was adjourned until Tuesday after a morning of jury selection. The prosecution is due to open its case later in the week.

Brand, who is on bail, left the court building beside the River Thames holding hands with his wife, Laura Gallacher. He had earlier arrived at court flanked by security guards and accompanied by his wife.

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. The charges involve six women and alleged offenses between 1999 and 2009. The trial is expected to last up to 10 weeks.

Prosecutors said at previous hearings that Brand is accused of raping a woman in a hotel room at a Labour Party conference, grabbing a TV worker's breasts and forcing her into a sex act in a toilet, and kissing and groping a radio station worker.

Known for risque stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" and "Get Him to the Greek."

In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
The Associated Press doesn't name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.

title: Billy Crystal on finding humor in the darkest of times
summary: In January 2025, the Pacific Palisades wildfire burned more than 5,000 homes, including Billy Crystal's. From the smoldering ruins of what was once his family home, Crystal found inspiration for his latest one-man Broadway show, "860."
story: If Billy Crystal is one of the kings of comedy, his family home in L.A.'s Pacific Palisades neighborhood was definitely his castle. "Sunday Morning" was invited there a few times for interviews,  and I'd usually end up getting schooled on his backyard basketball court.
It was, he acknowledged, a magical place: "Yeah, it kept me young, that place," he said.

It was his family's forever home, but things don't always last forever. In January 2025, a massive, wind-driven inferno tore through the Crystals' Pacific Palisades neighborhood, devouring more than 5,000 homes, including the Crystals'. The fire took everything, but in the smoldering ruins of what was once their family home, Billy Crystal and his wife Janice found inspiration.
Crystal is taking the story of his home, and his life, to Broadway, in his new one-person show, "860," talking about what he lost, and what he learned.
"Oh God, what a morning. Helicopters and sirens woke us up to the news that there was a big brush fire in the Highlands."
He describes the disaster moment by moment, and it's a harrowing tale. But he's still Billy Crystal.
"Janice is the more practical of the two of us. She's thinking about medicines and prescriptions. I'm thinking about that half a veal parmesan sandwich that's in the refrigerator."

"860" is now in previews, and opens October 21. Crystal wanted the audience to feel like they're really inside his house, so the "860" set is an exact replica of his home office, with everything just as it was. "Yes, we're fortunate to have this and have that, but that doesn't take away the hurt. That doesn't take away the loss," he said.
According to Crystal, nothing survived.
But there are some things that no fire could ever touch. The memories are all intact, and funny as ever.

The name of the show, "860," is actually the street address of the house he lost. Truth is, Crystal wasn't sure what to call it, until his dear friend Rob Reiner weighed in. "He said, 'What are you going to call it?' I had these other titles, and the third one was '860.' He went, 'That's the one. I love that. I like that.'"

And then, in a year that was already traumatic beyond belief, the unimaginable happened, In December 2025, Rob Reiner and his wife Michelle were killed in their home. For Crystal, it's all still too hard to process: "No, it's too big," he said. "It's so insane, because we were together the night before. We said goodbye, like, late that night, 10:30 or something, at the party we were at together for the holidays, and then …  what?!?"
But Crystal has found a way to process his grief, and maybe ours, too, sharing stories and laughter.

Asked how he can find humor in the darkest of times, Crystal laughed, "That's what I do! You have to, man. You got to, you got to … It's a healer. It always has been that way. You know, we say when life gets tough, all you can do is laugh."

Twenty-two years ago, Crystal did another one-man show: "700 Sundays," named for the approximately 700 Sundays he had with his father before he died. It was a major hit, and a ticket to a Tony Award. And for Crystal, it was a cathartic experience, which he said healed him. Asked if he thinks "860" will as well, Crystal replied, "It already has, 'cause I'm doing it, and I've been doing it. If I didn't get to perform it even, I'm OK. I've absorbed the biggest pains that people couldn't go through, the loss of home, dearest of friends. And I'm OK."
Still, he says the body blows of 2025 have changed his outlook a bit.

In "700 Sundays," he describes conversations with God. Asked if he has been talking to God over these past couple of years," he said, "No, 'cause I don't trust Him. Too many bad things have happened. The Earth is in bad shape. This is a weird, scary time. So no, not anymore."

"860" is a one-man show, but Crystal leaned on some Broadway heavyweights to bring it all to life: director Scott Ellis, and legendary composer Marc Shaiman, who remarked on Crystal's ability to extract humor from dark memories. "He can't help but find the humor," Shaiman said. "That's just who Billy is, and that's why he is who he is."

"But it is family," added Ellis. "That's the thing that is the core of it, is how do you move forward? You move forward with friends and you move forward with family. And that's what you want and need, and he's lucky to have it. Not a lot of people do."
The show is in a limited run in New York just until January. After that, Crystal says he hopes to bring it to the city where it all happened, Los Angeles.

The house might be gone, but the heart that built it is still there, strong as ever. "I'm 78 now,  and I feel really good," he said, "and I'm optimistic for what life is going to bring. And if we've gotten through this in the way that we've gotten through it, we're doing OK."

title: Who would oversee a flying car? We asked the DOT.
summary: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk unveiled Tesla's new Roadster Rocket, which he called a "flying car" equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks."
story: Who has oversight of a car that flies, hovers or otherwise defies gravity? We asked Department of Transportation officials, and the answer isn't readily clear.

Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk unveiled Tesla's new Roadster Rocket, which he called a "flying car" equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" — describing it as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company." The car — about a decade behind schedule — would go into production in 2028.

Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground, and Tesla's website notes that the flying model isn't approved for public road use. There's a non-flying version of the car, which would-be buyers can reserve online with a $5,000 deposit, but the Tesla website says the Rocket model with the "full flight system" will be offered by invitation only.

So, who will decide whether the Roadster is safe? There's time to work that out, but a senior Department of Transportation official, who expressed skepticism that the vehicle will actually be able to take off, acknowledged there's no clear answer.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration typically has regulatory oversight of vehicles — though it delegates safety certification to the automaker.

In a statement, the NHTSA said: "While the vehicle may appear to defy the laws of physics, the manufacturer must ensure that it does not defy applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and drivers must obey all local traffic laws. NHTSA will continue to monitor the situation and won't hesitate to act to protect the driving public."

If the Roadster is going to enter the public domain with the ability for off-ground "driving," that would seem to shift to the FAA, which regulates aircraft. The FAA tells CBS News: "The Tesla vehicle does not meet the FAA definition of an aircraft."

Thursday's Roadster demo showed the car launching from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolling over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.
CBS News reached out to Tesla to ask which agencies the company is working with. We will update if we hear back.

title: With Tesla Roadster debut, Elon Musk shows "flying cars are real"
summary: Elon Musk unveiled Tesla's new Roadster, which uses high-pressure air thrusters to leave the road entirely during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX facility in Texas.
story: Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a "flying" car, equipped with thrusters, during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX rocket company's facility on Thursday.
Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground.
Musk revealed Tesla's new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas.

During the demo, which was livestreamed on Tesla's X account, the car launched from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolled over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.
"Flying cars are real," Musk said during the event, adding that the vehicle's "success is not guaranteed" but "it will probably work."
Musk said the car was equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" to propel itself into the air.
The tech billionaire described the development as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company," referring to Tesla and SpaceX.
The vehicle would go into production in 2028, he said. Prices were not announced.
Tesla's website notes that the planned flying model is not approved for public road use.

Would-be buyers can place a reservation online, with a $5,000 deposit, for a non-flying model of the Roadster. A limited-edition Thrust model is also promised online but cannot be reserved. Tesla's website says the Rocket model, with its "full flight system," will be offered by invitation only.

"The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle, with production likely limited, and investors should not model it as a growth driver," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said in a research note. "What it does is restore the brand halo at the top of the market and put a spotlight on the engineering stack a week before the FY3Q26 print on October 21st."

It wasn't immediately clear what government agency would have oversight of the vehicle, CBS News senior transportation and national correspondent Kris Van Cleave reports. A senior U.S. Transportation Department official expressed some skepticism to CBS News that the vehicle will actually be able to take off, but acknowledged there wasn't a clear answer.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration typically has regulatory oversight of vehicles but delegates safety certification to the automaker. NHTSA didn't immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.
The Federal Aviation Administration told CBS News the vehicle doesn't meet the agency's definition of an aircraft.

The concept of flying cars has been around almost as long as motor vehicles themselves, with American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuting the first flying car prototype in 1917. But successful designs have been pursued more seriously only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.

Ives said the Roadster shows how Tesla and SpaceX can collaborate. The new vehicle "puts the Tesla and SpaceX relationship on the table in a tangible way, with propulsion, pressure-vessel, and control hardware developed at the rocket company sitting on a Tesla product, which in our view strengthens the case for the two companies operating as one engineering platform over time," he said.

Musk — a major GOP political donor known for an often close but sometimes tumultuous relationship with President Trump — has thrust his companies to the forefront of several major industries, and he continues pushing into new ones.

SpaceX announced a week ago that it had agreed to buy licenses for radio airwaves that will enable its Starlink Mobile satellite business to provide cellular service inside buildings, a move the company said would allow it to "become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said in an Oct. 8 social media post.

title: Looking for a pay bump? A "nondegree credential" can help.
summary: So-called nondegree credentials can significantly boost worker pay, Census data shows. Here's what to know.
story: You don't have to switch jobs or earn a promotion to get a pay bump.

So-called nondegree credentials (NDCs), such as professional certifications and licenses, can boost earnings, particularly for workers without college degrees, according to research from the U.S. Census Bureau.

These credentials, which demonstrate that a worker has completed training or developed a specific skill, can pay off in the job market. NDC holders had median earnings that were 16% higher than those of workers at the same level who lacked the credentials, the Census data shows.

Stacie Haller, chief career adviser at ResumeBuilder.com, said she's steering more job seekers toward alternative credentials as some employers stop requiring that candidates hold college degrees. Such certificates or licenses demonstrate "specific skills that will put you ahead of other candidates," she told CBS News.

NDCs are certificates or licenses that signal that a worker possesses a particular qualification or competency. They include vocational and educational certificates awarded by technical colleges or trade schools that focus on job skills and career preparation.

Workers can earn certificates in a variety of fields, from food service to healthcare, according to the Census Bureau. For some people, NDCs can also offer an alternative to pursuing a college degree.

Workers with job-specific knowledge and skills can also take exams to earn certifications and licenses, which usually expire and must be renewed. Boards and associations, such as the American Nurses Association, can issue certifications, as can private firms like Google. Licenses are required for certain professions, such as cosmetologists and barbers.
Roughly 40% of workers in healthcare support, food service, farming, fishing, forestry, construction and repair occupations hold NDCs.

"This is not surprising given the extensive credentialing requirements for healthcare workers and information technology-related certifications for various software, programs and equipment," Census Bureau researchers wrote. "Farm and craft trades, like agriculture and plumbing, similarly require credentialing to work with hazardous chemicals, heavy machinery and complex systems."
Just under 40% of workers in professional occupations, including management, STEM jobs, education, legal and other roles, hold NDCs.

Haller said determining which type of credential is most valuable in a given field can require extensive research. But there's one type of qualification she recommends that every job seeker obtain — a certificate or badge that demonstrates AI competency.
"Every company is figuring out how to use AI, and if you have that experience and know how to use it in a business setting, you'll be valued," she said.

title: More workers are skipping doctor's visits over money worries
summary: Roughly a third of employees said they put off or skipped medical or dental care in the past year because of financial concerns, a new survey found.
story: Rising financial strains on American workers are forcing them to make painful trade-offs, such as skipping medical care, to make ends meet, new research shows.
Financial security among U.S. employees dropped from 46% to 36% in 2026, its lowest level in seven years, according to a survey of 6,000 U.S. employees by benefits company Willis Towers Watson (WTW).
While workers report feeling better physically and say their social connections have improved, their sense of well-being has moved in the opposite direction regarding money matters, the firm said.
Barriers to healthcare

Financial pressures are also changing employees' attitudes toward seeking healthcare, shaping their views on retirement and affecting their performance at work, the survey found. Across all age groups, about one-third of employees say they put off or skipped a medical or dental appointment in the past year because of concerns over cost, and despite having health insurance, respondents told WTW.

"They feel the cost of healthcare is huge and are facing high deductibles and high out-of-pocket costs," Courtney Stubblefield, a WTW health and benefits practice leader, told CBS News. "Those kinds of features are becoming barriers to them getting the care they need."

Among different age groups, employees in their 40s reported feeling the least financially secure, according to the survey. Just 30% of workers in their 40s reported feeling financially secure, compared to half of workers 60 and over. More than 40% of people in their 40s said they delayed or skipped receiving medical care over money worries — the highest share among all age groups.
Mid-career workers often balance multiple responsibilities, including caring for both children and aging parents, Stubblefield said.

"These people are more likely to have kids and family healthcare coverage, so it costs more," she said. "They're also part of what we call the sandwich generation, so they have kids in school or approaching college and are also caring for elderly parents. They have peak levels of obligation in that decade."
Fading retirement dreams
Roughly two in three employees expect to be worse off in retirement than their parents' generation, citing healthcare costs as a barrier to saving for retirement, respondents told WTW.

Separate research from Prudential Financial recently found that more than six in 10 retirees with at least $500,000 in investable assets do not feel comfortable spending money for enjoyment. Many cite inflation, the rising cost of living, and healthcare costs as barriers to spending on entertainment in retirement.

Many older Americans are doing comparatively better than younger people. The 18 million households headed by someone 75 or older have the highest median net worth of any age group nationwide, according to Federal Reserve data. Americans in that demographic had a median net worth of $504,000 in 2025.
Between 2022 and 2025, households headed by 65- to 74-year-olds saw their wealth increase by 37%, the Fed concluded.

title: Amazon launches new AI devices that can listen and take notes
summary: The products include a silicone wristband that can be clipped to clothing and a device that magnetically attaches to the back of a phone.
story: Amazon launched two new AI gadgets on Thursday that the company says can listen to conversations, compose notes and issue reminders.

The first, the Bee Frontier, is a silicone wristband that can also be clipped to clothing and retails for $74.99. Amazon also announced the Bee Eclipse, a credit card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of a phone and goes for $99.99.
The new tech offerings are engineered by Bee, an AI wearable maker that Amazon acquired last year.

Equipped with microphones, Bee's "personal AI" devices transcribe meetings or everyday conversations, helping people document moments hands-free. The devices can then recommend "personalized goals and actions" based on the conversation, Amazon said.
"It takes note of the details you might otherwise forget and turns them into useful conversation summaries, to-dos, reminders, and insights," the company said in its release.
If someone is on a phone call planning a vacation, for example, the Bee Frontier or Bee Eclipse will create a summary of the trip, documenting details such as flight times or hotel reservations.

Amazon said users can also connect Bee to existing apps such as Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, allowing the AI technology to draft follow-up emails or create calendar invites based on what was discussed. The Bee devices can also be linked to Amazon's Alexa+ and Amazon.com.

Users can get conversation summaries, recaps and 14 days of memory for free; if they want more advanced capabilities, such as integration with Alexa+ and Amazon.com and suggested to-dos, they'll need a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $11.99 per month.

Amazon emphasized Bee's privacy protections, noting that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." The audio recordings are deleted after the Bee devices transcribe them, and no one can access your data unless you share it, the company said.

The Bee devices are part of a trillion-dollar market of AI gadgets that companies are marketing to consumers. Meta recently announced Muse, an AI assistant that comes in the form of a pocket-sized keychain. Microsoft, OpenAI and Samsung are among the other companies that have introduced AI-powered products aimed at consumers.

title: FTC issues subpoenas to Anthropic and OpenAI over safety incidents
summary: The demands come amid mounting public concerns about the potential risks posed by frontier AI models.
story: The Federal Trade Commission has subpoenaed Anthropic and OpenAI to gather information about potential consumer protection violations, a spokesperson for the agency confirmed.

The development, first reported by Axios, comes just two weeks after the FTC said it was investigating the artificial intelligence companies as part of a probe it launched this summer. The agency declined further comment about the probe.

The FTC is seeking documents on safety incidents, privacy policies and safeguards at Anthropic and OpenAI, Axios reported. The companies have come under public scrutiny in recent months after several incidents in which their AI models went rogue and hacked into websites.

The agency, which sent civil investigative demands to Anthropic and OpenAI on Wednesday, will also issue subpoenas to third-party organizations at a later date, according to Axios, which cited a person familiar with the matter.

The FTC could compel Anthropic and OpenAI to testify before Congress about their products, a move that would allow the government to press the companies about the safety of their technology as the public grows increasingly wary about its potential harms.

A recent poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that 64% of U.S. adults think AI is developing "too fast." Eight in 10 said it's "extremely" or "very" important for the U.S. government to ensure that AI stays under human control.

President Trump has resisted calls to slow the development of AI, saying that the technology is vital to U.S. national interests. He recently announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" to coordinate with the federal government on AI matters and engage with consumers, public interest groups and other stakeholders.

title: Why AI could end the price tag as we know it
summary: Retailers want to harness the power of artificial intelligence to set personalized prices for shoppers, a consumer protection expert says.
story: The humble price tag has long served as a common measure of value for consumers. Now, experts warn that artificial intelligence could allow retailers to charge people different prices based on their personal data.

Lindsay Owens, CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, a nonprofit think tank focused on economic policy, said AI threatens to upend universal prices for consumers. That could overturn norms that have been in place since the 1860s, when pioneering retailer John Wanamaker introduced fixed prices in his Philadelphia department store.

"The posted price has been paramount for consumers, and I do think the price tag is at risk of extinction," Owens, a consumer protection expert and author of "Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — and What That Means for Your Wallet," told CBS News. "Predictability is really essential if you're on a budget, and knowing how much something is going to cost from one week to the next is part of what the posted price offered."
A price tag just for you

AI-enabled pricing builds on so-called dynamic pricing, which companies have used for decades to adjust prices in response to shifting patterns of supply and demand, weather, time of day and other factors.

Firms aren't stopping there, however. Today, retailers are starting to test new ways of pricing goods based on who you are, where you live and myriad other insights gleaned from AI — an approach known informally as personalized or "surveillance" pricing, Owens said. AI also gives companies a powerful new tool to continually analyze vast amounts of disparate data to gain insights into consumer behavior.

"These technologies may empower firms to collect, process and analyze vast amounts of consumer data, leading to more granular, dynamic, and individualized pricing than previously observed," analysts with economic consulting firm Cornerstone Research said in a 2025 report.

The upshot: Retailers could use AI to tap the vast amounts of consumer data they already collect to set prices not on a product's value, but rather on the maximum amount they believe an individual shopper is willing to pay, Owens said.

Currently, this Uber-style pricing typically fluctuates based on, say, the number of drivers and passenger demand in a given market. But with AI, companies could also harness your consumer profile to set what amounts to a personalized price, Owens said. The result could amount to a form of AI-enabled haggling, in which consumers face perpetually shifting prices based on factors largely invisible to them.
"Technology is allowing companies to stop setting prices for products and start setting prices for you," she said.
A sign of prices to come?

In December, Groundwork Collaborative and Consumer Reports reported on a trial by grocery-shopping platform Instacart that used AI to simultaneously show customers different prices for the same goods from the same store. The pilot built on Instacart's 2022 purchase of Eversight, a software platform designed to enable AI pricing.

The AI-enabled tech ran experiments by setting different prices for different consumers and collecting insights into how people respond, including when they proceed with a purchase and when they walk away. The investigation found that grocery baskets containing identical items cost up to 23% more for some shoppers. That could translate into a swing of about $1,200 per year for a family of four, Groundwork and Consumer Reports concluded.

Instacart disputes the report's findings, telling CBS News that the $1,200 price gap among some shoppers reflects an "atypical" grocery basket with the greatest possible price difference for every item. The company also said it doesn't use consumers' personal data, including federally protected characteristics such as race or gender, to set prices.
In December, however, Instacart said it would stop using AI to let retailers charge customers different prices for identical items on its platform.

According to Owens, other companies have begun experimenting with using AI to charge consumers individualized prices based on their personal data, such as their online browsing habits, income level, ZIP code or family structure.

In separate Groundwork research released this month, the group said that Walmart had applied for patents on technology that would allow the retailer to compile comprehensive shopper profiles and use them to set individualized prices. The tech, such as electronic shelf labels, could be used to charge consumers a "different price than the customer in front of them in the checkout line," Owens and her co-author wrote.

One patent application indicates that Walmart has already developed technology to adjust prices based on items in a shopper's cart, according to Groundwork. "If a customer has tuna fish, they may be offered a different price for mayonnaise," the group claimed.
Walmart denies developing tools that would allow it to use customers' personal data or other factors to adjust prices.

"Walmart does not and will not use an individual customer's personal information, income, shopping history, urgency or willingness to pay to set an individualized price," Dan Bartlett, Walmart's executive vice president of corporate affairs, said in a public letter to Owens this month in response to her research. "We do not engage in dynamic pricing, raising prices in response to a hot afternoon or an approaching snowstorm, for example."

Jay Zagorsky, a senior lecturer at Boston University's Questrom School of Business, has also warned about the potential risks of using AI for personalized pricing, noting that businesses are unlikely to disclose such practices for fear of facing consumer backlash.

"Nothing positive is gained by a merchant stating they are doing this," he told CBS News, while expressing his belief that retailers are developing the tools to set individualized pricing. "The days when the price you saw stayed fixed for a relatively long period of time appear to have passed."

title: Inflation surged in September as U.S. energy costs jumped
summary: Gas prices, which jumped 9.1% in September from August, accounted for more than half the monthly rise in inflation.
story: Inflation accelerated across the U.S. in September, rising at an annual rate of 3.7% as energy costs jumped, according to new government data.
The latest Consumer Price Index shows that stubborn price pressures persist just weeks before Americans vote in the midterm elections.
By the numbers
The CPI tracks changes in prices over time for a basket of commonly purchased goods and services. Economists expected the index to rise at an annual rate of 3.6% in September, according to FactSet.

Inflation picked up after two months of holding steady at an annual pace of 3.4%. Core CPI, which excludes the more volatile energy and gas categories, rose 2.6% from a year ago, accelerating from a 2.4% rate in August and higher than economists' forecast of 2.5%.
Inflation has risen sharply since the start of the year due to soaring energy prices, sparked by the war in Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.

The Labor Department said Wednesday that gasoline prices, which rose 9.1% in September from the prior month, accounted for more than half the monthly increase in the CPI report. Energy prices rose 20.4% from a year ago, while gasoline jumped 34.2%.

Prices at the pump have cooled slightly in recent weeks but remain elevated. The national average for a gallon of gasoline was $4.33 a gallon on Wednesday, AAA reported, up from $2.98 before the war started. The national average for diesel, which hit a record high in late September, was $6.29 a gallon.
Higher diesel prices increase the cost of transporting goods around the U.S., often leading to higher prices for consumers on everyday items like groceries.
"The CPI was clearly hot, and there aren't many ways to sugarcoat it," Wall Street analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a note to investors on Wednesday.
Energy played a "huge role," he added, noting that prices may not head lower anytime soon as the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine escalate.
"Energy prices being so high for so long is starting to seep into the broader economy," he said.

One category of spending that saw large price increases last month was airline fares, which are up 22.4% from a year ago, according to the CPI report. Increases in shelter and used car costs also pushed up the core inflation figure, experts noted.
Nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their views of the economy, according to a CBS News poll released earlier this month.
What this means for the Fed and interest rates

Economists say the September inflation figures could put pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate later this month, as consumer prices rise faster than the central bank's 2% annual target.

"Today's hotter-than-expected CPI report shows that inflation is still well above the Fed's target, and that the current rate-hiking cycle isn't likely to end anytime soon," David Royal, chief finance and investment officer at Thrivent, a financial services firm, said in an email.
The spike in core CPI shows price pressures are broadening into other categories beyond energy,  experts noted, a sign inflation remains sticky.

In September, the Fed hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023, bringing the federal funds rate to between 3.75% and 4%. Fed officials also signaled that they expect to raise rates again later this year. The central bank has two more policy meetings this year, on Oct. 27-28 and Dec. 8-9.

"This is the type of move that could prompt the Fed to pull the trigger on another hike this month, rather than wait as Fed officials have recently suggested, with markets now shifting to a 50% chance of that happening, up from 20% prior to the data," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, said in a report.

title: Data center builder offers Kansas town residents $10,000
summary: Digital Realty is offering utility and property tax credits to residents of De Soto, Kansas, in a bid to win public support for a data center facility.
story: Amid a pronounced public backlash against data center construction in the U.S., one real estate developer is making an offer it hopes will win over one Kansas community: money.
Digital Realty is offering every household in De Soto, Kansas, where it plans to build a data center, $1,000 in utility and property tax credits for 10 years.

"Digital Realty builds critical infrastructure that enables the modern economy, and we believe we also have a responsibility to help strengthen the communities that make this growth possible," Andy Power, the developer's president and CEO, said in a statement on Wednesday.

The offer is part of a $20 million community investment Digital Realty is pledging in De Soto as the company paves the way for a 280-acre data center site. The company said the project, which will eventually cover 1,400 acres, will provide recurring tax revenue, create jobs and deliver other economic benefits to local residents.

Digital Realty, a publicly traded company based in Austin, Texas, with a market worth of more than $67 billion, said in a news release that it is working with De Soto to finalize distribution of the $1,000 credits to households.

The company, whose clients include Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Nvidia, expects to create 250 permanent jobs for local suppliers and contractors once the site is complete. The initial phase of development will also support "thousands of construction jobs over time," Digital Realty said in its news release.

A recent CBS News poll found that more Americans oppose than favor building a new data center in their area, citing concerns that the facilities harm the environment, drain local resources and raise utility costs.

title: On dating apps, men use AI to put their best face forward
summary: How much AI is too much when it comes to finding love on the apps? "It's very subtle," one dating app user said of his AI-enhanced photos.
story: Marissa, a 31-year-old Boston resident, downloaded dating apps because she is looking for love. But more and more, she finds herself looking for something else: AI-free photos.

The marketing professional said she routinely comes across dating app profiles that appear to be digitally altered. Usually, the changes are minor and can be easily made using tools like Photoshop, such as editing someone out of a photo. Sometimes, however, the photo appears to be completely AI-generated, she told CBS News, citing a photo she came across on Bumble of a man dressed in a suit tiling a bathroom wall.
"AI aside, I'm not sure what the appeal is there," she said (Marissa asked to withhold her surname for privacy reasons).

Numerous women on TikTok also report spotting photos of men on dating apps that appear to be AI-generated. Their accounts demonstrate how AI is blurring the line between what's real and what's fake in the already fraught arena of online dating. They also raise ethical questions about how far is too far when it comes to manipulating your online persona.

"People want authentic connections and conversations," Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor at Boston University who studies dating apps, told CBS News in an email. "I think AI has made people more wary and skeptical of others, especially people they don't know."

Of course, dating app users have long relied on filters and other editing tools to polish their photos. But AI tools are upping the ante, allowing people to create high-quality images within seconds, and in some cases, fabricate fake scenes.

"A dater has to think about how they're going to capture someone's attention in a few seconds or less," Coduto told CBS News. "This might mean making your photo look a little better than it might have before."
To be sure, this practice isn't exclusive to men. However, they appear more likely to use AI to spruce up their dating profiles than women, Coduto added.
"So far, men are more interested in AI in the dating space, which isn't surprising," Coduto said. "Women tend to receive more matches and messages, so men have a harder time standing out."
The "digital stylist" who helps men AI their photos

AI can create obvious distortions when it generates photos, such as omitting a finger from someone's hand. For Marissa, a telltale sign is the person's face, which sometimes looks "waxy" in AI-generated photos, she said.
Still, as technology improves, it's becoming harder to distinguish a real photo from one created by AI models.

Lana Li, a Brooklyn, New York, dating consultant who runs the Substack "Love Me Like a Robot," calls herself a "digital stylist." She uses AI to help men level up their dating app photos, and defends using the technology as long as the photos still genuinely represent who they are.

"I can take a picture of somebody and then put them in a different outfit or change their hairstyle a little bit, or put different shoes on them," she told CBS News. "Or if I think their body language doesn't look confident in the picture, I will have [ChatGPT] change that."
The 37-year-old also uses FaceApp to change men's facial expressions. She said the edits are subtle, such as slightly lifting the corner of someone's mouth to make them look "friendlier."

Despite her liberal approach to using AI, there are lines Li is unwilling to cross. For example, one client asked her to digitally alter a photo so that his head was on a marathon runner's body — a request she declined.
"I told him, 'I can't work with you if you want to not represent yourself accurately,'" she said.

Two men who spoke to CBS News on the condition of anonymity to maintain their privacy told CBS News they've used AI in their online dating photos, but in ways they feel stop short of being misleading and remain true to who they are.
A ban on Hinge
One man, a 30-year-old tech employee and client of Li's, said she used ChatGPT to digitally clothe him in more professional garb and to tame his frizzy hair.

"It's very subtle," the New York City resident said, saying he still looked like himself, even with the edits. He emphasized that he doesn't want to "catfish" anyone — a concern for singles even in the absence of AI.

Another man is pulling back after one of his AI photos backfired. The 50-something-year-old New York City resident said he fed photos of himself into Aragon.ai, an AI headshot generator, which produced a picture of him standing on a Manhattan roof with a sunset in the background. It immediately drew hits on his Hinge profile.

"This picture generally got the most likes," he told CBS News. "Now that could just be because it was the first thing they saw. But regardless, it was proving to be effective, and women seemed to like it."
That was, until Hinge banned him. He managed to get his account back but ultimately decided to delete the sunset photo, suspecting it was the reason for his removal from the app.
"How much AI am I OK with?"

Most popular dating apps have policies that limit the use of AI-generated images in people's profiles. Hinge emphasizes the importance of authenticity on its website, noting that people should be able to discern "fact from fiction."
"If you decide to include generative AI images, audio, or video in your profile, it should not be used to misrepresent yourself or your intentions," the company says on its AI policy page.

Hinge also uses automated tools and human reviewers to detect and remove "prohibited material," according to the company's terms of service. If users see suspicious AI material, they can confidentially report it through the app or online.

A spokesperson for Match Group, which owns Hinge, Tinder and a handful of other dating apps, told CBS that as generative AI evolves, the company is "watching closely and listening to daters, who tell us they want more transparency, more authenticity, and more confidence that a real person is on the other end."

Bumble also uses tools to detect and weed out AI-generated content, and lets users report profiles that feature such images. A spokesperson said the company prohibits inauthentic profiles, and Bumble's community guidelines bar the use of "artificially generated photos or enhanced photos to deceive others."

"We enforce this through a combination of AI-powered tools, human moderation, verification features and member reporting, and we take action based on the severity of a violation, up to and including permanently banning accounts," the spokesperson said.
Marissa, the 31-year-old who lives in Boston, said that when she sees a person's profile whose photos bear the hallmarks of AI, she chooses to move along.
"The dating pool is already challenging, and this is just another thing we have to grapple with," she said. "How much AI am I OK with?"

title: U.S. banks dropped customers over political views, regulator says
summary: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency said nine of the top U.S. banks "debanked" customers over their political or religious views.
story: Top U.S. banks have "debanked" customers because of their political or religious views, as well as their business activities, according to a report from the Treasury Department's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

The report, released on Wednesday, examines a practice that President Trump has claimed discriminates against conservatives over their views. Debanking has also been highlighted by some cryptocurrency investors, who claim their accounts have been closed because banks are uncomfortable working with crypto industry clients.

The OCC said the report was in accordance with Mr. Trump's 2025 executive order requiring federal banking regulators to review complaints to identify financial institutions that had declined business with clients because of their views.

Some conservatives have argued that they've been unfairly targeted by financial institutions, although the OCC found that some banks had also refused to do business with Democratic-leaning organizations. Debanking can also occur for legal and regulatory reasons, such as if a bank detects potentially fraudulent activity or an account is overdrawn.

The OCC, which reviewed 100,000 complaints and hundreds of bank decisions between 2020 and September 2025, found that the nine largest national banks it supervises had policies that swayed their decisions based on political, religious or business activities.

"Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations or political views. Fair access to financial services is not a mantra — it is a mandate," said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould in a statement on Wednesday.

The incidents cited in the report include the payment processor WePay, which is now defunct and was acquired by JPMorgan Chase in 2017. WePay closed the accounts of several merchants selling MAGA- or Trump-related items, the OCC said.

"Our policies prohibit discrimination against customers based on political or religious views," a JPMorgan spokesperson said. WePay's processes "did not meet our expectations. We identified it, corrected it, and the business no longer operates."

The OCC also found that some banks turned away customers due to their industries. For instance, businesses involved in oil and gas exploration, coal mining or firearms were restricted from some financial services, the agency concluded.
Other banks cited in the report, including Citibank and Wells Fargo, declined to comment and pointed to a statement from the Bank Policy Institute, a trade group for the banking industry.

"The banking industry supports fair access to banking services and has been working to ensure that government regulations and policies enable banks to serve law-abiding customers," the Bank Policy Institute said in response to the OCC's findings.

The group added, "We support efforts to establish clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management, including the administration's recent efforts to prioritize supervisory attention on material financial risk and rather than reputational risk."

title: Netflix cutting workforce as its revenue growth slows
summary: The layoffs will affect the company's product, tech, legal and HR teams, Netflix leaders said in a memo to employees.
story: Netflix said it is laying off roughly 6% of its workforce, according to a memo to employees obtained by CBS News.
The cuts will impact the company's product, technology, legal and human resources departments, Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in the memo.

"Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full-year forecast," Sarandos and Peters said. "We'll continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation. Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors."
Netflix declined further comment on the planned layoffs.
The news was first reported by the Wall Street Journal. The news outlet said Netflix's job cuts will impact roughly 1,000 positions globally, the company's largest workforce reduction since 2022.
Netflix had roughly 16,000 full-time employees as of December 2025, according to a securities filing.
Netflix remains profitable. In its second financial quarter, the company earned $3.4 billion on revenue of nearly $12.6 billion, up 9% and 13%, respectively, from the year-ago period.
S&P Global estimates that Netflix had 327.7 million subscribers at the end of last year, up 8.6% from a year earlier.
Yet Netflix's growth has slowed in recent years amid mounting competition from other streaming platforms and a saturated North American market.
Netflix shares, which traded at just below $70 each on Wednesday, have fallen nearly 43% over the last 12 months. The company is scheduled to release its next earnings report on Oct. 20.

title: Social Security announces cost-of-living increase for 2027
summary: The 2027 cost-of-living adjustment is the largest since 2023. Here's how it will impact the typical benefit check starting early next year.
story: More than 75 million Americans will get a 3.6% boost to their monthly Social Security benefits next year, due to a cost-of-living adjustment announced Wednesday by the Social Security Administration.

The 2027 cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, represents the largest annual boost for Social Security recipients in four years. The bigger increase is meant to keep pace with higher inflation this year, driven in part by soaring fuel prices sparked by the war in Iran.
Starting in January, next year's COLA will increase the average Social Security payment by roughly $75 to $2,170 a month, the Social Security Administration said.
The Labor Department said Wednesday that the Consumer Price Index, a closely watched inflation gauge, rose at an annual rate of 3.7% in September.

The annual COLA helps older Americans, people with disabilities and other Social Security beneficiaries stay ahead of rising prices, ensuring their benefits don't lose purchasing power. Yet critics say the measure may fall short for many seniors struggling to cope with rising costs following a 2.8% benefits adjustment in 2026 — a rate that has lagged the CPI for the last seven months.

"While a 3.6% COLA is certainly welcome, it wouldn't necessarily restore the purchasing power seniors have already lost," Shannon Benton, executive director of the advocacy group Senior Citizens League, told CBS News. "The COLAs are designed to keep pace with inflation, not make up for years of falling behind."
She added, "The bottom line is that seniors aren't getting ahead. They're getting a slightly bigger check to pay bills that have gotten even bigger."
About 7.3 million people who receive Supplemental Security Income will see the new COLA reflected starting on Dec. 31, 2026, the agency said.
The 3.6% COLA lags September's inflation data, noted Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, an advocacy group for the program.
"People are getting crushed by prices," Altman said in an email. "As important as the Social Security COLA is, it is not keeping up with prices."
How Social Security calculates the COLA

Each fall, the Social Security Administration announces its inflation adjustment based on a metric known as the "Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers," or CPI-W, which tracks the average change in prices paid by workers for a basket of commonly purchased goods and services.

The COLA is based on that inflation data from July through September. However, some advocates for senior citizens say that the CPI-W doesn't accurately reflect spending by older Americans, who tend to spend more on healthcare than younger people. Those costs have tended to rise faster than overall inflation.
As such, some experts support using different measures to make Social Security's annual adjustment.

"We favor the adoption of the CPI-E (Consumer Price Index for the Elderly), which calculates the impact of inflation on seniors' true living costs," Max Richtman, president of the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, told CBS News.
The advocacy group has endorsed two congressional bills — the Social Security Expansion Act and the Social Security 2100 Act — that would make the switch to the CPI-E.
"Without adopting a more adequate COLA formula, seniors likely will continue to tread water or fall behind rather than 'catch up,'" Richtman said.

Medicare has not yet announced its 2027 premiums, which could eat into Social Security's inflation adjustment, experts said. Part B premiums, which pay for doctor visits and outpatient care, are automatically deducted from seniors' monthly Social Security checks.

"For some retirees, a significant portion of their COLA increase can be absorbed by healthcare costs before they even have a chance to spend it elsewhere," Tyler End, a certified financial planner and CEO of retirement planning firm Retirable, told CBS News.

End added, "Healthcare inflation runs 5.8% annually, while COLA averages 2.4%. Even on paper, a 3.6% COLA only goes so far if the costs retirees face most heavily continue to rise faster than their benefits."
More senior citizens in poverty

Social Security is the largest antipoverty program in the U.S., the Census Bureau said last month. However, the poverty rate among seniors has been inching higher for several years, rising to 15.4% last year from 14.2% in 2022, according to government data. Experts attribute that increase partly to issues such as rising healthcare costs, lagging Social Security benefits and insufficient retirement savings.

In an AARP survey taken ahead of the COLA announcement, about three-quarters of older Americans said a 3.5% inflation adjustment in their Social Security benefits wouldn't be enough to keep up with rising prices.

"There's a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: 1 in 5 have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last," AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement on Wednesday.

At the same time, Social Security's trust fund is projected to become insolvent in six years. Unless lawmakers agree on remedies, all Social Security recipients will see a benefit cut of more than 20% in 2032.
"Americans cannot afford cuts to the benefits they have earned, whether through changes to their hard-earned payments or the COLA," Minter-Jordan said.

title: Trump promised to lower prices for Americans. Here's what the data shows.
summary: Just weeks before the midterm elections, 90% of Americans say prices in the U.S. are the main factor shaping their view of the economy. These charts show why.
story: President Trump campaigned in 2024 on promises to lower Americans' cost of living, vowing to push gasoline prices below $2 a gallon and to deliver 2% mortgage rates. Two years later, consumers face sharply higher costs for many of the necessities he pledged to make more affordable.

Less than a month before the midterm elections, the gap between Mr. Trump's promises and the financial realities facing many Americans is fueling voter frustration over the economy. Although economic growth is solid and unemployment remains low, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their views of the economy, according to a recent CBS News poll.

The financial pressures affecting Americans predate Mr. Trump's return to the White House last year. Consumers are reeling from the cumulative impact of five years of post-pandemic inflation, economists note. But his campaign promises raised hopes that he would lower consumer prices.

At the same time, some of Mr. Trump's policies have exacerbated inflation. His tariff regime contributed about 2.9 percentage points to inflation through February, according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Without the tariffs, the price of goods would have declined, the researchers said.
Mr. Trump's decision to attack Iran in February has also led to a drawn-out conflict that has disrupted oil shipments and sharply driven up the price of oil, gas and diesel.

"It's undeniable that several of these supply shocks that the U.S. economy has been navigating through come from policy decisions made by the administration — namely, decisions to intervene in Iran and decisions to impose tariffs," Greg Daco, chief economist at investment advisory firm EY-Parthenon, told CBS News.
Inflation in September is forecast to have risen at an annual rate of 3.6%, up from 3.4% in August, according to economists polled by FactSet — well above the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target.
Ryan Bourne, an economist at the libertarian Cato Institute, said that consumers "judge the prices they're paying against the prices they paid four or five years ago, and are still shocked by it."
He added, "As a result of that, they think the economy's doing very, very badly."

The White House said that Mr. Trump's agenda "stopped Biden's inflation crisis" while creating jobs and economic growth. The administration's policies "will continue to deliver economic wins over the next two years," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News.

"The President has delivered tangible wins for American families: He signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals that put American workers first and sent 401(k)s to record highs," Rogers added.
The following charts show how U.S. costs have changed for expenses ranging from groceries to car insurance.
Groceries
"A vote for Trump means your groceries will be cheaper." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Pittsburgh on Nov. 4, 2024.
For consumers, each visit to the supermarket is a fresh reminder of inflation's impact on food costs, which have continued to rise since Mr. Trump vowed to lower grocery prices.

The cost of food prepared at home has climbed 4% since November 2024, according to Consumer Price Index data, when Mr. Trump said a vote for him would lead to lower costs. That increase comes on top of a 23% jump in food prices during the prior four years. Because consumers tend to remember what they spent on groceries before the pandemic, they get a jolt each time they visit the supermarket, said Daco of EY-Parthenon.

"Whether it's talking about gas prices or grocery prices or restaurant prices or travel prices, everybody talks about inflation," he said. "The salience of prices is what is driving this downbeat consumer morale."

Food costs are continuing to rise due to a number of factors, ranging from the elevated price of gas and diesel, which are needed to fuel farm equipment and ship items to stores, to the Trump administration's tariffs, economists said.
Gasoline

"Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon, bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares, and housing costs."  — Mr. Trump in a speech at the Economic Club of New York on Sept. 5, 2024.

Gas prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. As of Oct. 9, the national average price for a gallon of gasoline was $4.37. That's up 47% from $2.98 on Feb. 27, one day before the war began, according to CBS News data. Prices at the pump are at a record high for October, according to AAA.

Diesel prices rose to a record high of $6.53 per gallon on Sept. 22 and now hover around $6.28. Diesel, which is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, is a factor in consumer prices for nearly every type of good, including groceries.

Gas prices tend to have an outsized impact on consumer sentiment, influencing their views on future inflation and the broader economy, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.
Energy and electricity

"By contrast, I'm announcing today that under my leadership, the United States will commit to the ambitious goal of slashing energy and electricity prices by half, at least half." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.

Consumers' energy bills have continued to increase this year. Data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows that average monthly residential electricity costs rose 12.5% between December 2024 and July of this year. Electricity bills are rising as utilities spend more to upgrade the nation's aging power grid, and overall energy demand grows amid the data center buildout.

Natural gas is also more expensive. Average monthly residential prices for natural gas rose 106% between December 2024 and July 2025, according to the EIA. Energy Innovation, a nonpartisan policy and research firm, attributes the jump to geopolitical conflict, an increase in domestic exports, extreme weather linked to climate change and rising infrastructure costs.

A July report from advocacy groups The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers found that the national average utility bill reached $280 per month in early 2026, up 12% since the end of 2024, just before Mr. Trump took office.

Many people could face even higher energy prices this winter. Americans are forecast to spend an average of $1,030 to heat their homes between mid-November and mid-March 2027, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, a policy organization. Homeowners who use heating oil are projected to pay an average of $2,627 over that three-month period, up roughly 50% from last year, the group said.
Car insurance

"Car insurance is up 70% to 100%, and you can't get it. … But prices will come down. You just watch, they'll come down, and they'll come down fast." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.
Car insurance costs are one area where consumers are seeing some modest relief. Data shows motorists are paying 5.5% less for vehicle coverage since premiums hit a recent high in February.

Still, insurance prices have soared in recent years along with the cost of both new and used vehicles. Yelena Shulyatyeva, senior U.S. economist for The Conference Board, a nonprofit that represents businesses, attributed the recent dip in premiums to increased industry competition, rather than public policy actions.
"Some of the deceleration was a result of a pushback from consumers, rather than some legislative or other action," Shulyatyeva told CBS News.
Housing and mortgage costs

"We will drive down the rates so you will be able to pay 2% again, and we will be able to finance or refinance your homes drastically at much lower costs." — Mr. Trump at a campaign rally in Tucson, Arizona, on Sept. 12, 2024.

Mortgage rates were climbing from pandemic-era lows for several years before President Trump returned to office in January of 2025. The average rate on a conventional 30-year mortgage now stands at 7.28%, up from 7.04% when Mr. Trump took office, according to Freddie Mac.
But home loan rates have been volatile, briefly dipping below 5% in February before climbing amid surging government bond yields, rising inflation and geopolitical tensions.

Borrowing costs are just one side of the struggle: Home buyers are also contending with high prices, keeping many on the sidelines as they wait for more affordable options. The median list price for a home in August was $408,333, up 4% from $392,967 since Mr. Trump took office, according to Zillow.
The gap between the income needed to afford a home, $126,487, and the U.S. median income, $86,490, is now the widest since 2005, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.
Credit card rates

"We're going to put a temporary cap on credit card interest rates. We're going to cap it around 10%. We can't let them make 25% and 30%." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Uniondale, New York, on Sept. 18, 2024.

President Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates at 10% while campaigning, an issue he also highlighted after taking office in 2025. But while the effort drew bipartisan support, the proposal fizzled.

Currently, the average credit card rate across all commercial bank accounts is 20.94%, down from 21.58% when Mr. Trump resumed office, according to Federal Reserve data. Credit experts said the rate-cap proposal would have hindered consumers' access to credit.

"Obviously, we'd love for everyone to have low rates and be free from debt. But the unintended consequence of a 10% cap would be the loss of access to credit, because banks say they wouldn't be profitable with it capped at that low rate," Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling firm, told CBS News.
Airfare
"We're going [to] … bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares and housing costs." — Mr. Trump in a speech at the New York Economic Club on Sept. 5, 2024.

Along with promising to reduce energy prices, Mr. Trump pledged to lower airfare costs for travelers. In recent months, fares have eased slightly, although CPI data shows that they remain 17% higher than in January 2025.

The war in Iran has disrupted global oil supplies and raised jet fuel costs, which are the second- biggest expense for airlines after labor costs. Facing significantly larger fuel bills, carriers are raising prices to cover the added costs.

Jet fuel now costs $4.34 a gallon, up 85% from an average of $2.35 per gallon in January 2025, according to the Energy Information Administration. Aviation analysts also point to the May shutdown of budget carrier Spirit Airlines as another factor behind higher fares.
ACA health insurance
"I will make the ACA much, much, much better for far less money (or cost) to our greatest American citizens. …" — Mr. Trump in a Truth Social post on March 26, 2024.

Millions of Americans with an Affordable Care Act health insurance plan face sharply higher costs than a year ago. Average monthly premiums have risen to $178, or $2,136 per year, up 58% from 2025, according to a May analysis from nonprofit health group KFF.

Obamacare plan deductibles have soared from an average of $1,027 per person to $3,786, up 37% over the same period, KFF found. Prices for ACA plans spiked after Congress allowed a tax subsidy designed to lower plan costs to expire at the end of last year.
In an effort to offer relief, the Trump administration began sending $500 checks in September to nearly 1 million ACA participants in 30 states.
Prescription drugs
"When reelected as president, I will continue my efforts to protect Americans from unaffordable drug prices …" — Mr. Trump in an interview with AARP Magazine on Oct. 2, 2024.
Prescription drug prices have dropped since Mr. Trump took office in his second term, falling 3.9% after peaking in February 2025, government data show.

Mr. Trump has credited his policies lowering drug costs, with the White House stating in August that the president "has delivered" on his campaign promise. The administration cited policies such as its "most favored nation" approach, which links U.S. drug prices to those paid in other developed nations.

Experts said that while the Trump administration's policies have helped, other factors are also at play. For instance, manufacturers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are cutting their prices amid increased competition, while the nonpartisan Brookings Institution notes that more generic drugs are entering the marketplace, tempering healthcare costs.

title: Character.ai declares bankruptcy, citing legal and business woes
summary: AI company has faced multiple lawsuits from families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using its platform.
story: Character.ai said it has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, with its chief executive attributing the chatbot provider's financial problems to "significant legal, regulatory and operational headwinds."

The company said it will continue operating as it seeks to sell its business, and added that The Walt Disney Co. has agreed to pay $20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual license to Character.ai's intellectual property.

Character.ai's financial struggles follow scrutiny and litigation over its technology, which uses artificial intelligence to create custom bots consumers can chat with. In early 2026, Character.ai and Google, which had a licensing deal with the AI company, agreed to settle several lawsuits filed by families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using Character.ai's platform.

The company settled a wrongful death lawsuit earlier in 2026 — the first filed in the U.S. against an AI company — with a Florida family who said their teen son died after conducting an emotional and sexual relationship with a chatbot known as "Dany." The family said in their lawsuit that Character.ai had no mechanisms in place to protect their son or notify an adult when teens were spending too much time interacting with Chatbots.
The company added several safety features designed with teens in mind after several lawsuits alleged its chatbots inappropriately interacted with underage users.

Several states have also sued Character.ai over its technology, with Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman alleging in January that its chatbots "preyed on children and led them into self-harm." In May, Pennsylvania sued Character.ai after one of its chatbots allegedly claimed to be a licensed psychiatrist in the state and provided a "fake Pennsylvania license number."
In a statement issued late Monday, Character.ai said it believes the company will be sold by late November or early December.

"After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders," Character.ai CEO Colin Adams said in the statement. "As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging user experience for our Character.ai community remains a top priority."
Is Character.ai shutting down?
The company said on Monday that its services continue to operate and that subscriptions remain active.
"If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance," Character.ai said.

In a blog post, the company said customer data "continues to be protected under our Privacy Policy." That policy states that data Character.ai collects from users — including chat transcripts, voice recordings, and images and videos — could be disclosed in connection with a sale or a negotiation to sell the company or its assets.
"As a reminder, you can delete your account or export your data through the app or the Character.ai website," the company said.

title: Six Flags stock slides 16% following fatal roller coaster accident
summary: The company's stock is taking a hit after officials confirmed a person died at one of the theme park's locations, extending a slide that started in September.
story: Shares of Six Flags slid as much as 16.3% after officials confirmed that a 42-year-old man died during an incident at one of the amusement park's locations in Georgia.
Six Flags Entertainment Corporation stock, which trades under the ticker symbol FUN, fell 12% in early trading. By late morning, the stock was trading at $9.98, down 16.3%.

The person died on Monday during a ride on one of the roller coasters at Six Flags Over Georgia, located in Austell, Georgia. According to witness testimony provided to the Cobb County Police Department, the man was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction. Several people were injured during the incident, according to the Cobb County Police Department.

Officials did not confirm which roller coaster was involved in the incident, although CBS News Atlanta cameras showed the park's Goliath ride, described as an "intense 7­­­0­­­-­­­m­­­i­­­l­­­e­­­-­­­p­­­e­­­r­­­-­­­h­­­o­­­u­­­r thrill ride," had shut down.

Dennis Speigel, founder and owner of consulting firm International Theme Park Services, said incidents like these are normally the result of an engineering issue, operating issue or rider responsibility issue.
He expects it will have very little, if any, impact on sales at the theme park.

"The public knows that the company is going to go in, examine, and figure out exactly what happened on this issue," Speigel said, adding he's seen "situations similar to this over the last 50 years with basically no impact."
An investigation is ongoing in Georgia to determine what happened Monday.

In the short term, the company's stock is taking a hit, extending a slide that started in September. Shares are down 33.8% since the start of the year. That comes as Six Flags faces high CEO turnover in the last decade and financial struggles following a 2024 merger with Cedar Fair, Speigel said.
The "merger really put the company in a very difficult position, [and] dug a very big hole for them," he said.
Following the incident in Georgia, Six Flags closed several other roller coasters across its parks, including the Goliath roller coaster in Los Angeles, CBS News LA reported.
"Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily closed similar attractions across our parks," a Six Flags spokesperson said Monday.

title: Anthropic warns "AI worms" could soon infect smart home devices
summary: Small AI models could clone themselves and infect internet-connected devices such as smart TVs and appliances, the researchers warned.
story: Anthropic is sounding the alarm about a new risk posed by artificial intelligence: Self-replicating "AI worms" could soon infest your "smart" home devices.

In a report released on Monday, Anthropic safety researchers said small AI models may be only "months away" from gaining the ability to clone themselves and spread across internet-connected devices, such as smart ovens, TVs and vacuum cleaners. The ability to reproduce themselves without human control would make it hard to control such agents because there's "no centralized point to shut off," said Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot.
Stronger AI models are already capable of what the researchers called "end-to-end replication," a threshold they say smaller models could reach by year-end, according to Anthropic.
AI worms, a type of AI-powered malware, can quickly spread across networks and devices while evading detection, according to cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks.

Smart devices in people's homes, as well as internet-connected devices such as security cameras, are vulnerable given that internet-enabled devices tend to have weaker security protections, the Anthropic researchers said. In what they described as a worst-case scenario, a swarm of AI agents — bots that work together to accomplish a shared goal — could propagate across computer hardware using "replication schemes."

The researchers said they are unsure of what form these attacks could take, noting that the AI models could be distributed as "digital slime mold" or as more powerful models capable of hacking into data centers.

"We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay," the Anthropic researchers wrote in the report.

title: Squeezed by inflation, more Americans fall behind on their debts
summary: Credit card and auto loan delinquencies are near historic highs as rising prices leave more people struggling to keep up with payments.
story: Rising U.S. prices are squeezing household budgets, causing more Americans to fall behind on their debt payments, recent financial data shows.

The share of seriously delinquent auto loan balances has hit a record high this year, while nearly 13% of credit card balances are seriously past due — close to their 2010 peak in the aftermath of the housing crisis — according to recent data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
The share of households behind on their mortgages reached a six-year high, although the measure remains far below its peak during the Great Recession.
Student loan delinquencies have also jumped in the past year, with the rise tied to the end of pandemic-era protections and a Biden administration repayment plan.
Other signs that more Americans are struggling with debt:

Almost 9% of U.S. households spent more than 40% of their income on debt repayment in 2025, the highest level since 2010, according to the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances.Nearly 20% of households were late on a debt payment in 2025, a jump from about 12% in 2022, the same survey found.More Americans over 70 are struggling with debt, with their share of auto loan accounts in delinquency at its highest level since the New York Fed began tracking the metric in 2000. Credit card delinquency among people over 70 is at its highest level since 2011, the analysis also found.
Almost 9% of U.S. households spent more than 40% of their income on debt repayment in 2025, the highest level since 2010, according to the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances.
Nearly 20% of households were late on a debt payment in 2025, a jump from about 12% in 2022, the same survey found.

More Americans over 70 are struggling with debt, with their share of auto loan accounts in delinquency at its highest level since the New York Fed began tracking the metric in 2000. Credit card delinquency among people over 70 is at its highest level since 2011, the analysis also found.

More than half of Americans relied on credit cards to pay for basic needs like groceries, rent and utilities, according to a March survey from Debt.com. Almost six in 10 said inflation was causing them to carry a bigger credit card balance than a year earlier, the same survey found.

Many Americans are frustrated with the U.S. economy, even as measures such as GDP growth and unemployment remain relatively solid. After five years of elevated inflation, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their economic outlook, according to a recent CBS News poll.
The worsening debt situation reflects the impact of inflation on household finances, said Kelly Regan, a certified financial planner at financial advisory firm Girard.

Credit cards are "kind of like the safety valve if you have no emergency savings left," Regan told CBS News. "We have an issue that if prices are increasing, especially more than people's wage growth, we're going to have a gap where things are going to cost more. And if you don't have any savings or are able to find those savings somehow in your budget, you're going to accrue debt."
Lagging wage growth

Adding to the crunch is that wage growth is lagging inflation, meaning that millions of households have lost purchasing power. That's also depressing consumer sentiment and squeezing people coping with higher prices, according to economists.

More than half of U.S. consumers said they intend to cut back on spending in the next year, the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers said in a report last week. The most common items they intended to cut back on included food and groceries, household items, cars, dining out, and vacations, the poll found.

"Frustration over cost of living continues to mount, as consumers across the political spectrum believe that the trajectory of the economy has weakened since the beginning of the year," Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers, said in a statement.
