title: 9 fired FBI employees who worked on Trump documents case sue
summary: Nine former FBI employees sued the bureau, saying they were unlawfully terminated for working on the investigation into President Trump's classified documents case.
story: Washington — Nine former FBI employees sued the bureau on Thursday, saying they were unlawfully terminated merely for working on former special counsel Jack Smith's investigation into President Trump's retention of classified records after his first term in the White House.

The former special agents, intelligence analysts and staff operation specialists worked on counterintelligence investigations and were fired over the course of two days in February 2026 — just as the United States and Israel were set to begin military strikes against Iran.

The nine plaintiffs represent the latest in a growing number of former FBI agents and other personnel who have filed lawsuits against the Justice Department and the bureau after they were abruptly terminated. Many of the fired employees worked on matters that displeased Mr. Trump and his allies.
The plaintiffs "were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President's personal vendetta," the lawsuit alleged.

"The firings did not follow any internal investigation or disciplinary process within the FBI, and Plaintiffs were not given any notice, a hearing, or an opportunity to appeal. Instead, Patel claimed to rely solely upon 'Article II' to support the firings," the suit said, referring to FBI Director Kash Patel and Article II of the Constitution, which lays out the president's executive powers.

The 70-page lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and names the FBI, Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche and the Department of Justice as defendants. CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department and FBI for comment.

FBI agents executed a search warrant at Mar-a-Lago in August 2022 and allegedly recovered more than 100 documents with classified markings. In 2023, Smith's office indicted Mr. Trump on more than three dozen charges related to his alleged retention of the records and efforts to obstruct the government's attempts to get them back. The charges were ultimately dismissed by the federal judge overseeing the case, who said Smith was unlawfully appointed special counsel. The Justice Department formally abandoned its appeal of the ruling after Mr. Trump won the 2024 election.
Thursday's lawsuit cites public comments made by top Justice Department officials and the president directed toward the plaintiffs as evidence the firings were motivated by political animus.

For example, Blanche, who was deputy attorney general when the employees were let go, stated that the administration had "cleaned house" at the FBI by firing employees associated with investigations involving the president.
The lawsuit contains some new details about the circumstances surrounding the firings.

In the case of counterintelligence section chief Jennifer Bacon, she learned she was being let go shortly after an agent named Miles Starr had requested access to the classified investigative files about Plasmic Echo, the codename given to the documents investigation.
Starr, the lawsuit said, was a member of Kash Patel's Director's Advisory Team, a group staffed by agents from around the country who support his policy goals.

He also was the lead case agent who testified in the since-dismissed indictment charging former FBI Director James Comey with lying to Congress. That testimony later was criticized by a federal magistrate judge, who accused the FBI of numerous missteps, including a failure to filter out potentially privileged materials.
On Feb. 23, Starr emailed Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky to tell him that he urgently needed access to the Plasmic Echo case files, the lawsuit said.

"Starr did not explain what he needed, but stated that he was on instructions from Patel to access the case file. Bacon granted him access to all Plasmic Echo files in the FBI's case management system, with the exception of one specific subfile. The files Starr had access to contained the names of all nine Plaintiffs," the lawsuit says.
Less than 48 hours later, Bacon and the others were all fired.

The lawsuit also suggested that the firings may have been an attempt to distract from negative press about Patel, who was spotted on Feb. 22 at the Olympic Games in Milan "chugging a beer and, in a display of wild immaturity and lack of personal control, flinging alcohol around the U.S. men's hockey team's locker room."

A special agent in charge who was assigned to inform former special agent Zach Feldman he was being terminated even surmised that the firing might be "related to the news reports from earlier that day about Director Patel drinking alcohol at the Winter Olympics," the lawsuit said.
The military strikes against Iran began on Feb. 28.

"This scandal proved politically perilous for Patel: he drew widespread criticism for his conduct, with numerous sources suggesting that his status with President Trump and position as Director of the FBI were in jeopardy as a result," the lawsuit said.
On Feb. 25, Patel gave an interview to Reuters in which he disclosed that his phone records and those of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were subpoenaed as part of Smith's investigations.
Eight of the nine plaintiffs were fired the same day, and the ninth was fired the following day.

"With over a century of experience among them, these former FBI agents and analysts served our country with honor and distinction as they investigated leaks of national security and defense information, thwarted threats and attacks from our enemies, and responded to critical incidents like the Boston Marathon bombing," attorneys Margaret Donovan, Abbe Lowell and Rebecca Tinio said in a joint statement.
"In return for their service, they were fired because they did their jobs, as they always did, to follow the facts and the law without bias or favor."

title: As Jolly runs for Florida gov., he confronts prior ties to alleged fraudster
summary: Shortly after David Jolly launched his campaign for Florida governor, his former boss was indicted for taking over $100 million from a disability nonprofit. Jolly says he wasn't aware of the scheme.
story: Less than two weeks after David Jolly launched his Democratic campaign for Florida governor last year, a Tampa grand jury indicted his former boss for allegedly siphoning over $100 million from a nonprofit set up to manage the assets of people with disabilities.

Jolly has called the alleged actions of businessman Leo Govoni "raw cruelty." He has also distanced himself from Govoni, telling voters in a July video that he "was an employee of Mr. Govoni's at a separate company from which the theft later occurred," and "from public filings, his activities appear to have occurred almost exclusively after we left his employment."

While Jolly didn't work at the nonprofit that was the source of the allegedly stolen money, he did work at a for-profit firm where the money was allegedly sent. Federal prosecutors said Govoni had used the firm to enrich himself. And a forensic accountant found that millions of dollars moved from the nonprofit to the firm during the period when Jolly worked there, according to filings from a related court case reviewed by CBS News.

Nothing in the court documents suggests that Jolly knew about or was involved in the scheme laid out in the indictment, and he has not been accused of any wrongdoing. He told the Tampa Bay Times he was not aware of the transfers described by the indictment.

Jolly campaign senior advisor Mark Riddle said in a statement: "Congressman Jolly has been forthright with the public and the press since he learned of this matter when the rest of the world did last year, upon the arrest and public filings against Leo Govoni. Congressman Jolly was one of over 100 W-2 employees among Govoni's many companies. He never served as an officer or in a position of any fiduciary responsibility, nor did he ever have any visibility into the finances of Mr. Govoni or his companies. Congressman Jolly has never been contacted by investigators in the criminal case against Mr. Govoni nor been a subject of the investigation."

Jolly — a former Republican who left the party early in the Trump era — is vying for the governor's mansion against GOP Rep. Byron Donalds. Florida hasn't elected a Democratic governor in this century, but Jolly thinks discontent with the GOP could give him an opening.

Jolly worked at Govoni's Boston Finance Group from 2012 until early 2014, when Jolly won his first election for a Tampa-area U.S. House seat. In 2013, the future congressman earned $250,000 at the firm, according to House financial disclosures. One 2013 statement from his House campaign describes Jolly as a vice president at Boston Finance Group.

Govoni also donated to Jolly's various political campaigns and served as finance co-chair of Jolly's 2016 Senate run. Jolly's wife worked for another Govoni-run firm while he was a House member, and Govoni's son worked in Jolly's congressional office in 2014.

Riddle told CBS News that Jolly "has done something that no Republican politician has done: returned Mr. Govoni's political contributions to his victims. Congressman Jolly calls on the other beneficiaries of Mr. Govoni's contributions to do the same."

Govoni's alleged scheme left behind a trail of alleged victims. After Colorado resident Chase McMinn was shot at work, over $1 million from legal settlements was placed in a trust managed by Govoni's nonprofit to pay for his 24/7 care, according to his father. Between $200,000 and $360,000 disappeared, his father said, and it's not clear if it will ever be returned.
"What [Govoni] did was just so evil," Chase McMinn's father, Milt, told CBS News.
An attorney for Govoni did not comment, saying he would let the case speak for itself. CBS News has reached out to Govoni's son for comment.
Charges against Govoni mention firm where Jolly worked
The federal criminal charges against Govoni describe a complicated web of companies set up by the Clearwater-based businessman and his associates.

At its center is the Center for Special Needs Trust Administration, or CSNT, a nonprofit co-founded by Govoni in 2000 to help manage and invest the financial assets of people with disabilities. Prosecutors say it eventually became one of the country's largest operations of its kind, managing around $200 million in assets across more than 2,000 trusts as of 2024.
Between 2009 and 2012, prosecutors allege, CSNT agreed to lend up to $100 million to Boston Finance Group, a firm run by Govoni that was in the business of offering loans to other companies.
After CSNT declared bankruptcy in 2024, a federally appointed trustee set out to track down the money and sued Boston Finance Group to claw back the loan.

Court papers filed in that lawsuit show that the loan was set up as a revolving line of credit that allowed Boston Finance Group to borrow chunks of money from CSNT over time. In January 2012, Boston Finance Group was granted a $100 million credit line and was required to pay back the money by 2017, with quarterly interest payments until then.

Boston Finance Group drew money from CSNT almost every quarter for a decade, starting in 2010, according to an analysis by a forensic accountant hired by the bankruptcy trustee who pored through both CSNT and Boston Finance Group's bank records.
From March 2013 to February 2014, during Jolly's tenure at Boston Finance Group, the company drew down more than $10 million from CSNT, the accountant's analysis shows.

Two accounting experts told CBS News the forensic accountant who carried out the analysis appeared to follow the correct procedures: Suresh Govindaraj, a professor at Rutgers Business School, and Francine McKenna, a professor at Montclair State University and independent journalist who covers accounting issues at public and pre-IPO companies.
Court records do not mention Jolly or suggest that he was personally aware of those transfers.

By late 2024, the accountant found, Boston Finance Group had borrowed just shy of $100 million from the nonprofit and only paid back around $19 million. The nonprofit was owed around $120 million net, including interest, the accountant said. A judge later found Boston Finance Group liable for the full sum, brushing off the firm's argument that it owed less.

Federal prosecutors say the "overwhelming majority" of the money that Boston Finance Group borrowed from CSNT wasn't invested in order to help clients, and instead, much of it was "distributed … to other GOVONI-controlled entities for illegitimate, non-investment purposes, including the personal enrichment of the defendants and others."

The indictment said Boston Finance Group "functioned as a slush fund and passthrough entity." It is not clear exactly what happened to the money that was transferred during Jolly's time at the firm, or whether those funds played a role in the alleged scheme. The indictment alleges several 2020 transfers from Boston Finance Group to other Govoni-linked entities constituted wire fraud.

"Govoni used his victims' money to live a lavish life, complete with luxury boxes at Tampa Bay Buccaneers games and the Kentucky Derby, pay off his own home mortgage, enable his use of private planes, and cover the living expenses of his friends and family," the Justice Department alleged in one court document last year. "He even distributed some of his victims' money directly into his own personal bank account."
Federal prosecutors charged Govoni with conspiracy, fraud and other charges. He pleaded not guilty and was ordered detained ahead of a trial set for next year.

Milt McMinn told CBS News his son Chase relied on money held by CSNT after he was shot in the head by a customer at an auto shop in the Denver area. The 2017 shooting left him quadriplegic, nonverbal and in need of 24/7 care.
"His life right now is basically a bed and a wheelchair," Milt McMinn said. He described his son as a "great young man."
Chase McMinn's family was able to recover more than $1 million in legal settlements, and a judge directed the money to be managed by Govoni's nonprofit, his father said.
In 2024, the FBI notified the family that it was investigating issues with the trust.
Milt McMinn said he and his wife have had to pay for many of Chase's needs out of pocket, including a rehab center and expenses for Chase's daughter.
The father said he is "really angry" about Govoni's alleged crimes.
"I just don't understand why he would do that," he said.
Govoni and Jolly's relationship

Over the summer, Jolly told the Tampa Bay Times he met Govoni when they were both members of an elder affairs committee at Stetson University. He said Govoni initially brought him on as a consultant, and later hired him at Boston Finance Group in 2012 to help Govoni recover $30 million from a former business partner.

Financial disclosures show Jolly worked at Boston Finance Group from some point in 2012 until March 11, 2014, when he won a special congressional election to replace his late boss, GOP Rep. Bill Young. Over that period, Jolly reported $468,750 in income from the firm.

Govoni and employees of his companies donated thousands of dollars to Jolly's congressional campaigns, and Govoni served as finance co-chair for his 2016 Senate run. Govoni has donated to other politicians, a point Jolly raised over the summer, saying he "worked hard to surround himself with elected officials across Florida."
After he was elected to Congress, Jolly says his wife also worked for Govoni. House financial disclosures list his wife as an employee of Boston Holding Company in 2015 and 2016.

Meanwhile, Govoni's son worked for Jolly's office, the gubernatorial candidate said over the summer. According to his LinkedIn account, LJ Govoni worked as a senior legislative aide from April 2014 to December 2014. LJ Govoni's profile on the site doesn't mention that he worked for Jolly, but says his job "wasn't a career move — it was a personal ask."

"When a close contact was elected to Congress, he asked me to come to Washington and help build the office: establish process, install leadership infrastructure, and make sure the operation ran the way a serious legislative office should," he wrote. "I came, did the work, and returned to the private sector when the foundation was set."

        contributed to this report.

title: Trump calls off plan to livestream Fort Hood shooter's execution
summary: "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," President Trump wrote on Truth Social.
story: Washington — President Trump said Thursday that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will not be streamed, a decision that comes after his administration faced significant backlash over the Pentagon's initial plan to allow the American people to watch Hasan's death by firing squad.

"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed."
The president said the immediate families of the victims can view the execution in person if they choose to.
"They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said.

Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 at Fort Hood in 2009, is set to be executed by firing squad at 1 p.m. on Dec. 3 at the Texas Army installation, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said earlier this month.
The plan to allow the public to watch Hasan's execution was revealed by Hegseth last week in an interview with far-right political activist Jack Posobiec.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," he said.
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's chief spokesman, said Hegseth and Mr. Trump spoke about the decision to cancel the planned livestream before the president announced it on social media.
"The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," Parnell said in a statement.
But the plan sparked broad outcry from Republicans and Democrats, who warned that livestreaming Hasan's death diminished the United States and could fuel radicalization.

House Speaker Mike Johnson told CBS News national correspondent and chief Washington analyst Robert Costa that "the concern would be that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists." Vice President JD Vance acknowledged that he would not watch the execution.
CBS News reported Tuesday that Trump administration officials were leaning against streaming the death by firing squad.

If the Trump administration had followed through with its plan, it would have placed the United States in a small group of nations carrying out public executions. Afghanistan and Iran are the only two nations that conducted known public executions last year, according to Amnesty International.

It appears the last public execution in the U.S. took place in 1936. An estimated 20,000 people gathered to watch the hanging of Rainey Bethea, a Black man who confessed to the rape and murder of a 70-year-old White woman, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

The last military execution took place in 1961, when U.S. Army Private John Bennett was hanged. Hasan's death by firing squad would be the military's first using that method since 1945, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

title: Trump invokes executive privilege in Kennedy Center legal fight
summary: President Trump has formally invoked executive privilege to shield certain records from a Democratic congresswoman who sits on the Kennedy Center board.
story: Washington — President Trump has formally invoked executive privilege to shield certain records from Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio as part of her ongoing legal challenge to the president's effort to temporarily shutter the Kennedy Center for renovations.

White House deputy counsel Joshua Hoyt informed a federal judge on Wednesday of Mr. Trump's formal assertion of the presidential communications privilege, a form of executive privilege. Hoyt said it covers information, documents or communications between Mr. Trump, his advisers and Kennedy Center employees about the president's duties and "the effective functioning" of the performing arts institution.

Hoyt argued that because the president appoints members of the Kennedy Center's board and a related Advisory Committee on the Arts, he must "familiarize himself" with the institution's management, operations, fundraising efforts and planned activities.

"I believe that, without the protection of the presidential communications privilege over the communications described above, presidential advisors and their staff members would be chilled from gathering relevant information, exploring alternatives, and providing fully informed recommendations regarding the performance of the President's duties," the White House lawyer wrote in a declaration.
In a separate filing, Justice Department lawyers accused Beatty of conducting a "fishing expedition" that raises separation-of-powers concerns.

"Even though the President's statutory duties and the Chairman's trust duties overlap, what matters for the purpose of executive privilege is that Plaintiff seeks information, documents, and communications concerning the President's actions in his official capacity," they argued.
Executive privilege is not absolute and can be overcome by an adequate showing of need for the information at issue.

The Kennedy Center's board of trustees, composed of Trump administration officials and the president's allies, elected Mr. Trump as its chairman last year, making him the first sitting president to hold the role. His effort to invoke executive privilege to shield records relating to the Kennedy Center raises new and untested questions of whether the protection extends to the president's actions as chairman of the performing arts institution, which was created by Congress in 1958 and is funded through a mix of federal dollars, ticket revenue and private donations.

The president asserted executive privilege over a number of records relating to his attempt to close the Kennedy Center for two years to allow for renovations, its financial condition, the effort to add Mr. Trump's name to the building's facade and the possibility that the Kennedy Center could be demolished.

Concerns that the building could be razed emerged after Mr. Trump said last month that the Kennedy Center will close and "end up being ripped down" if he and his administration did not get recognition for raising money and spearheading repairs to the institution.
Mr. Trump was also photographed on Air Force One looking at a placard that appeared to say "Kennedy Center Demolished."

The brewing fight over executive privilege comes as part of a lawsuit Beatty filed in December challenging the board's move to change the center's name to the Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts and shutter the institution for two years for renovations. Beatty is an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center's Board of Trustees.

In May, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked the center's closure and ordered Mr. Trump's name to be removed from the building's facade. Construction crews stripped the president's name from the exterior in June, but the front portico of the building has since been covered by a tarp, concealing most of its name.

Cooper has also allowed Beatty to collect information from the Kennedy Center about the decision to close the main building and any potential demolition, and to take depositions, a process known as discovery.

But Beatty's lawyers said that the Justice Department sought to block her inquiries about any input and instructions Kennedy Center staff received from Mr. Trump in his capacity as the board's chair and refused to turn over any documents related to those communications.
They accused the Justice Department of "improperly asserting a blanket privilege in an unprecedented fashion" and asked Cooper to order the Kennedy Center to turn over the material Beatty is seeking.

In response to Beatty's inquiries, Justice Department lawyers said late last month that "to the extent the discovery requests seek communications involving the President or White House personnel, they are inappropriate because they may have the effect of seeking information protected by the presidential communications privilege."

During a deposition with Matthew Floca, executive director and chief operating officer of the Kennedy Center, last week, a Justice Department lawyer repeatedly instructed Floca not to answer certain questions from one of Beatty's lawyers based on a protective assertion of executive privilege.

title: Talarico announces record-breaking $64 million fundraising haul
summary: The Talarico campaign said that brings his total fundraising to $134 million since he announced his candidacy last year.
story: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico raised a record-breaking $64 million in three months — more than any Senate candidate ever in the third quarter — his campaign announced Thursday.
The campaign said that brings Talarico's total fundraising to $134 million since he announced his candidacy last year.

His Republican opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton, said earlier this month that he had raised $18 million in the same period. Talarico broke Jamie Harrison's record of $57 million, raised during the third quarter in his unsuccessful 2020 Senate campaign in South Carolina.

Although a Democrat hasn't won a Senate election in Texas since 1988, Democrats there have been powerhouse fundraisers. In 2018, candidate Beto O'Rourke raised a then-record $38 million in the same three-month period.
Recent polls have shown Talarico with a slight lead over Paxton.

Incumbent GOP Sen. John Cornyn, a prolific fundraiser, lost the primary earlier this year to Paxton, who has long struggled as a fundraiser. Republicans have dumped hundreds of millions into the race to support Paxton, even as there have been leaks of audio clips of Paxton appearing to disparage national involvement in the race.
President Trump, who backed Paxton in the primary against Cornyn and is a longtime ally, has traveled to Texas three times in a month to campaign for Paxton.
CNN hosted a town hall with Talarico on Wednesday night, and said Paxton had been invited but declined to respond. CNN and CBS are both owned by Skydance.

At the town hall, Talarico drove home the economic theme of his campaign, telling voters, "We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis." He also addressed issues ranging from abortion to his recent absence from the campaign trail, confirming that he had the flu and slamming online conspiracy theories about it.

"That decision to stay home for a week sent my opponent and his conspiracy theorists spiraling. I opened up social media and learned that I had apparently dropped out of the race, flown to a mental health facility in Ohio, that I had died," Talarico said. "This is crazy. I mean, these false claims got millions of views online."
Paxton announced Wednesday that his campaign is kicking off a two-week bus tour this weekend near Fort Worth that will wrap up the night before Election Day at the Alamo.
Early voting starts Monday in Texas.

title: DOJ tells California to review whether noncitizens got mail ballots
summary: The Justice Department has ordered California to review a list of people who the federal government believes may have received mail-in ballots for the upcoming election despite not being U.S. citizens.
story: Washington — The Justice Department has ordered California to review a list of people who the federal government believes may have received mail-in ballots for the upcoming November election despite not being U.S. citizens, according to a letter reviewed by CBS News.

In the Oct. 13 letter, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter imposed a 48-hour deadline to review the list of names, which were provided on a password-protected thumb drive, to determine the citizenship status of each individual.

"For individuals whom you cannot independently confirm citizenship status, we request that you immediately instruct the appropriate elections official to segregate — not cancel — those individuals' vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined," McCotter wrote.

"If individuals on the list have not yet been sent a vote-by-mail ballot, take all immediate and reasonable steps to not provide a ballot to those individuals until we confirm their citizenship status," he added.

In a statement, California Secretary of State Shirley Weber confirmed that her office received a letter from the Justice Department, but said the federal government "did not provide the list [of alleged noncitizens] to our office."
"The USDOJ's relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," Weber said.
Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder/county clerk of Los Angeles County, confirmed he had received the letter but said the records were on a USB drive that his office had not yet accessed.

"The letter included a USB drive purportedly containing the referenced records, along with a handwritten note providing a password. We have not accessed the drive because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols," Logan said in a statement. "We do not consider the device a secure medium. Additionally, the letter does not specify the number of individuals involved or describe the information contained in the records."

He added: "Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established — and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching."

Similar letters were also mailed out to other counties in the state, a person with knowledge of the matter said. The move comes after Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in July told California's secretary of state that the government believed there were noncitizens listed on its voter rolls.
Reuters was the first to report on the letter.
McCotter's demands represent the latest effort by the Trump administration to press blue states on whether they have people who are unlawfully registered to vote on their rolls.

The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.
So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.
It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.
Since President Trump took office, the department has criminally charged more than 100 people with voter fraud-related crimes.
The crackdown comes as the president has continued to allege, without evidence, that the 2020 election was stolen due to voter fraud.
Experts have repeatedly found across multiple studies that the incidents of voter fraud are minimal and have not been numerous enough to impact the outcome of an election.

A data analysis published last month by Reuters found that states may have added more than 30,000 self-declared noncitizens to voter rolls since 2000 because of software glitches and clerical errors that came about during the processing of driver's licenses and state IDs.
That figure is small relative to the number of registered voters. In the 2024 election, Census data showed there were about 174 million people registered to vote.

title: Ilhan Omar's relatives subpoenaed as part of immigration probe
summary: The subpoenas were issued on Friday, just days before Omar's home in Washington, D.C., was searched early Monday morning by investigators from ICE's investigative unit.
story: Multiple relatives of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar received grand jury subpoenas, as part of the ongoing criminal investigation into her family's history for evidence of possible fraud and false statements in their immigration paperwork, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
The subpoenas were issued on Friday, just days before Omar's home in Washington, D.C., was searched early Monday morning by investigators from ICE's investigative unit.
Omar's personal cell phone was taken by Homeland Security Investigations during the search, two sources told CBS News.
The subpoenas were first reported by the New York Times.

The decision by the Justice Department to take those overt investigative steps so close to the midterm elections has sparked criticism. It appears to run contrary to the DOJ's own internal guidelines, which stipulate that federal prosecutors and agents "may never select the timing of any action" for the "purpose of affecting any election, or for the purpose of giving an advantage or disadvantage to any candidate or political party."

Customarily, the Justice Department has operated under an unwritten, so-called "60-day rule" cited in a 2016 DOJ inspector general report. It refers to the general practice of prosecutors to avoid the public disclosure of investigative steps related to electoral matters or the return of indictments against a candidate for office within 60 days of a primary or general election.

Omar, a frequent critic of President Trump's — and a frequent target of Mr. Trump and his allies — has denied any wrongdoing, and she has accused the Trump administration of attempting to "target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."

Mr. Trump said Monday that he had "nothing to do with" the raid. Sources said Attorney General Todd Blanche, however, was aware of the search. The Public Integrity Section, which handles the nation's most politically sensitive criminal investigations, was consulted, the sources also said.

But that section was largely gutted by the Trump administration last year, with only two attorneys remaining in its ranks. It was not immediately clear what type of guidance the section may have provided to the department before the search was executed at Omar's home.

It was also not immediately clear why the government moved to execute the warrant so close to the election, since some of the documents in question date back to Omar's childhood and were completed by her late father.

The warrant to search Omar's home was only approved by a magistrate judge in Washington after an extended back-and-forth discussion with Justice Department attorneys about how to address concerns stemming from the United States v. Rayburn House Office Building case, sources with knowledge told CBS News. That crucial 2007 D.C. Circuit Court case held that in a criminal investigation of a sitting member of Congress, the executive branch can't review information that is seized in a search without allowing that member to first screen it for legislative privilege under the Constitution's Speech and Debate clause.

Initially, the warrant did not take the Rayburn case into account because the investigators searched the congresswoman's home and not her congressional office, but the magistrate judge ordered them to include protocols that would allow Omar and her counsel to review the materials and assert legislative privilege, one of the sources added. CBS News has not yet been able to determine who Omar's lawyer is in this case.
Homeland Security Investigations, or HSI, the department's criminal investigative arm, is leading the investigation, with the Department of Justice assisting.
This is at least the second active criminal investigation involving Omar and her family.

Two sources familiar with the matter previously told CBS News that the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C., is also conducting a criminal investigation into the valuation of several of her husband's businesses — which D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro confirmed during a Fox News interview this week.

The businesses run by her husband Tim Mynett came under scrutiny after financial disclosures she was required to file as a member of Congress showed the value of the businesses had jumped to being worth between $6 million and $30 million.
Omar later blamed the valuation calculations on an accounting error and filed an amended form that listed the couple's joint assets as being valued between $18,004 and $95,000.

title: Mars rover sets new driving record on surface of another world
summary: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover has set a new record for the longest distance traveled on the surface of another planet, the space agency said.
story: NASA's Perseverance rover set an otherworldly driving record this week, traveling the farthest of any vehicle ever on the surface of another planet.

The space agency said its rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, had driven 28.1 miles as of Sunday, exceeding the previous record set by NASA's Opportunity rover, which drove 28.06 miles during its 15-year exploration of the red planet, from 2004 to 2018.

Perseverance reached the milestone distance while traveling along the western rim of of Mars' Jezero Crater, where the rover has been tasked with investigating what scientists believe may be some of the oldest terrain in the solar system. They hope Perseverance will find traces of ancient hydrothermal systems — underground networks that heat water — in that area.

The rover has made important discoveries at the Jezero Crater since first landing on Mars in February 2021. Several years into its mission, Perseverance had collected enough data for scientists to develop a timeline of the crater's formation, dividing its history into "three major periods" after water originally entered it. In 2023, NASA said it was possible that microbial life once existed there.

Perseverance has been able to cover as much ground as it has in a relatively short time, compared with its predecessors, because of its self-driving capabilities. The rover is equipped with an autonomous navigation system, called AutoNav, that allows it to collect images of surrounding terrain, map out hazards and plan its own route as it's rolling along.

Scientists overseeing the rover have dubbed that skill "thinking while driving." They said Perseverance is also able to navigate itself while traveling at top speeds, up to 1,351 feet over the course of one sol, which is how scientists count a single solar day on Mars.

"It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine," said Steven Lee, the project manager of the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in a statement.

Lee said the rover has "blown well past" the 12.4 miles of driving initially expected during the mission, and now, it's likely that Perseverance will "keep adding to this record for many years to come."
NASA said it recently extended the Perseverance mission to allow to explore the rim of the Jezero Crater until the end of 2028.

title: Spectacular launch sends cargo ship on voyage to space station
summary: Along with crew supplies and equipment, the Cargo Dragon is delivering two rollout solar arrays to complete a major power system upgrade.
story: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket boosted an unpiloted Dragon cargo ship into orbit Tuesday, setting up a rendezvous with the International Space Station early Thursday to deliver more than 6,300 pounds of research materials, spare parts and crew supplies.
Also on board are two new rollout solar array blankets, the final sets in a major upgrade to compensate for age-related degradation of the station's original eight solar wings.

Six "IROSA" blankets were installed during spacewalks starting in June 2021. The seventh and eighth IROSA arrays on board the Cargo Dragon will be installed during spacewalks later this month and in early November.

The Falcon booster's nine first-stage engines thundered to life at 6:33 a.m. EDT, throttled up and smoothly pushed the rocket away from Pad 40 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station atop 1.7 million pounds of thrust.

Two-and-a-half minutes later, now out of the dense lower atmosphere, the first stage fell away and headed back toward Cape Canaveral for a return-to-launch-site landing while the second stage continued the climb to orbit.

At almost the same moment, viewers at the Kennedy Space Center were treated to a stunning view of the space station passing 260 miles overhead, a brilliant "star" moving from southwest to northeast. The Falcon 9's launch was timed to ensure the rocket climbed away into that same orbital plane, a requirement for rendezvous missions.

As the second stage continued the ascent, the exhaust plume from its single engine expanded in the low pressure of the extreme upper atmosphere, growing into an enormous teardrop shape visible for hundreds of miles around, backlit by the rising sun.

The first stage, meanwhile, heralded by two ground-shaking sonic booms, landed within a few hundred feet of its launch pad at 6:41 a.m. One minute and 10 seconds later, the second-stage engine shut down and the Cargo Dragon was released to fly on its own.
If all goes well, the spacecraft will catch up with the space station Thursday, moving in for an automated docking at the forward Harmony module's space-facing port at 11 a.m.

The Cargo Dragon is loaded with more than 6,300 pounds of supplies and equipment, including 844 pounds of supplies for the crew, 1,307 pounds of science gear, 417 pounds of spacewalk equipment and 880 pounds of vehicle hardware and computer gear.

Also on board: fresh food for the crew, including "oranges, apples, grapefruit, tomatoes, blueberries, baby carrots and mini sweet peppers," said Bill Spetch, space station program manager. "There's also the always popular pizza kit, cookies and candy, as well as some special holiday items."
The IROSA solar arrays, tipping the scales at 2,635 pounds on Earth, are mounted in the Dragon's unpressurized trunk section.
Each IROSA blanket generates 20 kilowatts of power and, acting in concert with the original arrays, boosts power output back to factory-fresh levels.

"The new arrays are installed on top, over in front of the existing solar arrays," Dana Weigel, director of low-Earth orbit operations at the Johnson Space Center, said earlier. "The exposed portion of the old arrays will still be generating power in parallel with the new arrays."

"Those new IROSA arrays have solar cells on them that are more efficient than our original cells, they have a higher energy density, and together in combination, they generate more power than what (an) original array, when it was new, did on its own," Weigel said.

title: With Tesla Roadster debut, Elon Musk shows "flying cars are real"
summary: Elon Musk unveiled Tesla's new Roadster, which uses high-pressure air thrusters to leave the road entirely during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX facility in Texas.
story: Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a "flying" car, equipped with thrusters, during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX rocket company's facility on Thursday.
Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground.
Musk revealed Tesla's new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas.

During the demo, which was livestreamed on Tesla's X account, the car launched from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolled over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.
"Flying cars are real," Musk said during the event, adding that the vehicle's "success is not guaranteed" but "it will probably work."
Musk said the car was equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" to propel itself into the air.
The tech billionaire described the development as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company," referring to Tesla and SpaceX.
The vehicle would go into production in 2028, he said. Prices were not announced.
Tesla's website notes that the planned flying model is not approved for public road use.

Would-be buyers can place a reservation online, with a $5,000 deposit, for a non-flying model of the Roadster. A limited-edition Thrust model is also promised online but cannot be reserved. Tesla's website says the Rocket model, with its "full flight system," will be offered by invitation only.

"The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle, with production likely limited, and investors should not model it as a growth driver," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said in a research note. "What it does is restore the brand halo at the top of the market and put a spotlight on the engineering stack a week before the FY3Q26 print on October 21st."

It wasn't immediately clear what government agency would have oversight of the vehicle, CBS News senior transportation and national correspondent Kris Van Cleave reports. A senior U.S. Transportation Department official expressed some skepticism to CBS News that the vehicle will actually be able to take off, but acknowledged there wasn't a clear answer.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration typically has regulatory oversight of vehicles but delegates safety certification to the automaker. NHTSA didn't immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.
The Federal Aviation Administration told CBS News the vehicle doesn't meet the agency's definition of an aircraft.

The concept of flying cars has been around almost as long as motor vehicles themselves, with American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuting the first flying car prototype in 1917. But successful designs have been pursued more seriously only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.

Ives said the Roadster shows how Tesla and SpaceX can collaborate. The new vehicle "puts the Tesla and SpaceX relationship on the table in a tangible way, with propulsion, pressure-vessel, and control hardware developed at the rocket company sitting on a Tesla product, which in our view strengthens the case for the two companies operating as one engineering platform over time," he said.

Musk — a major GOP political donor known for an often close but sometimes tumultuous relationship with President Trump — has thrust his companies to the forefront of several major industries, and he continues pushing into new ones.

SpaceX announced a week ago that it had agreed to buy licenses for radio airwaves that will enable its Starlink Mobile satellite business to provide cellular service inside buildings, a move the company said would allow it to "become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said in an Oct. 8 social media post.

title: Amazon launches new AI devices that can listen and take notes
summary: The products include a silicone wristband that can be clipped to clothing and a device that magnetically attaches to the back of a phone.
story: Amazon launched two new AI gadgets on Thursday that the company says can listen to conversations, compose notes and issue reminders.

The first, the Bee Frontier, is a silicone wristband that can also be clipped to clothing and retails for $74.99. Amazon also announced the Bee Eclipse, a credit card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of a phone and goes for $99.99.
The new tech offerings are engineered by Bee, an AI wearable maker that Amazon acquired last year.

Equipped with microphones, Bee's "personal AI" devices transcribe meetings or everyday conversations, helping people document moments hands-free. The devices can then recommend "personalized goals and actions" based on the conversation, Amazon said.
"It takes note of the details you might otherwise forget and turns them into useful conversation summaries, to-dos, reminders, and insights," the company said in its release.
If someone is on a phone call planning a vacation, for example, the Bee Frontier or Bee Eclipse will create a summary of the trip, documenting details such as flight times or hotel reservations.

Amazon said users can also connect Bee to existing apps such as Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, allowing the AI technology to draft follow-up emails or create calendar invites based on what was discussed. The Bee devices can also be linked to Amazon's Alexa+ and Amazon.com.

Users can get conversation summaries, recaps and 14 days of memory for free; if they want more advanced capabilities, such as integration with Alexa+ and Amazon.com and suggested to-dos, they'll need a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $11.99 per month.

Amazon emphasized Bee's privacy protections, noting that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." The audio recordings are deleted after the Bee devices transcribe them, and no one can access your data unless you share it, the company said.

The Bee devices are part of a trillion-dollar market of AI gadgets that companies are marketing to consumers. Meta recently announced Muse, an AI assistant that comes in the form of a pocket-sized keychain. Microsoft, OpenAI and Samsung are among the other companies that have introduced AI-powered products aimed at consumers.

title: FTC issues subpoenas to Anthropic and OpenAI over safety incidents
summary: The demands come amid mounting public concerns about the potential risks posed by frontier AI models.
story: The Federal Trade Commission has subpoenaed Anthropic and OpenAI to gather information about potential consumer protection violations, a spokesperson for the agency confirmed.

The development, first reported by Axios, comes just two weeks after the FTC said it was investigating the artificial intelligence companies as part of a probe it launched this summer. The agency declined further comment about the probe.

The FTC is seeking documents on safety incidents, privacy policies and safeguards at Anthropic and OpenAI, Axios reported. The companies have come under public scrutiny in recent months after several incidents in which their AI models went rogue and hacked into websites.

The agency, which sent civil investigative demands to Anthropic and OpenAI on Wednesday, will also issue subpoenas to third-party organizations at a later date, according to Axios, which cited a person familiar with the matter.

The FTC could compel Anthropic and OpenAI to testify before Congress about their products, a move that would allow the government to press the companies about the safety of their technology as the public grows increasingly wary about its potential harms.

A recent poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that 64% of U.S. adults think AI is developing "too fast." Eight in 10 said it's "extremely" or "very" important for the U.S. government to ensure that AI stays under human control.

President Trump has resisted calls to slow the development of AI, saying that the technology is vital to U.S. national interests. He recently announced the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" to coordinate with the federal government on AI matters and engage with consumers, public interest groups and other stakeholders.

title: On dating apps, men use AI to put their best face forward
summary: How much AI is too much when it comes to finding love on the apps? "It's very subtle," one dating app user said of his AI-enhanced photos.
story: Marissa, a 31-year-old Boston resident, downloaded dating apps because she is looking for love. But more and more, she finds herself looking for something else: AI-free photos.

The marketing professional said she routinely comes across dating app profiles that appear to be digitally altered. Usually, the changes are minor and can be easily made using tools like Photoshop, such as editing someone out of a photo. Sometimes, however, the photo appears to be completely AI-generated, she told CBS News, citing a photo she came across on Bumble of a man dressed in a suit tiling a bathroom wall.
"AI aside, I'm not sure what the appeal is there," she said (Marissa asked to withhold her surname for privacy reasons).

Numerous women on TikTok also report spotting photos of men on dating apps that appear to be AI-generated. Their accounts demonstrate how AI is blurring the line between what's real and what's fake in the already fraught arena of online dating. They also raise ethical questions about how far is too far when it comes to manipulating your online persona.

"People want authentic connections and conversations," Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor at Boston University who studies dating apps, told CBS News in an email. "I think AI has made people more wary and skeptical of others, especially people they don't know."

Of course, dating app users have long relied on filters and other editing tools to polish their photos. But AI tools are upping the ante, allowing people to create high-quality images within seconds, and in some cases, fabricate fake scenes.

"A dater has to think about how they're going to capture someone's attention in a few seconds or less," Coduto told CBS News. "This might mean making your photo look a little better than it might have before."
To be sure, this practice isn't exclusive to men. However, they appear more likely to use AI to spruce up their dating profiles than women, Coduto added.
"So far, men are more interested in AI in the dating space, which isn't surprising," Coduto said. "Women tend to receive more matches and messages, so men have a harder time standing out."
The "digital stylist" who helps men AI their photos

AI can create obvious distortions when it generates photos, such as omitting a finger from someone's hand. For Marissa, a telltale sign is the person's face, which sometimes looks "waxy" in AI-generated photos, she said.
Still, as technology improves, it's becoming harder to distinguish a real photo from one created by AI models.

Lana Li, a Brooklyn, New York, dating consultant who runs the Substack "Love Me Like a Robot," calls herself a "digital stylist." She uses AI to help men level up their dating app photos, and defends using the technology as long as the photos still genuinely represent who they are.

"I can take a picture of somebody and then put them in a different outfit or change their hairstyle a little bit, or put different shoes on them," she told CBS News. "Or if I think their body language doesn't look confident in the picture, I will have [ChatGPT] change that."
The 37-year-old also uses FaceApp to change men's facial expressions. She said the edits are subtle, such as slightly lifting the corner of someone's mouth to make them look "friendlier."

Despite her liberal approach to using AI, there are lines Li is unwilling to cross. For example, one client asked her to digitally alter a photo so that his head was on a marathon runner's body — a request she declined.
"I told him, 'I can't work with you if you want to not represent yourself accurately,'" she said.

Two men who spoke to CBS News on the condition of anonymity to maintain their privacy told CBS News they've used AI in their online dating photos, but in ways they feel stop short of being misleading and remain true to who they are.
A ban on Hinge
One man, a 30-year-old tech employee and client of Li's, said she used ChatGPT to digitally clothe him in more professional garb and to tame his frizzy hair.

"It's very subtle," the New York City resident said, saying he still looked like himself, even with the edits. He emphasized that he doesn't want to "catfish" anyone — a concern for singles even in the absence of AI.

Another man is pulling back after one of his AI photos backfired. The 50-something-year-old New York City resident said he fed photos of himself into Aragon.ai, an AI headshot generator, which produced a picture of him standing on a Manhattan roof with a sunset in the background. It immediately drew hits on his Hinge profile.

"This picture generally got the most likes," he told CBS News. "Now that could just be because it was the first thing they saw. But regardless, it was proving to be effective, and women seemed to like it."
That was, until Hinge banned him. He managed to get his account back but ultimately decided to delete the sunset photo, suspecting it was the reason for his removal from the app.
"How much AI am I OK with?"

Most popular dating apps have policies that limit the use of AI-generated images in people's profiles. Hinge emphasizes the importance of authenticity on its website, noting that people should be able to discern "fact from fiction."
"If you decide to include generative AI images, audio, or video in your profile, it should not be used to misrepresent yourself or your intentions," the company says on its AI policy page.

Hinge also uses automated tools and human reviewers to detect and remove "prohibited material," according to the company's terms of service. If users see suspicious AI material, they can confidentially report it through the app or online.

A spokesperson for Match Group, which owns Hinge, Tinder and a handful of other dating apps, told CBS that as generative AI evolves, the company is "watching closely and listening to daters, who tell us they want more transparency, more authenticity, and more confidence that a real person is on the other end."

Bumble also uses tools to detect and weed out AI-generated content, and lets users report profiles that feature such images. A spokesperson said the company prohibits inauthentic profiles, and Bumble's community guidelines bar the use of "artificially generated photos or enhanced photos to deceive others."

"We enforce this through a combination of AI-powered tools, human moderation, verification features and member reporting, and we take action based on the severity of a violation, up to and including permanently banning accounts," the spokesperson said.
Marissa, the 31-year-old who lives in Boston, said that when she sees a person's profile whose photos bear the hallmarks of AI, she chooses to move along.
"The dating pool is already challenging, and this is just another thing we have to grapple with," she said. "How much AI am I OK with?"

title: OpenAI employee accused of planting recording device in office
summary: A Saudi national who worked at OpenAI as an engineer is suspected of planting a recording device in one of the company's conference rooms.
story: An OpenAI employee suspected of secretly planting a recording device in one of the company's conference rooms has been arrested on criminal charges, the Justice Department said Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and made his initial appearance in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on Tuesday. Alfozan was charged with trying to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
Prosecutors said that Alfozan had worked at OpenAI as an engineer since July 2025.

On Sept. 30, the company's employees discovered the audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television inside an executive conference room. The company later determined that the recording device had been concealed in toilet paper and installed about two days before it was discovered.

The meeting room where it was hidden was often used by OpenAI's employees to discuss highly confidential and proprietary matters, including research, product plans and business development, the Justice Department said.
In a statement, OpenAI said that after discovering the device, it contacted the FBI and has terminated the employee accused of planting it.

"The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work. At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the company said.

"We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats."
FBI Director Kash Patel said in a post on X that the FBI and its partners had carried out the arrest and that the investigation is ongoing.

Alfozan's attorney, William Pernik, noted to CBS News that his client is presumed innocent, and cautioned against "jumping to conclusions at this very early stage of the case when very little information is known," or seeking to "politicize" a prosecution based on factors like nationality.

The criminal complaint, made public on Tuesday, alleged that Alfozan used a productivity tool to make inquiries about OpenAI's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, and locations of "leadership and exec" and external partner meetings.

Other evidence gathered in the investigation, meanwhile, showed that a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse had also submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30, related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating and remote accessing a continuous audio recording device.
A photograph included in the complaint also shows that Alfozan entered the conference room where the device was hidden on Oct. 5 and looked behind the television.

That same day, the complaint says Alfozan left his bag unattended in another room, and the company's security personnel opened it and found his ID, wallet and another recording device similar to the one planted in the conference room.
Alfozan is due to appear in federal court again on Oct. 19 for a detention hearing.

title: Character.ai declares bankruptcy, citing legal and business woes
summary: AI company has faced multiple lawsuits from families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using its platform.
story: Character.ai said it has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, with its chief executive attributing the chatbot provider's financial problems to "significant legal, regulatory and operational headwinds."

The company said it will continue operating as it seeks to sell its business, and added that The Walt Disney Co. has agreed to pay $20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual license to Character.ai's intellectual property.

Character.ai's financial struggles follow scrutiny and litigation over its technology, which uses artificial intelligence to create custom bots consumers can chat with. In early 2026, Character.ai and Google, which had a licensing deal with the AI company, agreed to settle several lawsuits filed by families who claimed their teenage children died by suicide or harmed themselves after using Character.ai's platform.

The company settled a wrongful death lawsuit earlier in 2026 — the first filed in the U.S. against an AI company — with a Florida family who said their teen son died after conducting an emotional and sexual relationship with a chatbot known as "Dany." The family said in their lawsuit that Character.ai had no mechanisms in place to protect their son or notify an adult when teens were spending too much time interacting with Chatbots.
The company added several safety features designed with teens in mind after several lawsuits alleged its chatbots inappropriately interacted with underage users.

Several states have also sued Character.ai over its technology, with Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman alleging in January that its chatbots "preyed on children and led them into self-harm." In May, Pennsylvania sued Character.ai after one of its chatbots allegedly claimed to be a licensed psychiatrist in the state and provided a "fake Pennsylvania license number."
In a statement issued late Monday, Character.ai said it believes the company will be sold by late November or early December.

"After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders," Character.ai CEO Colin Adams said in the statement. "As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging user experience for our Character.ai community remains a top priority."
Is Character.ai shutting down?
The company said on Monday that its services continue to operate and that subscriptions remain active.
"If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance," Character.ai said.

In a blog post, the company said customer data "continues to be protected under our Privacy Policy." That policy states that data Character.ai collects from users — including chat transcripts, voice recordings, and images and videos — could be disclosed in connection with a sale or a negotiation to sell the company or its assets.
"As a reminder, you can delete your account or export your data through the app or the Character.ai website," the company said.

title: Anthropic warns "AI worms" could soon infect smart home devices
summary: Small AI models could clone themselves and infect internet-connected devices such as smart TVs and appliances, the researchers warned.
story: Anthropic is sounding the alarm about a new risk posed by artificial intelligence: Self-replicating "AI worms" could soon infest your "smart" home devices.

In a report released on Monday, Anthropic safety researchers said small AI models may be only "months away" from gaining the ability to clone themselves and spread across internet-connected devices, such as smart ovens, TVs and vacuum cleaners. The ability to reproduce themselves without human control would make it hard to control such agents because there's "no centralized point to shut off," said Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot.
Stronger AI models are already capable of what the researchers called "end-to-end replication," a threshold they say smaller models could reach by year-end, according to Anthropic.
AI worms, a type of AI-powered malware, can quickly spread across networks and devices while evading detection, according to cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks.

Smart devices in people's homes, as well as internet-connected devices such as security cameras, are vulnerable given that internet-enabled devices tend to have weaker security protections, the Anthropic researchers said. In what they described as a worst-case scenario, a swarm of AI agents — bots that work together to accomplish a shared goal — could propagate across computer hardware using "replication schemes."

The researchers said they are unsure of what form these attacks could take, noting that the AI models could be distributed as "digital slime mold" or as more powerful models capable of hacking into data centers.

"We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay," the Anthropic researchers wrote in the report.

title: Feds probing suspicious letters to election officials, lawmakers
summary: Federal investigators said they are looking into suspicious letters containing unknown substances that were mailed to state election officials and congressional offices.
story: Washington — Federal investigators said Thursday that they are looking into "suspicious" letters mailed to state election officials and congressional offices, some of which contained unknown substances.

At least seven Democratic Senate offices were sent the letters, most of which were intercepted before they were delivered. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's office was one of those targeted, CBS News has learned.

The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating the "suspicious mailings," according to Brendan Donahue, the deputy chief inspector at the USPIS. Donahue told reporters earlier in the day that some letters have contained an unknown substance and that they were sent to "various addresses nationwide," including "secretary of state offices and the related election offices."

"We are committed to protecting our nation's election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable," Donahue said. "Our partners, including the FBI and we at the Postal Inspection Service, will bring all of our resources to bear on these investigations."

The Senate sergeant at arms also issued a notice to congressional staff informing them of the investigation. The message, which was obtained by CBS News, said congressional offices were among those who received the suspicious letters.

A spokesperson for Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester told CBS News that a state office received a suspicious letter that contained a white powder. The letter was not opened in the office, the spokesperson said.

A letter meant for New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand was found at the senator's office in New York City and postal inspectors were on the scene to investigate, an aide for the senator said. A letter intended for one of Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks' former state office was intercepted by the Postal Service, her office said Friday.
A spokesman for Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut also said his office was "sent a letter with a suspicious substance."

"Our office was promptly informed of the letter by FBI, SAA, and Capitol Police, and we continue to work closely with them and federal law enforcement," said Josh Sorbe, a spokesman for Murphy. "Due to those efforts and various safety protocols, the Senator and staff were not in immediate danger."
A letter was also sent to Sen. Alex Padilla's office, according to a spokesperson for the California Democrat.
"We received the notification from the FBI that one of our offices was mailed a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted by USPS," the spokesperson said.
A suspicious letter was sent to the office of Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, according to a spokesperson, who said the office was "working with law enforcement."
The House sergeant at arms sent a notice to the lower chamber's offices stating that no House members were known to have been targeted.

Federal officials are working to identify the responsible parties and have intercepted some of the letters, Donahue said. Donahue declined to provide an exact number of incidents or discuss possible connections, citing the ongoing investigation. He added that investigators would bring their full resources to bear on the cases.
The development comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections. Federal investigators also probed a series of suspicious letters ahead of the 2024 elections.
In addition to the congressional offices, top election officials in at least eight states have reported that their offices were sent suspicious packages in recent days.

Delaware's Department of Elections said in a post on X that it "received and opened a letter which was discovered to contain a white powdery substance" on Thursday. "Staff members followed security and USPS instructions on handling suspicious mail," the post said.
Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry said Tuesday that an employee in her office's Elections Division opened a package and found a white powder.
"Law enforcement responded to today's incident and conducted tests that found no evidence of harmful substances," she wrote on Facebook, adding that no one was injured.
The Oklahoma State Election Board said it received an envelope containing "suspicious" white powder Tuesday morning, and its office was evacuated.
Paul Ziriax, secretary of the election board, said no one was hurt as a result of the incident, and law enforcement is investigating.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission said it received a "suspicious mail piece" on Wednesday, but "field testing confirmed no hazardous material was detected."

The secretaries of state in Pennsylvania, Maryland, New Hampshire, Ohio and Mississippi said their offices were also sent suspicious mail, but the deliveries were intercepted by the U.S. Postal Service or law enforcement before they arrived.

title: Who would oversee a flying car? We asked the DOT.
summary: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk unveiled Tesla's new Roadster Rocket, which he called a "flying car" equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks."
story: Who has oversight of a car that flies, hovers or otherwise defies gravity? We asked Department of Transportation officials, and the answer isn't readily clear.

Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk unveiled Tesla's new Roadster Rocket, which he called a "flying car" equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" — describing it as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company." The car — about a decade behind schedule — would go into production in 2028.

Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground, and Tesla's website notes that the flying model isn't approved for public road use. There's a non-flying version of the car, which would-be buyers can reserve online with a $5,000 deposit, but the Tesla website says the Rocket model with the "full flight system" will be offered by invitation only.

So, who will decide whether the Roadster is safe? There's time to work that out, but a senior Department of Transportation official, who expressed skepticism that the vehicle will actually be able to take off, acknowledged there's no clear answer.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration typically has regulatory oversight of vehicles — though it delegates safety certification to the automaker.

In a statement, the NHTSA said: "While the vehicle may appear to defy the laws of physics, the manufacturer must ensure that it does not defy applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and drivers must obey all local traffic laws. NHTSA will continue to monitor the situation and won't hesitate to act to protect the driving public."

If the Roadster is going to enter the public domain with the ability for off-ground "driving," that would seem to shift to the FAA, which regulates aircraft. The FAA tells CBS News: "The Tesla vehicle does not meet the FAA definition of an aircraft."

Thursday's Roadster demo showed the car launching from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolling over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.
CBS News reached out to Tesla to ask which agencies the company is working with. We will update if we hear back.
