title: Billy Joel says he can't drive, unsure about touring future after brain disorder diagnosis
summary: Billy Joel revealed his hydrocephalus diagnosis means every concert is like getting a concussion, and he's not allowed to drive a vehicle.
story: Gooding Christie's founder David Gooding told Fox News Digital that Billy Joel is a "genuine enthusiast" who loves all kinds of motorcycles.
Billy Joel's touring future remains uncertain due to his ongoing health issues.
Joel, 77, revealed in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter that he's also not allowed to drive a vehicle after being diagnosed with normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) in 2025.
"What the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it’s like you’re getting a concussion," Joel said.
'PIANO MAN' BILLY JOEL'S PRIZED MOTORCYCLE COLLECTION HITS THE AUCTION BLOCK
Billy Joel can't drive and is unsure about his touring future after brain disorder diagnosis. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images)
When asked about his current status, Joel said that his "health is good," but still isn't sure when he'll be able to tour again.

"I have this thing called hydrocephalus," he told the outlet. "It used to be called water on the brain, so it affects your balance, it affects your memory, it affects your vision, your hearing. But I’m OK."
"They call it a brain disorder, but it’s not that serious. It’s just something that affects your balance mostly."
LIONEL RICHIE HOSPITALIZED IN ST LOUIS AFTER SUMMER OF HEALTH SCARES AND CANCELED CONCERTS
As far as going back on the road again, Joel admitted he can't perform quite like how he used to.
Billy Joel said that while his health is "good," he has new limitations due to his NPH diagnosis. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images)

"I have to take a series of tests before I know, but I can’t drive right now," he said. "I’m not allowed to drive. And I can’t do performances because what the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it’s like you’re getting a concussion."
He added, "So they have to test me further to see if I can go back and do performing again, which I would like to be able to do."

The "Uptown Girl" singer underwent brain surgery after revealing his normal pressure hydrocephalus diagnosis in May 2025. NPH affects his vision, hearing and balance, according to a statement Joel released on social media at the time.

He delved more into his recovery process during a recent appearance on his self-titled SiriusXM show, "The Billy Joel Channel," and said doctors told him that performing loud rock 'n' roll music caused damage to his brain nerves.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Joel remembered his medical team saying, "Well, we drill a hole through your skull, and we stick a shunt inside your brain."

"I didn't want to do that, but then I read up on it and I realized it can help improve your balance and can help your memory," he noted. "You know, I don't want to lose my marbles. It's hard to tell what's age and what's a condition, so I agreed to do the shunt and I had a surgery. And they implanted a shunt in my brain, and it actually improved things."
Billy Joel has been nominated for dozens of Grammy Awards and won multiple trophies, including Album of the Year for "52nd Street." (Getty Images)

"My memory got better. My balance got a little better. My ability to function was better, and I realized, and the doctors told me this, because of my job, which is playing rock and roll music very loud, that it was giving me something like a concussion every time I did a show."
Joel shared more about his diagnosis ahead of the sale of more than 70 lots from his personal collection of motorcycles heading to the auction block next month with Gooding Christie's.

"Well, I ended up having over a hundred motorcycles, and the truth is you can only ride one at a time. I’m into my 70s now, and I realized I can’t ride as much as I used to," he told the outlet. "I don’t want to die like a bug on a windshield. So I thought I’d put a lot of them on auction."
Gooding Christie’s announced the world-famous Billy Joel Motorcycle Collection as a leading consignment for its upcoming inaugural sale at the Javits Center in New York City. (Billy Joel Archives)
"And also I have a condition called hydrocephalus, which makes driving a little bit iffy. So I realized it’s time for me to turn it over to somebody else."
The collection includes a number of his most cherished motorcycles, in addition to Ducati, BMW, Moto Guzzi, Harley-Davidson, Yamaha, Triumph, Honda, Kawasaki, and more.

"One of the stars of the sale is a 1978 Triumph T140 Bonneville that was gifted to Billy Joel by Madison Square Garden to commemorate 150 sold out shows," Gooding Christie's founder David Gooding explained to Fox News Digital of the bike, which is expected to retrieve anywhere from $10,000 - $15,000.

Among the most captivating motorcycles in the collection is a 1978 Triumph T140 Bonneville gifted to Mr. Joel by Madison Square Garden on the occasion of his 150th sold-out show at the world-famous venue. (Mike Maez, Gooding & Company, LLC.)
"He still holds the record for the most sold out show of anyone ever at Madison Square Garden. And this bike is painted with a keyboard on the tank. It's really, really a special, special item."

title: Hayden Panettiere’s final moments revealed in frantic 911 call from boyfriend’s brother
summary: The newly released 911 call captures Zach Hickerson performing CPR on Hayden Panettiere as Brian Hickerson administered Narcan inside a South Carolina apartment.
story: The Greenville County Coroner released the cause of death for 36-year-old actress Hayden Panettiere, ruling it a tragic accident from the toxic effects of fentanyl and other substances. Fox News chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt reports from Los Angeles on her sudden death in South Carolina.

Hayden Panettiere’s final moments were captured in a frantic 911 call as the brother of her on-and-off boyfriend desperately tried to revive the actress after finding her unconscious at a South Carolina apartment Aug. 16.
"​​Oh, God, oh, my God — you do like CPR or something?" Zach Hickerson asked the dispatcher in the newly released audio obtained by ABC News and CBS News.
The seven-minute call reveals Hickerson performing CPR on Panettiere while Brian Hickerson administered Narcan.

Panettiere, 36, was found unresponsive at the Greenville residence    Aug. 16. Zach told the 911 operator that he had arrived at the apartment after returning from church and discovered his brother and Panettiere inside.
HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S BOYFRIEND’S BROTHER REVEALS WHAT HAPPENED INSIDE AIRBNB BEFORE ACTRESS'S DEATH
Hayden Panettiere died at age 36 on Aug. 16. (Getty Images)
"He woke up, and his girl ... she’s unconscious," Zach said.
The dispatcher asked whether Panettiere was breathing.
POLICE SHOW UP AT HOME LINKED TO HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S ON-AND-OFF BOYFRIEND DAYS AFTER HER SUDDEN DEATH
"No, I don’t think so," Zach replied.
The operator then instructed Zach to lay Panettiere flat on her back and begin CPR while emergency crews rushed to the scene.
HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S REP SLAMS ‘GOSSIP AND SPECULATION’ AS DEATH INVESTIGATION DEEPENS
"OK, we need to start CPR," the dispatcher said. "I’m going to tell you how to do CPR, OK?"
The operator proceeded to walk Zach through chest compressions and mouth-to-mouth resuscitation.
Panettiere’s major breakthrough came as Claire Bennett, the seemingly indestructible cheerleader at the center of NBC’s superhero drama "Heroes," which ran from 2006 to 2010. (Getty Images)
HAYDEN PANETTIERE'S OVERDOSE SHOWS FENTANYL CRISIS 'DOESN'T DISCRIMINATE,' STANFORD PSYCHIATRIST SAYS
"We’re going to do this 500 times or until help can arrive," the dispatcher said, according to ABC News.
Zach continued performing CPR until first responders arrived. Brian reportedly administered Narcan, a medication used to reverse the effects of an opioid overdose.
HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S MOM DISCLOSES HEARTBREAKING ULTIMATUM IN THEIR FINAL PHONE CALL BEFORE ACTRESS’ DEATH
In a statement to TMZ shortly after Panettiere’s death, Zach said he called 911 after he and Brian tried to wake up the actress.

"When we went in and tried to wake Hayden up, we realized she was unconscious," he said. "I immediately called 911, and Brian gave her Narcan. We then jointly performed CPR while 911 was on speaker until fire and EMS arrived."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Hayden Panettiere and Brian Hickerson in Los Angeles Jan. 31, 2019. (Gotpap/Bauer-Griffin)
Panettiere was pronounced dead at 2:32 p.m.
Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine, according to the Greenville County Coroner's Office. The manner of death was ruled an accident.

"On August 16, 2026, at approximately 1:51 PM, a 911 call was received regarding a reported cardiac arrest at 701 Easley Bridge Road in Greenville," the Greenville County Coroner's Office said in a release obtained by Fox News Digital.

"First responders and Emergency Medical Services arrived on scene and located a female in cardiac arrest. EMS personnel initiated advanced cardiac life support measures; however, resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful, and the individual was pronounced deceased at 2:32 PM.

"The Greenville County Coroner’s Office responded to the scene and initiated a parallel investigation with the Greenville City Police Department. title: 'Big Bang Theory' stars were 'outraged' over request to take pay cut for new co-stars, Chuck Lorre claims
summary: Chuck Lorre's memoir "Sitcom" reveals Charlie Sheen's final chaotic day on set, his Scientology past and CBS initially rejecting Melissa McCarthy.
story: Hollywood in Toto founder Christian Toto reacts to Lorre’s speech at a charity event, where the comedy producer criticized President Donald Trump, compared first lady Melania Trump to an escort and took aim at Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Chuck Lorre is spilling all his secrets in his new memoir.

The prolific television producer and writer wrote about his life and his many decades in the industry in his new memoir, "Sitcom," in which he gave tons of behind-the-scenes stories from some of his most popular TV shows.
Whether it was his final days working with Charlie Sheen, him going to bat with the network over casting choices or shocking refusals from cast members regarding salaries, Lorre didn't hold back.
Chuck Lorre spills secrets from his life and from his many sets in his new memoir, "Sitcom." (Presley Ann/Getty Images for Lucas Museum of Narrative Art)
Here are some of the biggest bombshells from his memoir.
MACKENZIE PHILLIPS SAYS SHE AND VALERIE BERTINELLI DRANK WINE, DID COCAINE DURING SITCOM BREAKS
'The Big Bang Theory'

"The Big Bang Theory" cast members Kaley Cuoco, Johnny Galecki, Melissa Rauch, Kunal Nayyar, Simon Helberg, Jim Parsons and Mayim Bialik pose with producers Steven Molaro, Chuck Lorre and Bill Prady at the People’s Choice Awards on Jan. 6, 2016, in Los Angeles, Calif. (Smallz & Raskind/Getty Images for The People's Choice Awards)
One of Lorre's most successful sitcoms is "The Big Bang Theory," which had a large ensemble cast.

In his memoir, Lorre recalled bringing in Mayim Bialik and Melissa Rauch towards the end of season three and upgrading them to series regulars in the fourth season, noting without them, "the show would likely have run out of gas after seven, maybe eight seasons."

Lorre writes about Charlie Sheen and other actors he worked with in his new memoir, "Sitcom." (Dey Street Books)

After a while, he remembered the network getting pressure to raise the episodic fees for Bialik and Rauch, noting TV executives Les Moonves and Bruce Rosenblum approached the main cast, who were earning $1 million an episode plus profit points, "to ask them to take a 10 percent cut in pay to accommodate that raise."

"I assumed they’d quickly agree, you know, all for one, one for all," he wrote. "That effusive attitude of gratitude actors display at award shows. Wrong again. They were outraged that they would even be asked to take a small cut in order to reward the two newer cast members. Moonves and Rosenblum had to slink out of the room, scrotally impaired."
Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for stars Jim Parsons, Kaley Cuoco, Johnny Galecki, Kunal Nayyar and Simon Helberg for comment.
Charlie Sheen's last day on set
Sheen starred in "Two and a Half Men" for eight seasons. (Tony Esparza/CBS via Getty Images)
Lorre and Charlie Sheen worked together on "Two and a Half Men" for eight seasons before the actor's behavior led to his exit.
In his memoir, Lorre explained that the show "was a blast to do" for the first seven seasons, but "it all began to unravel" during season eight, when Sheen "started calling in sick all the time."

"The typical excuse was food poisoning, usually bad clams," Lorre wrote. "There were a lot of emergency dental appointments. Once I was informed he would not be attending rehearsal because his BIC lighter had exploded and burned off his eyelashes. Another time, his manager bragged to me about having to fly across the country, with a bag full of cash, in order to purchase a home video sex tape starring his client."
Despite his antics, they continued to film the show, with Lorre noting they "worked in a constant state of anxiety," wondering what Sheen was going to do next.
Sheen allegedly couldn't remember his lines and needed help staying upright during his last day on set. (Gale Adler/CBS via Getty Images)
His behavior soon became too much to handle, and it was clear to those around him that his health and wellbeing were at risk.

"The last scene we shot was with Charlie and Melanie Lynsky," Lorre wrote. "He couldn’t remember any of his lines and had to use the furniture to keep himself upright. Melanie was terrified. It was clear to everyone that this man, whom we’d all grown to love, was in trouble. I had no choice but to shut down the show."
Lorre wrote that after refusing to get help for his drug problem and later trashing him on television, Warner Bros. decided they no longer wanted Sheen on their lot, and he was let go.
Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for Charlie Sheen for comment.
JULIA LOUIS-DREYFUS REVEALS ‘TONS’ OF FRICTION BEHIND THE SCENES OF ‘SEINFELD’
Casting controversy
Lorre shared that he had to fight for Melissa McCarthy to be the lead in "Mike & Molly." (Cliff Lipson/CBS via Getty Images)
During his career as a television writer and show creator, Lorre encountered pushback from studio executives many times when it came to choosing actors to star in his shows.

In his memoir, Lorre explained the casting decisions behind some of the most popular shows from the past few decades, noting executives initially didn't want to cast Jon Cryer on "Two and a Half Men," or Nayyar on "The Big Bang Theory."

Despite the success of these actors in their respective roles, studio executives challenged him once again when it came time to cast the female lead in "Mike & Molly."

"The casting of Molly was, like with Jon Cryer, a tortuous journey," he said. "Once again, my brilliant casting director, Nikki Valko, brought in a comic genius. Melissa McCarthy. And once again, CBS hated her. Believe it or not, they wanted a hot young woman to play a woman struggling with her weight. It was even suggested by one exec—a female exec—that I consider casting a more attractive actress and put her in a fat suit."
Lorre recalled feeling smart when McCarthy starred in "Bridesmaids." (Frederick M. Brown/Getty Images)

Lorre explained that at this point he had learned his lesson and did not take no for an answer, insisting that McCarthy be given the role, "end of discussion," adding that "when 'Bridesmaids' came out, I felt pretty god-damn smart."
Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for CBS for comment.
'MIKE & MOLLY' STAR BILLY GARDELL REVEALS WEIGHT LOSS SURGERY 'PROBABLY SAVED' HIS LIFE
Scientology
Lorre revealed he was once a member of the Church of Scientology. (Michael Tullberg/Getty Images)
When discussing his life prior to making it big as a TV writer, Lorre revealed he was once a part of the Church of Scientology.

He recalled going to the Church of Scientology in Columbus, Ohio, after being invited by the sax player at a bar. He wrote that he "had no idea what Scientology was," but since he had nothing to do and his car was in a junkyard, he decided to go, and was quickly taken with the "pretty girls" there.

Lorre explained that after taking a communication class, he had an out-of-body experience, and sought out the Church of Scientology when he was in Los Angeles. There, he found himself presented with a one billion year contract to join Scientology's Sea Org.

"Now, I didn’t want to give up my dead-end music career, but I was broken, outnumbered, and overwhelmed," he wrote. "I caved in and signed. Next thing I knew, I was saving homo saps by passing out free personality test invites to homeless people in MacArthur Park. I lasted two days. Which means contractually, I owe the Church of Scientology a billion years of labor minus two days."
Age gap regrets
Lorre admitted entering into an age-gap marriage was not the best decision. (Allen Berezovsky/Getty Images)
Lorre touched on his marriage to his third wife, Arielle Mandelson, saying entering into an age-gap relationship was not the best decision.

He explained that when their relationship began, he "convinced myself that age was an arbitrary thing" and that "you're only as old as you think" and that "the heart wants what it wants, but as time went on he came to the conclusion that all that ‘turned out to be bulls---’ and 'sometimes the heart's an idiot.'"

"Age is not only a huge chasm, it widens with time. No bridge can span the distance between Taylor Swift and Bruce Springsteen," he wrote. "The speed of physical and mental decline between sixty and sixty-five is horrifyingly quick. Between thirty and thirty-five, infinitesimal."

Lorre claimed that initially he was "wary about the age thing" as he was older than Mandelson's parents, but that anytime he brought that to her attention, "she accused me of being ‘ageist,’" adding, "eventually she wore me down."
Lorre said the two were miserable after seven years together. (VALERIE MACON/AFP via Getty Images)

"After seven years we were both miserable and agreed to separate. Eight months later we carpooled to a wedding," he wrote. "The night ended with a second consummation, followed by reconciliation, followed by another year of misery. This time we agreed to divorce. She got a whole bunch of money. I got the dog. I like to think I got the better end of the deal. The dog is always happy to see me."

title: Prince Harry, Meghan Markle accused of staging 'royal theatre' as King Charles faces new dilemma: expert
summary: Royal experts say the Sussexes' Nottingham charity visit risks defying Queen Elizabeth II's rule against a "half in, half out" arrangement.
story: Hugo Vickers, author of "Queen Elizabeth II: A Personal History," details how the Duke and Duchess of Sussexs exit and Oprah interview added strain during the late monarch's final years.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are being accused of playing royals on their own terms — and sidestepping the late Queen Elizabeth II's wishes in the process.

On Oct. 15, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex visited Nottingham for their first joint public appearance since returning to the U.K., Fox News Digital confirmed. The city holds special significance for the couple, as it was the first place they visited after announcing their engagement in November 2017.

Kinsey Schofield, host of the YouTube show "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital that, based on her sources, "there is frustration" inside Buckingham Palace as Harry and Meghan prepare to visit several charities in a manner resembling an official royal engagement.
KING CHARLES DRAWS ‘LINE IN THE SAND’ WITH PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE AFTER COUPLE CAUGHT OFF GUARD: EXPERT
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex during a visit with Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England.  (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle attend the Terrence Higgins Trust World AIDS Day charity fair at Nottingham Contemporary on Dec. 1, 2017 in Nottingham, England. The couple returned to the city on Oct. 15, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"Harry and Meghan are no longer working members of the royal family," Schofield said. "King Charles recently reminded his government that the Sussexes are private citizens. The Sussexes appear increasingly determined to recreate the optics of royal life without the responsibilities that come with it. … The charitable visits, the appearances, the photographers. It’s royal theatre without royal authority."

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex at Himmah Hub, which provides meals and a welcoming space for people experiencing financial hardship or isolation, during a visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Mark Cuthbert/Getty Images)

"Royal engagements aren't just photo-ops," Schofield said. "There's diplomacy involved. There's soft power. Working royals represent the sovereign, strengthen relationships and serve the interests of the country. Harry and Meghan appear more interested in faking the image of royalty than embracing its purpose. They can imitate the engagement, but they can't replicate the authority or constitutional significance."
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle gesture during a visit to Nottingham Academy in Nottingham, central England, on Dec. 1, 2017. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
"They are pushing to reclaim the spotlight they left behind," British broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital. "It's definitely a reboot — a pseudo royal reboot."
WATCH: PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE CAUSED QUEEN STRESS IN FINAL YEARS: AUTHOR

In January 2020, Queen Elizabeth II drew a firm line at the Sandringham Summit: There would be no "half in, half out" role for the Sussexes. They couldn't remain working members of the royal family while pursuing independent, income-generating ventures. The couple stepped back from royal duties that year, citing intrusive coverage by the British press and a lack of support from the palace.

From left: Queen Elizabeth II, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, watch a flypast marking the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace in London on July 10, 2018. (Getty Images)

"Following conversations with the duke, the queen has written confirming that in stepping away from the work of the royal family it is not possible to continue with the responsibilities and duties that come with a life of public service," Buckingham Palace said in a statement on Feb. 19, 2021.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex during a visit to Himmah Hub during their visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Annabel Lee-Ellis - Pool/Getty Images)
In response, the couple issued a statement of their own, saying: "We can all live a life of service. Service is universal."
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle returned to the U.K. six years after leaving for California. (Getty Images)

In Nottingham, the couple focused on charitable work. They visited a food bank, where Meghan reconnected with some of the women she supported at the Hubb Community Kitchen in London. As a working royal, Meghan helped produce "Together: Our Community Cookbook," which featured recipes from women associated with the kitchen.
Prince Harry is seen here during a visit to Himmah Hub on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. ( Annabel Lee-Ellis - Pool/Getty Images)
They also visited the Community Recording Studio, which helps young people affected by violence, and spent time at Epic Partners, which supports young people through mentoring and sports.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex visits the Hubb Community Kitchen in London on Nov. 21, 2018, to celebrate the success of their cookbook. The kitchen was set up by women affected by the Grenfell Tower fire, and the duchess wrote a foreword to the cookbook to help raise funds for the victims. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Although Harry and Meghan are free to support charities as private citizens, their visits are not official royal engagements, as they no longer represent the monarch. However, royal commentators argue that the couple's public appearances risk blurring that distinction.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, arrives for a visit to the Community Recording Studio in St. Anns on Sept. 9, 2025, in Nottingham, England. (Getty Images)

"The Sussexes have not been given permission to behave like working royals, and yet they seem to have gone ahead with their own plans to recapture the spotlight in the U.K.," Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," told Fox News Digital. "These are worthy causes that the couple was supporting previously, so that obviously takes some of the sting out of it."
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle visit the Terrence Higgins Trust World AIDS Day charity fair at Nottingham Contemporary in Nottingham, England, on Dec. 1, 2017. (Getty Images)

Several royal experts told Fox News Digital that the couple's public appearances put King Charles in an increasingly uncomfortable position. While Harry and Meghan are no longer working royals, their titles, global profile and carefully choreographed public appearances can still look strikingly similar to official royal duties, even though they do not carry the authority of the crown. This, they argued, leaves the monarch to decide how firmly to enforce the boundary his late mother drew.
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"Kate!: The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen" by Christopher Andersen is available now. (Gallery Books)
"King Charles faces a severe problem because Harry and Meghan appear determined to ignore the late queen's instructions," Schofield said.

King Charles III meets guests during a reception to celebrate the Commonwealth Diaspora ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda at St. James's Palace in London on Oct. 14, 2026. (Getty Images)

"They’ve retained their titles and international recognition, allowing them to stage appearances that resemble official engagements, despite no longer representing the crown. The king has demonstrated throughout his life that he can be decisive when protecting his interests and the institution. The question is whether he’s prepared to demonstrate that same strength when it comes to his youngest son."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex during a visit to Himmah Hub during their visit to Nottingham on Oct.15, 2026, in Nottingham, England.  ( Annabel Lee-Ellis - Pool/Getty Images)

Andersen noted that the king is "weary of having to deal with all this drama" and of being "a sort of referee between his sons." However, Andersen said, the king may ultimately have little choice but to act if the Sussexes continue to blur the line between private citizens and working royals.

The outlet reported that while the Sussexes reunited with King Charles and Queen Camilla in July, they are not believed to have seen the king in person since moving back to Britain. According to People, Harry and his father have remained in contact by phone. Harry and his older brother, Prince William, reportedly haven't spoken in years. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex visit Epic Partners during their visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Joe Giddens - Pool/Getty Images)

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that, as private citizens, Harry and Meghan have the freedom to pursue their own projects without requiring the blessing of the king or the Prince of Wales.

"There are suspicions that Harry and Meghan are trying to create an alternative royal family," he said. "Their first joint event together has raised eyebrows in some royal circles. But as they are now private citizens, 'The Firm' have very little, if any, power over them. This, in some ways, could be a blessing for Harry and Meghan and a curse for those in royal circles."

title: Canadian singer Joni Mitchell officially becomes American citizen after 62-year journey
summary: Joni Mitchell shared a photo and video from her naturalization ceremony, becoming a U.S. citizen at 82 while retaining Canadian citizenship.
story: Country music superstar Chris Janson joins 'Fox & Friends' at Liberty House in Jersey City, N.J., for the America 250 celebration. Janson articulates his profound patriotism, stating he's 'never been shy' about loving the flag, troops and freedom.
Joni Mitchell has officially become an American citizen at age 82, more than six decades after she first moved to the United States.
The music icon, who hails from Canada, announced the news on Instagram, sharing a photo of herself beaming while holding an American flag along with a video from her naturalization ceremony.
"A journey that began 62 years ago," Mitchell wrote in the caption of her post.
Joni Mitchell has become a U.S. citizen after 62 years in America. (Joni Mitchell Instagram)
ART GARFUNKEL JOINS GROWING LIST OF CELEBRITIES CONSIDERING A MOVE ABROAD OVER TRUMP PRESIDENCY

Mitchell wore a red and navy blue floral cardigan that had an American flag pin along with a red beaded necklace, a red beret and black pants with black boots while posing in between an American flag and a Department of Homeland Security flag.
In the video Mitchell uploaded, she was seated in the front row at the ceremony as the speaker announced, "And Joni Mitchell, Canada" to cheers and applause from the audience.
According to KSL, Mitchell will also retain her Canadian citizenship because the U.S. and Canada legally permit dual citizenship.
The legendary singer-songwriter was born Roberta Joan Anderson in Fort Macleod, Alberta, to Royal Canadian Air Force flight Lt. William Andrew Anderson and teacher Myrtle Marguerite.

Mitchell's family lived on several bases during World War II before eventually settling in Saskatoon, which the singer has often referred to as her hometown. She went on to attend the Alberta College of Art in Calgary before dropping out and relocating to Toronto, where she played gigs at coffee houses and folk clubs.

The "Both Sides Now" songstress moved to the United States in 1965 at age 21 after marrying American folk singer Chuck Mitchell. The former couple, who lived in Detroit, Michigan, performed together as a folk duo before divorcing in 1967.
The legendary singer-songwriter was born in Canada and moved to the U.S. in 1965. (Getty Images)
After their divorce, Mitchell left Detroit and moved to New York City, where she became part of the Greenwich Village folk scene and performed along the East Coast.

By 1968, Mitchell moved to Los Angeles, settling in Laurel Canyon, which was becoming a hub for singer-songwriters including David Crosby, Graham Nash and others. In the mid-1970s, Mitchell moved to LA's Bel Air neighborhood, where she lived in a historic 1920s home for decades.
Mitchell built her legendary music career while living in California, where she recorded many of her most acclaimed albums, including "Blue," "Court and Spark" and "Ladies of the Canyon."
Mitchell has won 11 Grammy Awards and was inducted into both the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1997.
Mitchell lived in Detroit before moving to New York City and then Los Angeles. (Redferns)
She was also recognized with the Kennedy Center Honors in 2021 and received the prestigious Library of Congress Gershwin Prize for Popular Song in 2023.
The musician lives in Santa Barbara, California.
Mitchell is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump and expressed frustration that she couldn't vote in U.S. elections because she was Canadian.
CHRIS ROBINSON, BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN FACE BACKLASH AS 'AMERICANS HAVE HAD ENOUGH' OF BEING LECTURED: EXPERT
She has won 11 Grammy Awards.  (Getty Images)
During a performance at the Hollywood Bowl in LA in October 2024, Mitchell slammed Trump while performing her 1985 song "Dog Eat Dog," according to Billboard.
After singing a lyric about wealthy financiers, she added, "Like Donald Trump!"
Following her performance of the song, Mitchell responded to an audience member who shouted an anti-Trump remark.
"'F--- Donald Trump.' I love that song," she said, apparently referencing rapper YG's 2016 protest song "FDT (F--- Donald Trump)" featuring the late rapper and activist Nipsey Hussle.
Mitchell is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump.  (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
She then encouraged Americans to participate in the 2024 U.S. presidential election, in which Trump ran against Democratic nominee former Vice President Kamala Harris.
"Everybody get out and vote. This is an important one. I wish I could vote . I'm Canadian. I'm one of those lousy immigrants," Mitchell said.
Months before becoming an American citizen, Mitchell criticized the political climate in the U.S. while accepting a lifetime achievement award at Canada's Juno Awards in March.
The 2012 Kennedy Honors recipient slammed Trump at a concert in 2024. (Getty Images)
At the ceremony, Mitchell praised Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, saying, "I'm so glad to be back in Canada. This man is a blessing. You guys are so fortunate."

She also appeared to take a swipe at the Trump administration while contrasting Canada with the U.S.
"I'm living in the states, and you know what's happening there," she said.
After Mitchell's comments at the Juno Awards, the White House issued a dismissive response.

When asked about her remarks, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told The Independent, "Who the hell is Joni Mitchell?"

title: John Stamos says Beach Boys legend Mike Love is facing 'serious health challenges'
summary: John Stamos revealed Mike Love is facing serious health challenges, but the Beach Boys legend insisted on performing at the Ryman over the weekend.
story: ‘Full House’ star John Stamos told Fox News Digital he ‘made sure’ Mike Love performed at the Ryman amid health challenges.
John Stamos performed with the Beach Boys on Sunday at the Ryman Auditorium in Nashville.
Before the show, the actor was overcome with emotion talking about Beach Boys legend Mike Love, who is facing "serious health challenges."
Stamos, 63, shared a carousel of images on social media with his "musical hero and mentor" before admitting he was "struggling" to put his feelings into words.
ROD STEWART CONFIRMS FINAL TOUR AFTER HEART PROCEDURE AND HEALTH SCARES

"My beloved friend, father figure, musical hero and mentor, Mike Love, is facing serious health challenges," he wrote. "We hope he’ll be doing what he loves for years to come, but we don’t know what the future holds. We have tonight."
At Tuesday's Hot Cuisine fundraiser for the Scleroderma Research Foundation (SRF), Stamos told Fox News Digital it was his mission to get Love to the Ryman Auditorium for a performance of a lifetime.
John Stamos shared an emotional update about Beach Boys legend Mike Love before the Nashville performance. (John Lamparski)

"Our goal was to get him up at the Ryman this weekend. He wanted it," Stamos said. "I've been spending a lot of time with him, you know, quiet time. We've been listening to music. … Doo-wop. He loves Doo-Wop.
"And I said, ‘You gotta tell me, do you really think you can do these shows this weekend?’ He said, ‘Yes, and I really want to.’ I said, 'We'll make it happen.'

"Everybody told him not to — doctors, his family — but it was something he wanted to do. He's made all my dreams come true and all my wishes. So, I had to fulfill his wish, and we made sure that he got there and did a good job."

SRF presented John Stamos with the Bob Saget Legacy Award, recognizing his steadfast support for scleroderma research and his commitment to following in Bob’s footsteps by shining a spotlight on scleroderma and raising funds toward a cure.
Love's representatives did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. It's unclear what health struggles Love faces.
Stamos and Love's son, Brian Love, delivered speeches prior to the show.
"One thing about him is he's stubborn, and he's steadfast, and he did not want to miss the Ryman. I mean, for good reason," Brian said, via Variety.

"Look at this place. So, we are happy. We're going to be positive. We're gonna sing along. But I still remember something he told me when I was a child, and it stuck with me. I said, ‘Dad, why do you do so many shows?’ I mean, we are talking about a guy who's done over 100 concerts a year well up into his 80s."

"That's just incredible, right? So, he told me, ‘Well, if you don’t do as many concerts, you don't see as many towns, and then that means less people get to hear the amazing Beach Boys personally.' So, he's always cared for the small towns, the fairs. … This is obviously a much more well-known, beautiful venue. But he cares about the listener, and I think it's such an honor to be part of that. And we've gotta live in the moment."

Stamos said, "All we have is tonight really, and I think it's going to be very, very special. Mike, he insisted on being here. … He's done over 7,000 live shows. And tonight'll be 7,422, I think exactly. I think that's where we're at. He's counting. … We love you, and have the greatest night ever, and God bless you all."
After the curtains opened, Love was already seated on stage, the outlet reported.
He sang in his seat along with his bandmates but did not do his lead vocals.

During the performance, the Beach Boys legend addressed concerns about his health, saying, "Obviously, I’ve been going through some health issues for quite a while. But I didn’t want to miss being at the Ryman with y’all."
Variety reported that Love was helped up by Brian and Stamos at the end of the show as the song "We Are The Champions" by Queen played.
JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY ENDS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN SHOW AFTER HEALTH SETBACK
In his social media post, Stamos acknowledged that Love "is a fighter," and despite "doctors, family and friends urging him to focus on his health, he insists on being on stage."

"He says he needs his band, the audience, his friends and drummer surrounding him to lift him up," Stamos wrote. "I’ve played with Mike for 41 years. I never imagined how deeply it would affect me to see someone larger than life face something so human and fragile."
Love and Stamos performing on the Palomino Stage on the final day of Stagecoach Country Music Festival at the Empire Polo Club in Indio. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
The Beach Boys have been touring in support of the 60th anniversary of their groundbreaking 11th studio album, "Pet Sounds."
Stamos noted that "the Mike Love we see tonight may not be exactly the Mike we’ve always known. But he’s still every bit the Mike we love."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
"His lyrics, optimism, unforgettable hooks and more than 7,000 concerts have brought joy to generations," Stamos wrote. "What he’s given me personally is immeasurable.
John Stamos has performed with the Beach Boys for more than four decades. (Vinnie Zuffante)
"Forty-one years of stages, airplanes, hotel rooms, laughter and moments nobody else saw. He married Caitlin and me. He’s shared experiences with my family, and now my son."
The "Full House" star noted that Love didn't only give him a spot in the band. He "gave me a place in his life."
WATCH HERE: JOHN STAMOS FULFILLS BEACH BOYS LEGEND MIKE LOVE'S WISH TO PLAY IN NASHVILLE
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"He taught me how to entertain, hold a stage, connect with an audience and make people feel something. I carry those lessons everywhere," Stamos said. "He’s made me a better musician, entertainer and man.
The Beach Boys (L-R) — Carl Wilson, Bruce Johnston, Brian Wilson, Mike Love and Al Jardine — pose for a portrait session May 1, 1987, in Los Angeles. (Harry Langdon/Getty Images)
"This life with Mike and the Beach Boys has become part of my identity. I’ve felt entrusted with being a steward of this extraordinary music, carrying it to new generations."

Stamos wanted to "be completely present" performing with Love at the Ryman over the weekend and "hear every harmony, familiar joke and cheer. Feel that first chord hit and watch age, illness and time disappear. Just a bunch of guys making music together."
He wrote, "Maybe the hardest part of loving someone is becoming so accustomed to the miracle of having them there that you forget it’s a miracle at all.

"Tonight, I won’t forget," Stamos wrote. "I want to cherish every second without feeling those seconds slipping away. That’s what I’m giving him.
The Beach Boys rose to fame in the '60s with hits, including, "God Only Knows" and "Good Vibrations." (Michael Ochs)

"We don’t know what tomorrow brings. But we have tonight."

title: Selma Blair's on-off boyfriend asks fans to 'pray' for actress after Delta flight incident, assault charges
summary: Selma Blair's on-off boyfriend Andy Kiernan asked fans to "pray for Selma" as the actress faced assault charges following an alleged Delta flight incident at JFK.
story: The actress was arrested Sunday after allegedly attacking crew members on board a Delta flight into New York City. (Credit: Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News)
Selma Blair's on-again, off-again boyfriend pleaded for compassion after the actress' arrest and subsequent assault charges following an alleged mid-air incident aboard a Delta flight to New York.

title: Ethan Hawke blasts Hollywood's 'greedy bastards,' predicts massive rebellion against powerful elites
summary: Ethan Hawke predicts massive rebellion in music and live theater against Hollywood's "greedy bastards" who he says control the entertainment industry.
story: Ethan Hawke celebrates Willie Nelson’s 90th birthday and tells Fox News Digital ‘a lot of people disagree, but a lot of people can agree about Willie Nelson’
Ethan Hawke isn't holding back when it comes to the powerful forces he believes are controlling the entertainment industry.

During a new interview with GQ, the Oscar-nominated actor took aim at wealthy power players, blasting "greedy bastards" who think they control every aspect of Hollywood and predicting a major rebellion against the industry.

"I believe in rebellion. And I think people are going to wake up and punch back and there’s going to be massive movements in music and massive movements in live theater and massive movements of people getting together," Hawke said.
FROM ‘SCREAM’ TO STREAM: JAMIE KENNEDY REVEALS HOW HOLLYWOOD LOST ITS WAY AND WHY HE WON'T GIVE UP ON LA
Ethan Hawke spoke about the "greedy bastards" who believe they control Hollywood. (Getty Images)

"So don’t worry that the money and the greedy bastards that think they control everybody, they always lose in the end," he continued. "And they’re all going in the grave eventually. They think they’re winning, but they’re losing because their lives are worthless."
Hawke also expressed frustration with the financial pressures shaping Hollywood, arguing that the projects actors care about most often come with the smallest paychecks.
TRUMP, SCHIFF FORGE UNLIKELY ALLIANCE AS HOLLYWOOD BLEEDS JOBS
"There's a direct correlation. I find that the more you love a project, the less you get paid," he said. "If you want to beat the algorithm, it's very difficult to do that and be paid."
Hawke found fame at a young age. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images)
This isn't the first time Hawke has spoken about the pitfalls of Hollywood.
ROBERT DOWNEY JR. SLAMS MODERN CELEBRITY CULTURE AS 'ABSOLUTE HORSES---'
Last year, the actor called celebrity a "poison" for a young actor's brain.
During an appearance on "The Joe Rogan Experience," Hawke got candid about his start in Hollywood as a young man and reflected on the psychological effect of becoming famous at a young age.

"I think celebrity is like a tiny drop of mercury. Or it's poison. It's poison for your brain," the actor said. "To be a professional actor at a young age, it's dangerous in extremely insidious ways that are very, very hard to perceive when it's happening," Hawke said.

Rogan compared the experience of becoming famous as a child to concrete. If concrete is made incorrectly, with the wrong amount of water or cement, that's it, he explained. Rogan added that once it dries there is no way to repair or fix it.
Ethan Hawke at the 2026 BAFTAs on Feb. 22. (Getty Images)
DISNEY ALUM CHRISTY CARLSON ROMANO RIPS HOLLYWOOD FOR FAILING CHILD STARS AFTER HAYDEN PANETTIERE’S DEATH

"That analogy works for all walks of life. Really. If you have something really traumatic happen in childhood, it's very hard to recover. It's a tremendous amount of work to recover. And I agree with you, like I think celebrity is like a tiny drop of mercury. Or it's a poison. It's a poison for your brain," Hawke said.
During his GQ interview, Hawke expressed the same sentiment.

"I wouldn’t be the first person to say that there’s an aspect of celebrity that is like a disease," he said. "And you can handle little bits of it, but too much of it — we can see what happened to Elvis and we can see Michael Jackson. It’s a form of isolation. It’s like being put in a zoo, and zoo animals go nuts. So do human beings."

"And it seems like a kind of nice isolation because people are giving you money, and they’re telling you you’re wonderful, but nobody’s being real with you," he continued. "And that makes people insane. And they start scratching, trying to find some real life. And sometimes people do that with drugs, some people do that with acting out or getting in fights or whatever the ways that people do it."
Hawke once referred to celebrity as a "poison." (Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for BFI)
Last year, fellow actor Dakota Johnson also ripped into Hollywood, calling the industry an absolute "mess."
During her appearance on the show "Hot Ones," Johnson was asked why "Hollywood is risk-averse."

"I think it’s hard when creative decisions are made by a committee, and it’s hard when creative decisions are made by people who don’t even really watch movies or know anything about them … that tends to be what’s occurring a lot," Johnson shared with host Sean Evans.
Johnson, who has grown up in the business as the daughter of actors Melanie Griffith and Don Johnson, is no stranger to the inner workings of Hollywood.
The "Fifty Shades of Grey" actress’ comments come as studios continue to create sequels and remakes, with original storytelling often sidelined.
Actress Dakota Johnson called Hollywood an absolute "mess." (Photo by Christopher Polk/CBS via Getty Images)

"When something does well … studios want to keep that going so they remake the same things," she claimed. "But humans don’t want that. They want fresh. They want to feel new things, experience new things, see new things."
She added, "So I don’t know, I guess it’s all just a bit of a mess right now, isn’t it?"

title: 'Jon & Kate Plus 8' star Collin Gosselin accuses mom of trying to 'bury' him to ‘protect her reputation’
summary: Collin Gosselin alleges Kate Gosselin tried to "bury" him to protect her reputation, detailing childhood abuse claims and demanding accountability.
story: ‘In the Shadow of Eight’ author tells Fox News Digital he's willing to hear from estranged mom Kate Gosselin but insists she must own up to her alleged treatment of him during childhood.

Collin Gosselin is taking aim at his estranged mother, Kate Gosselin, accusing the former reality TV star of trying to "bury" him to protect her public image as he makes allegations of childhood abuse in his new memoir, "In the Shadow of Eight."

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, the "Jon & Kate Plus 8" alum said he has not spoken to Kate since he was 13 and would need an apology and accountability before considering reconciliation.
"I'd like an apology, simply put, an apology and for her to admit, and just take accountability for what she did," Collin, 22, said.
COLLIN GOSSELIN SENDS CRYPTIC SIGNAL TO MOM KATE AFTER CLAIMS SHE'S 'SPIRALING' OVER HIS UPCOMING MEMOIR
Collin Gosselin claimed his mother, Kate Gosselin, had him institutionalized against his will. (Michael Simon)

"And to say, you know, 'I'm sorry that I've soiled your name, and I've made every effort to bury you, to protect my reputation,' I think that'd be very honest and very powerful for her to say that … just show accountability because everything she's done to protect her reputation, it's all been at my cost."

In his memoir, "In the Shadow of Eight: Surviving the Reality of My Childhood," Collin alleged he endured physical abuse, isolation and forced psychiatric medication as a child. He also compared his experience in a treatment facility to being sent to a juvenile detention center, saying it left lasting scars.
Kate continued filming with her children following her split from Jon Gosselin. (Donna Svennevik/Disney General Entertainment Content)
Kate recently spoke out for the first time following her estranged son's book release.

On Oct. 10, the former reality star posted a video on TikTok with an update about her dog. The video's comments section of the video was later filled with TikTok users discussing Collin's memoir. Over the following days, Kate responded to some select comments.

One commenter wrote, "I know you already know this, but you have the support of so many. Most importantly your seven precious children." Kate shares eight children with her ex-husband, Jon Gosselin. The TikTok user added that their feed was "flooded with such terrible lies. It should be illegal to defame someone that way, but I just wanted to say you are doing a great job keeping your head up through all of this. We love you!"
"I know rational logical ppl or anyone who has dealt with mental illness understands what’s going on here :)," Kate replied.
Kate Gosselin shared her first comments following the release of her son Collin's memoir. (Getty Images)

Kate also liked another comment in the thread that claimed "he will regret all of this someday" and alleged that he'd been "encouraged and enabled by other dysfunctional and mentally ill people." The commenter added, "I'm just sorry that you have to relive this over and over."
Kate later replied, "Exactly! I had nothing to do with it, except for consent because it was medically necessary."
Fox News Digital has reached out to Kate for comment.
Kate Gosselin shared her thoughts in the comments section of her TikTok video, which was an update on her dog. (David Buchan/Variety/Penske Media via Getty Images)

Collin’s memoir accused Kate of restraining him with zip ties, hitting him when he failed to perform for cameras and isolating him in the family’s basement. The mother and son had been estranged for years, and Collin eventually moved in with his father, Jon, after his parents’ 2009 divorce.
KATE GOSSELIN CALLED A 'MONSTER' IN SOCIAL MEDIA COMMENTS AFTER SON COLLIN ANNOUNCES MEMOIR
Meanwhile, Collin told Fox News Digital he held on to hope even during what he described as his darkest moments.
"I had very little hope, but I always had some, and I hung on to that … I just kept telling myself that there's a better future for me and there will be a time where I will be past this," he said.
The former child star said sharing his story had weighed on him for years before he finally decided to speak publicly.
WATCH: COLLIN GOSSELIN BLASTS MOM KATE FOR 'BURYING' HIM TO SAVE HER REPUTATION
"It was heavy on my heart, my whole life, but especially now, it was just, I just felt like it was the time to do that," he said.
The rift with Kate remains deep. Collin recalled a visit from his mother when he was 13, claiming the encounter left him with a painful final memory.
"She berated me for all of 20 minutes after not seeing me for over a year," he said.
KATE GOSSELIN DEFENDS HERSELF AGAINST SON COLLIN AS HE PREPARES TO RELEASE SHOCKING NEW MEMOIR
Collin Gosselin accuses his estranged mother, Kate Gosselin, of physical abuse, isolation and forcing him to take psychiatric medication during his childhood. (Getty Images)

Collin also described the effects of the psychiatric medication he said he was allegedly forced to take as a child, saying it left him feeling like a "zombie." In his memoir, he portrayed his childhood away from the cameras that made his family famous as deeply isolating.
WATCH: COLLIN GOSSELIN DETAILS ALLEGED ABUSE, CONFRONTS FAMILY TRAUMA
Despite the estrangement, Collin said he had not ruled out taking a call from Kate. But forgiveness, he stressed, would not automatically mean reconciliation.
"Reconciliation requires action and accountability," he said.

Former "Jon & Kate Plus 8" star Collin Gosselin alleges his mother, Kate Gosselin, tried to "bury" him to protect her public image. (Donna Svennevik/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images | Brad Barket/WireImage for Discovery Communications)

"I think we can all say, 'I'm sorry,' but if we're not willing to take the actions and take accountability for what has happened in the past and what happened my entire childhood, then what does that really mean, you know?"
Collin said he remains open to hearing from his mother, hoping she might acknowledge what he alleges happened during his childhood.

WATCH: COLLIN GOSSELIN RECLAIMS CONTROL OF HIS TV CAREER AS AN ADULT
"I think I'd take the call out of curiosity and just to hope that maybe she would admit to the things that she did to me when I was a child," he said.

Now, Collin is stepping back into the spotlight on his own terms as a contestant on the fifth season of FOX's "Special Forces: World's Toughest Test," a move he said carries special significance after growing up on reality television.
Contestant Collin Gosselin appears in Season Five of "Special Forces: World's Toughest Test," premiering Thursday, September 24, on Fox. (FOX TV)

"It was so powerful to be able to come back to TV on my own terms as an adult and rather than being a young child being pressured to perform on the daily," he said.
He also stressed that children should have a say in whether their lives are broadcast to the public.
Collin Gosselin opens up about his troubled childhood and strained relationship with his mother, Kate Gosselin, in his new memoir, "In the Shadow of Eight." (Michael Simon/Getty Images)

"When a child does not want to be on TV, that should be their decision to make. And we should let them make that decision," he said.

Collin and his seven siblings shot to fame on "Jon & Kate Plus 8," which chronicled Kate and Jon Gosselin raising their twin daughters, Mady and Cara, now 26, alongside sextuplets Collin, Alexis, Hannah, Aaden, Leah and Joel, now 22.

The series aired from 2007 to 2009 before returning as "Kate Plus 8" in 2010. After the couple divorced, Collin was institutionalized as a preteen before Jon was awarded custody and he moved in with his father.
Collin's memoir, "In the Shadow of Eight: Surviving the Reality of My Childhood," is out now.

title: Kelly Clarkson 'has put us in danger,' Brooklyn store owner claims as bird's price tag soars to $15M
summary: Adam Rubin claims Kelly Clarkson's viral dispute over a mechanical singing bird has led to threats and doxxing against his Brooklyn curiosity shop.
story: Jay Aldebert says Clarkson’s first step should have been to contact the store’s owner and try to resolve the issue privately. If the owner dismissed her concerns or was rude, he says, she could then consider using her social media platform.
Kelly Clarkson's public clash with a Brooklyn shop has left its owner concerned about more than a lost sale.

Adam Rubin, co-owner of Art of Play and a children’s author, spoke with Fox News Digital inside the Brooklyn store Tuesday morning, claiming the singer has put his business in danger after their viral dispute over a $15,000 mechanical singing bird.
The bird at the center of the controversy now has a staggering $15 million price tag.
KELLY CLARKSON SLAMS BROOKLYN STORE OVER ‘PRETTY WOMAN’ TREATMENT
Art of Play co-owner Adam Rubin poses with Molly, a mechanical singing and dancing bird that has become a fixture at the Brooklyn shop. (Fox News Digital)
"But I am afraid for the safety of our shop. Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger," Rubin told Fox News Digital.
Rubin claimed the backlash has extended beyond angry comments online, with people associated with the business allegedly facing threats and having their personal information exposed.
"We've got incredible support from our neighbors and fans over the past few days, and all of them have been attacked, threatened, doxed," he said.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Rubin also accused Clarkson of an "abuse of power," arguing that the singer's enormous platform has intensified the backlash against his small business.
Rubin argued that Clarkson's celebrity status carries a responsibility.
"You can't just try to squash somebody like a bug and expect everybody to give you a pass," he said.

Rubin also questioned why strangers would go to such lengths to attack a small business on behalf of a celebrity, expressing frustration that people who had never visited his store were joining the backlash.
The mechanical bird that sparked the dispute has also undergone a dramatic price change.
A photograph taken Tuesday by Fox News Digital shows a new sign beside Molly identifying the bird as a creation of artist Bliss Kolb, with an eye-popping price of $15 million.
Molly, a mechanical singing bird designed by Bliss Kolb, is displayed at Art of Play in Brooklyn alongside a $15 million price tag and a look at its intricate inner workings. (Fox News Digital)
The sign describes Molly as "The world's most famous singing bird automata!" and lists its price as "$15,000,000."
The new figure is 1,000 times the original $15,000 price at the center of Clarkson's complaint.

Art of Play previously explained in a public statement that the original $15,000 figure referred to a nearly identical automaton available from artist Bliss Kolb, while Molly herself is permanently attached to the wall and serves as a fixture in the store's magic performances.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Rubin also addressed the dramatic price change during his conversation with Fox News Digital, pointing to the attention Molly has received since Clarkson's visit.
He described the new figure as a matter of "supply and demand," while the store has maintained that the bird is not for sale.
Rubin suggested Molly's sudden notoriety has made her one of the most recognizable mechanical birds in the world.
The new sign offers a striking contrast to the original $15,000 price tag that Clarkson cited in her complaint.

The price change adds another twist to a dispute that began Saturday when Clarkson visited the Brooklyn shop and later accused an employee of treating her as though she couldn't afford its merchandise.
KELLY CLARKSON'S STORE CALLOUT SHOWS THE 'POWER' OF CELEBRITY STATEMENTS: EXPERT
Clarkson initially took to social media to describe what she considered a humiliating shopping experience, comparing her treatment to Julia Roberts' character in the 1990 film "Pretty Woman."

"Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," Clarkson wrote.
"Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale."
The singer later doubled down on her account after Art of Play disputed her version of events.
Clarkson maintained that she had pointed to a $15,000 price tag and was told the bird was available for purchase, but that an employee suggested finding her something comparable.
"So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar. Got it," Clarkson wrote in a follow-up post.
Art of Play has maintained that the encounter was a misunderstanding.
In its public response, the store explained that Molly is a permanent fixture in the shop and that employees had offered Clarkson the opportunity to purchase a similar bird from its creator.
KELLY CLARKSON SAYS 'AMERICAN IDOL' PRODUCERS 'LIED' ABOUT $1M PRIZE
Kelly Clarkson rose to fame after winning the inaugural season of "American Idol" in 2002 and has since built a successful career as a singer and television host. (Art Streiber/NBC via Getty Image)
The business also said another singing bird automaton, priced at approximately $2,000, was available.
For Rubin, however, the controversy has become much more personal than a disagreement over an unusual piece of merchandise.
During his conversation with Fox News Digital, the co-owner revealed that he had recently undergone a medical procedure and was not supposed to be working.
"I'm not even supposed to be here today. I got a cancer removed from my face last week," Rubin said.
"I'm getting the stitches out tonight."
Rubin said his concern about the store's safety was the reason he came in despite recovering from the procedure.
The co-owner also wanted to explain what Art of Play represents beyond the dispute that has suddenly brought it national attention.
"This is a curiosity shop," Rubin told Fox News Digital.
He described a business built around objects intended to inspire curiosity, including spinning tops, kaleidoscopes, puzzles, games and playing cards.
"And the reason this place exists is to make people feel like a kid again," Rubin said.

Kelly Clarkson is returning to "The Voice" as a coach for Season 30. (Trae Patton/NBC via Getty Images)
The business began online before operating a small location in San Diego. Rubin said the Brooklyn shop opened approximately two years ago.
Rubin, who is also a children's book author and magician, has spent years working in the world of illusion and performance.

The Brooklyn store also houses a small theater that hosts close-up magic performances, with Molly serving as the opening act, according to Rubin. Art of Play has previously maintained that the bird is permanently attached to the wall and was not available for purchase.
Despite the public dispute, Rubin said Clarkson would still be welcome back at the shop.
"We messaged her. I don't know if she saw it. I don't know if she cares," Rubin said.

title: Joe Manganiello's secret seven-year health battle that nearly killed him
summary: Joe Manganiello reveals Sofia Vergara made the life-saving call to remove his large intestine while he was unconscious during a secret health crisis.
story: ‘America’s Got Talent’ judge Heidi Klum tells Fox News Digital if she would ever set up Sofia Vergara on a date.
Joe Manganiello is opening up about the secret health battle that nearly "took his life" over seven years.
Manganiello sat down with "CBS Mornings" to discuss his health and his newly released memoir, "Bloodlines."
During his appearance, the actor told Gayle King he was offered the role as the main villain, Deathstroke, in Ben Affleck's canceled "Batman" movie.
He wrote in his memoir that, at the same time as the job offer, he was "dying." Manganiello received the call to appear in the movie in 2016.
Joe Manganiello had to have his entire large intestine removed to save his life in 2016. (Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

"I got the call about a month out of the hospital after I collapsed on another set," Manganiello told King. "After about a year of feeling these mystery symptoms, I went into the hospital for two months straight and, at the end of my stay, they wound up having to remove my entire large intestine to save my life.
JOE MANGANIELLO DENIES SOFIA VERGARA’S CLAIM MARRIAGE ENDED BECAUSE HE WANTED A BABY: ‘SIMPLY NOT TRUE’

"They had split me open. My entire large intestine had turned to pus, and it was about to explode," he continued. "They took it out, and the surgery left me with an ostomy bag. And in the wake of that, I lost 60 pounds in two weeks. I couldn't walk. My eye went cross-eyed. I lost my voice. I had five catheters."
"I went into the hospital for two months straight and, at the end of my stay, they wound up having to remove my entire large intestine to save my life."
Manganiello explained that, after he was released from the hospital, he was in the process of trying to gain the weight back when he got the call to meet Affleck and appear in the "Batman" movie.
The actor told King he was still married to Sofia Vergara at the time, and she was the one who ultimately made the decision for the doctors to save his life and remove his large intestine.
Sofia Vergara and Joe Manganiello were married from 2015-2023. (WireImage)

"They had to call her as my next of kin and give her options of what she thought I would want done to me while I was unconscious. She chose the right one, and it bought me time," Manganiello said. "It didn't solve the problem. The doctors still had no idea what was causing this, how to treat it. But it bought me enough time."
"But we do have to credit her for saving your life. For making that decision," King replied.
"Absolutely," Manganiello said.

King went on to cite Manganiello's memoir in which he wrote that his mystery illness put a strain on his marriage to Vergara. The former couple married in 2015 and announced their separation in 2023. Their divorce was finalized in 2024.
Joe Manganiello's "mystery illness" symptoms began shortly after he married Sofía Vergara. (FilmMagic)

"That kind of pain was like a flood in my life. You can't predict how that's going to affect people. It affected me a certain way, it affected her," he said. "It was seven years long. People didn't know about it. I was living in secret with this. Only the closest people around me knew."

King mentioned that Vergara's son, Manolo Gonzalez Vergara, 35, shared a post about a "narcissistic" man on Monday.
Sofia Vergara's son, Manolo Gonzalez, allegedly shared a post that compared qualities of narcissistic men. (Christopher Polk/Getty Images)

"Her son posted a thing about, ‘This is what happens when you deal with a narcissistic man,’ and she has liked that post," King began. "They appear to be saying that, basically, it’s terrible what happened to you, but the bottom line is that you’re a narcissist. What do you say to that?"
Joe Manganiello has released his new memoir. (Michael Simon)

Manganiello appeared a bit shocked before he replied, "Well, I think anybody who said that should read the book first and understand what the book is actually about because it’s not about that. It’s about the suffering I went through."

title: Billy Crystal says he no longer trusts God after losing home of 46 years then his longtime friend Rob Reiner
summary: Billy Crystal says he no longer trusts God after losing his Pacific Palisades home in the wildfires and the death of close friend Rob Reiner.
story: Legal expert Donna Rotunno analyzes Nick Reiner's probable cause hearing in the murder case of his parents, Rob and Michele Reiner, and explains the low legal standard required to advance the case to trial. Rotunno also discusses the defense's strategy to dismiss charges against the man accused of fatally mowing down NHL star Johnny Gaudreau and his brother, a complex issue involving blood plasma vs. whole blood testing.
Billy Crystal is opening up about how a devastating year changed his relationship with God.

During an interview with CBS Sunday Morning, the comedian, 78, opened up about how losing his longtime Pacific Palisades home in the January 2025 wildfires and the death of his close friend Rob Reiner greatly impacted his faith.

Crystal was asked whether he had been speaking with God after the painful losses. The actor referenced his previous one-man show, "700 Sundays," in which he described conversations with God, before offering a stark response.
BILLY CRYSTAL DESCRIBES PAIN OF LOSING HOME IN PALISADES FIRE AT FIREAID BENEFIT CONCERT: ‘FELL TO MY KNEES’
Billy Crystal says he no longer trusts God after a year of loss.  (Getty Images for Peabody Awards)
"No, ’cause I don’t trust Him," Crystal said.
"Too many bad things have happened," he added. "The Earth is in bad shape. This is a weird, scary time. So no, not anymore."

Crystal’s longtime home was destroyed in the Palisades fire after he and his wife, Janice, lived there for 46 years. The couple raised their children and grandchildren in the house, which Crystal described as a "magical place."
Speaking at a benefit weeks after the disaster, Crystal recalled visiting the remains of what was once his home.
ERIKA KIRK PENS ESSAY ON GRIEF AS READERS GAIN INSIGHTS INTO WRENCHING PAST YEAR

"When we were finally able to get back to our house in the Palisades, which I lived in for 46 years, like thousands of you, our house now looked like this," Crystal said, before a photo of the aftermath of the Palisades Fire appeared on the screen.
Billy Crystal lost his home of 46 years in the Pacific Palisades fire in 2025.  (Getty Images)

"I stepped onto the grounds and fell to my knees and I wailed. I had not cried like that since I was 15 years old, and I was told that my father had just died. I remember looking in the mirror back then with my whole life ahead of me thinking, ‘What’s my life gonna be like without him?'"
"And now folks, I'm 76-years-old, without a mirror and a lot less life to ponder thinking, ‘What is my life going to be like without our home?’" Crystal asked.

title: 'Moonshiners' stars challenge notorious warning that outlaw liquor can make you go blind
summary: Mark Ramsey and Digger Manes from "Moonshiners" challenge stereotypes about Appalachia's distillers as home distilling battles reach the Supreme Court.
story: Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes of "Moonshiners" discuss the history of Appalachian moonshining, its misunderstood reputation and why they believe the tradition will survive.
Moonshine’s reputation is enough to make your eyes water.

For generations, Americans have been warned that the notorious outlaw liquor could leave them blind. But "Moonshiners" stars Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes say there's more behind that warning than most people realize.
"There's a huge different thought process behind moonshine than there was, say, in the '40s, '30s, early years," Manes told Fox News Digital.
KENNY LAW, 'MOONSHINERS' STAR, DEAD AT 68

Mark Ramsey and his distilling partner Digger Manes are starring in the new season of Discovery Channel's "Moonshiners." New episodes air Tuesday nights at 8 p.m. on the Discovery Channel. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"There was a lot of propaganda out there. It was said that it could make you go blind, make you die, make you go crazy, make you get the jack leg. The government was the one that was poisoning the industrial alcohol the people were stealing to make bathtub gin."

Historical records support part of Manes' account. During Prohibition, the federal government required industrial alcohol to contain toxic additives to discourage people from drinking it, according to the Smithsonian Channel. Some of that alcohol was diverted into the illegal liquor market and sold for consumption, although it was distinct from traditionally distilled moonshine.
Mark Ramsey learned about producing moonshine as a young man. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

The consequences were deadly. According to the Smithsonian Channel, 66 people died in New York City on Christmas Day 1926 after consuming poisoned industrial alcohol. The city's medical examiner, Charles Norris, blamed the federal government's practice of adding toxic substances to industrial alcohol, including those involving methyl alcohol, also known as methanol, which can cause blindness and death.
WATCH: ‘MOONSHINERS’ STARS REVEAL THE TRUTH BEHIND A MISUNDERSTOOD TRADITION
But not every warning about illicit liquor was a scare tactic.
Ramsey acknowledged that moonshine posed genuine health risks in earlier generations, particularly when distillers unknowingly used dangerous materials to build their equipment.
Eric "Digger" Manes (pictured here) and Mark Ramsey have mastered the craft of distillation. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"Back in the day, there were people who had health issues because of moonshine," Ramsey explained. "The solder that they used to build the pots had lead in it back in the day, and they didn't know that it was happening. So once it was discovered that the solder had lead in it, even the old timers here, when they built their stills, they no longer soldered their joints on the inside of the pots. All the solder connections were on the outside where the mash never touched the solder anymore."

A moonshine still recently confiscated by the Internal Revenue Bureau is photographed at the Treasury Department between 1921 and 1932. A man stands next to the still and looks at the contents of a glass. (Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
"So yeah, it caused some issues, but it was strictly an accident," he said. "They just didn’t know any better."

While moonshine does not inherently cause blindness, improperly produced spirits can contain dangerous levels of methanol, a toxic form of alcohol. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that methanol poisoning can damage the optic nerve, causing permanent vision loss or death.
According to Discovery.com, "A dozen surviving moonshiners must join forces to fight for their way of life, before it's gone forever." (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"Moonshiners," which is now in its 16th season, premiered in 2011. The series follows "a diverse group of people living in Appalachia who carry on a 200-year-old tradition passed down from their forefathers, making moonshine," according to the show's synopsis.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Discovery Channel's "Moonshiners" has been airing since 2011. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

Distillers can legally produce and sell spirits marketed as moonshine if they comply with federal, state and local licensing, taxation and other requirements. Federal law generally prohibits producing distilled spirits at home for personal consumption, according to the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, although recent court rulings have challenged the constitutionality of certain restrictions.
According to The Washington Post, federal appeals courts have issued conflicting rulings on a federal restriction on home distilling dating back to 1868.
Mark Ramsey, Amanda Bryant, Kelly Williamson and Eric "Digger" Manes are seen here during the filming of "Moonshiners." (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

In April 2026, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a federal restriction prohibiting distilled spirits plants from operating in homes and certain other locations was unconstitutional. Days later, the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reached the opposite conclusion, upholding the restriction as a "necessary and proper means" of collecting liquor taxes, the outlet reported.
Barrels of moonshine age at Casey Jones Distillery in Hopkinsville, Kentucky., on Aug. 16, 2017. (Getty Images)

The Hobby Distillers Association and four individual plaintiffs challenged the restriction in the 5th Circuit case, according to The Washington Post. Supporters of legal home distilling hope overturning the restriction could spark a "craft spirits revolution."

The legal battle has since reached the Supreme Court. In July, John Ream, the plaintiff in the 6th Circuit case, asked the justices to review the ruling. The Justice Department filed a separate petition in August, seeking to overturn the 5th Circuit's decision.
Eric "Digger" Manes and Mark Ramsey are the faces of Sugarlands Distilling Company. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)
Ramsey also challenged longstanding stereotypes about "moonshiners."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Seth Powers, a production staffer at Maine Craft Distilling, boxes bottles of blueberry moonshine. The company is one of several distilleries and breweries to use Maine farm products. (Portland Press Herald via Getty Images)

"A lot of times, people give it a bad name because they just see it as poison and a bunch of heathens out doing stuff they shouldn’t do," he said. "And moonshiners, as a rule, are very, very good people. They were just simply doing what they had to do to survive back in the day."

"[Moonshine] didn't actually sell in Appalachia," Ramsey said. "It went farther north: Ohio, Detroit, New York, the East Coast. ... One of my friends told me ... he took a load of liquor to Ohio and said, 'Them fellas up there, they get it. And every one of them said, 'God bless them hillbillies.'"
Ole Smoky Tennessee Moonshine is seen here on Dec. 10, 2013, at The Garage by Kenneth Cole in New York City. (Getty Images)

"The liquor business back in the day, the heyday of it, probably wouldn't have flourished here in Appalachia so prominently had it not been for our northern neighbors buying it," Ramsey said. "So we had a reason to make it, and they had a reason to want it."
The launch of Original Moonshine at Morrison Hotel Gallery in New York City is seen here on Sept. 11, 2010. (Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
"We were broke, but could make liquor," Manes added. "And they had money and could buy it."
Ramsey is also optimistic about the future of moonshine. He said a new generation of distillers is eager to carry on the tradition.
Mark Ramsey and Eric "Digger" Manes told Fox News Digital that moonshine became increasingly popular up north. (Courtesy of Discovery Channel)

"As we saw in previous seasons … we always want to know who's going to fill our shoes, who's going to carry the torch forward," he said. "[And] we have so many good distillers up and coming. I think it's got a future, a very healthy one. Things will change. It's been argued that the best drink of liquor hasn't been made yet, so they've got something to shoot for."
