title: 'Helicopter brain' could be making you feel sick: How to spot it and what to do
summary: Doomscrolling is linked to higher anxiety and psychological distress, but a neurologist says it may also trigger what he calls "helicopter brain."
story: Board-certified neurologist Dr. Steven Resnick discusses how overstimulation can lead to the "helicopter brain" effect, which can manifest as physical symptoms, and shares how to reverse it.

A new analysis of 44 studies has linked "doomscrolling" to higher levels of anxiety and psychological distress — but for some, information overload may also contribute to a phenomenon one neurologist calls "helicopter brain."

The research, published in Frontiers in Psychology, found associations between excessive consumption of negative online content and poorer mental health, although it did not establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Board-certified neurologist Dr. Steven Resnick uses the term "helicopter brain" to describe a nervous system that remains constantly on high alert, much like a "helicopter parent" who constantly hovers over a child to protect them from harm.
FUNCTIONAL MEDICINE EXPERT WARNS EVERYDAY HABITS MAY ACCELERATE CELLULAR AGING

"Imagine your own helicopter — that is your nervous system," Resnick, chief of the Division of Neurology and medical director of the Comprehensive Stroke Center at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, Florida, told Fox News Digital. "Your nervous system’s job is to protect you from harm."
Information overload may also contribute to a phenomenon one neurologist calls "helicopter brain." (iStock)
Information overload, overstimulation and uncertainty can keep the brain on high alert, activating the autonomic nervous system, the neurologist said.
"The brain is scanning for danger," Resnick said. "When it scans for danger, then you have that autonomic nervous system pushing the accelerator."
NEARLY 3 IN 4 AMERICANS ARE BATTLING THE SAME EXHAUSTING HEALTH PROBLEM, CDC REVEALS

The neurologist, who also hosts "The Healthy Mind" podcast, said he often sees patients experiencing symptoms they struggle to explain, including headaches, gastrointestinal issues, fatigue, sleep problems, tingling and dizziness.
In some cases, patients undergo evaluations by multiple specialists before identifying a potential explanation.
"The brain is scanning for danger," the neurologist said. "When it scans for danger, then you have that autonomic nervous system pushing the accelerator." (iStock)
"They end up going to see a neurologist, who sends them to the gastroenterologist, who sends them to the cardiologist, then the rheumatologist," he said.
"They don't understand what they're feeling is actually authentic, it's real — it's the nervous system that is actually activated."
THINK YOUR CORTISOL IS TOO HIGH? EXPERT REVEALS THE TRUTH BEHIND VIRAL WELLNESS CRAZE
Although constant information overload can contribute to this heightened state of alertness, Resnick said the same patterns can emerge in response to everyday stressors and deeply ingrained habits.
The neurologist outlined the following five strategies for recognizing these patterns, calming the nervous system and developing healthier responses to stress.
No. 1: Recognize what you’re feeling
When seeing patients, Resnick said his first step is to listen to them, to ensure that he understands what they’re feeling.

"I hear patients say, ‘I'm scared, I'm fearful, I'm concerned, I'm worried,’ and then you start to realize what their nervous system is telling you," he told Fox News Digital. "I would never have done that by just fixing the problem right away."
When seeing patients, Resnick said his first step is to listen to them, to ensure that he understands what they’re feeling. (iStock)
The nervous system can begin to calm when patients feel truly heard, safe, secure and connected, the neurologist said.
"The solution can be done later," Resnick said. "And we have to stop using the word ‘fixing,’ because a lot of things cannot be fixed — but over time, you can start feeling better."
No. 2: Name the pattern
Recognizing recurring patterns — in thoughts, behaviors and reactions — is an important first step toward changing them, Resnick said.
"Mindfulness is not just about meditation; it's about noticing," he said.

That could mean recognizing the same conflict happening repeatedly with a co-worker, lying awake each night with racing thoughts, or turning to food or cigarettes during periods of stress, according to Resnick.
THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS
When those behaviors repeat, people can begin operating on "autopilot," he said.

"The brain wants to resort to what is familiar, what is safe and what is known," Resnick said. "It keeps going back to that because the brain understands it, retrieves it and does the same thing over and over again."
Breaking that cycle requires recognizing the pattern and making a conscious effort to respond differently, he added.
No. 3: Catch the trigger
Next, the neurologist said it’s important to "catch the cue," or trigger, that kick-starts the pattern.
"It's a stimulus," he said. "It's something that is very sneaky. It goes under your level of consciousness."
"It could be your boss' face. It could be a telephone. It could be a chair or a couch in a room. It could be a smell or a feeling."
The neurologist said it’s important to "catch the cue," or trigger, that kick-starts the pattern. (iStock)
That cue can trigger an almost automatic behavior, Resnick said, such as procrastinating, eating, reaching for a drink or lashing out.
If the behavior provides pleasure or helps someone avoid an uncomfortable feeling or situation, the brain can become more likely to repeat it.
Even worrying can become part of that cycle. If the feared outcome doesn’t happen, Resnick said, the brain may interpret the worry as protective, reinforcing the habit.
ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES
Breaking the pattern starts with identifying the specific cues that set it in motion, according to the neurologist.

Rather than viewing anxiety or overthinking as something that happens "all the time," Resnick encourages patients to pinpoint a specific episode, consider what triggered it and recognize the behavior and potential reward that followed.
No. 4: Reward the new habit
The next step is replacing the unwanted behavior with a healthier habit that provides a noticeable reward, Resnick said.
"Give your new habit a reward you can feel," he advised.
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID

That reward does not have to be significant. After an early-morning workout, for example, it might be a sense of accomplishment or an improved mood. A healthy shake after the workout could provide another small reward.
"Give your new habit a reward you can feel."
"Even checkboxing something on a piece of paper feels good," Resnick said.
These immediate, positive reinforcements can help the brain begin associating the healthier behavior with something rewarding.
"Rewards are very important," the neurologist said. "Even the small ones are important."
No. 5: Float instead of fight
Finally, when anxiety or panic strikes, Resnick recommends taking a counterintuitive approach: "Float instead of fight."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
In many cases, he said, people are not only afraid of a particular situation, but of the anxious feelings that may result.
Someone with claustrophobia, for example, may fear getting an MRI because they anticipate the physical sensations of anxiety that could arise inside the machine.
A person with claustrophobia may dread getting an MRI because they expect to experience anxiety-related physical sensations while inside the machine. (iStock)
"Don’t fight it," Resnick advised. "You want to allow it. You want to feel it."
Avoiding a situation can reinforce the brain’s perception that it poses a threat, he said, while safely experiencing it can help create a new association.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"After you have that experience where you felt safe, and you went toward it, then your brain and body … pair it as being safe," Resnick said.
The goal, he added, is "to teach the brain safety through your body and through your brain and mind."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
While these strategies may help people better manage stress and anxiety, Resnick emphasized the importance of recognizing the patterns behind the symptoms.
People experiencing persistent or unexplained physical symptoms should seek medical evaluation to rule out underlying health conditions.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: New belly fat injection cuts dangerous fat surrounding organs by 12% in early human trial
summary: CBL-514 injection triggers apoptosis only in fat cells to reduce visceral fat by 12% in early trials, with implications for insulin resistance.
story: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. cautions that the nature of GLP drugs means there might be unknown side effects in a ‘Saturday in America’ town hall.
Early human trials of an experimental injection called CBL-514 have shown the potential for reducing deadly visceral fat.
Visceral fat, which sits deep inside the abdomen wrapped around internal organs, affects metabolism and influences insulin resistance. It can impact the development of type 2 diabetes.
Research published in March by the American Heart Association found that visceral fat had a stronger association with the risk of heart failure than body mass index (BMI).
YOUR WAISTLINE COULD REVEAL A HIDDEN HEART RISK YOUR BMI MISSES, MAJOR STUDY FINDS

The trials tested whether the injection could diminish visceral fat deposits. They were conducted by Dr. W. Timothy Garvey of the University of Alabama at Birmingham and Yu-Fang Ling of Caliway Biopharmaceuticals in New Taipei City, Taiwan.
Previous phase 2 trials had already shown that the drug could reduce subcutaneous fat, the layer of fat directly beneath the skin.
An experimental injection called CBL-514 has been shown to reduce visceral fat in early human trials. (iStock)
MRI scans from two phase 2 trials exhibited a decrease in visceral fat in participants who received the CBL-514 drug, while the visceral fat increased in those who received a placebo drug.
Participants who were given CBL-514 received injections into their lower abdomen every three weeks for up to 12 weeks, with doses of up to 600 milligrams.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The number of injections given to participants depended on the thickness of their abdominal fat.
As the fat layer decreased in volume, the number of injections also decreased.
The amount of injections that participants received depended upon the thickness of their abdominal fat. (iStock)
The CBL-514 injection selectively sparks apoptosis — a process that causes cells to self-destruct — but only in fat cells, leaving nearby cells unharmed.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Four weeks after the final treatment, the average volume of fat had lowered by 12.01% in the group given CBL-514, while it had increased by 5.68% in the group that received a placebo, SciTechDaily reported.
Participants who were given CBL-514 received injections into their lower abdomen every three weeks for up to 12 weeks — with doses of up to 600 milligrams. (iStock)
The potential cosmetic effects, such as a flatter stomach due to subcutaneous fat loss, are appealing to patients, Garvey acknowledged.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

What’s even more important, he noted, however, is the decrease in body weight, improved blood pressure and cholesterol, and the loss of visceral fat that the injection can cause — as these factors impact overall health.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Liposuction, a common surgical cosmetic procedure, cannot remove visceral fat, and thus cannot reduce the health risks caused by a high amount of visceral fat.
Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Hidden clues could help predict a woman’s breast cancer risk years in advance
summary: An AI tool developed at NYU Langone Health analyzes years of 3D mammograms to predict breast cancer risk up to five years before a diagnosis.
story: AI technology is transforming breast cancer screening by assisting doctors in identifying women at higher risk years before cancer develops. Mount Sinai's Breast Surgery Director and author of 'The Breast Advice' Dr. Elisa Port highlights how AI uncovers hidden tumors and slashes false positive results, especially for women with dense breasts. This advancement aims to increase screening adherence among the 30-40% who currently don't get regular mammograms.
An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance, according to new research.

In a new study, published in the American Journal of Roentgenology, researchers at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center tested an AI model designed to estimate a woman's risk of developing breast cancer within five years.
The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time, rather than looking only at the latest scan, according to the researchers.
NEW ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TEST PREDICTS WHO IS LIKELY TO DEVELOP DEMENTIA IN 5 TO 10 YEARS
The model was developed using more than 313,000 mammograms from more than 161,000 women, according to the study.
An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance. (iStock)

Connie Lehman, a Massachusetts-based breast imaging specialist and professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital that AI could help identify women whose increased risk might otherwise go unnoticed.

"For decades, as a doctor and breast imaging specialist, I have cared for women who were shocked by a breast cancer diagnosis," Lehman said. "Again and again, I heard: 'How can this be? No one in my family has had breast cancer.'"
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Traditional risk assessments can consider factors such as family history and genetic mutations, while AI can look for additional clues within a woman's breast tissue, according to Lehman.
The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time. (iStock)
"A mammogram can tell us more than whether cancer is visible today — it can also provide information about a woman's risk of developing cancer in the years ahead," she said.
That information could eventually help doctors tailor breast cancer screening to a woman's individual risk, Lehman said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Women identified as being at increased risk could discuss additional screening, such as MRI, with their health care providers, while women at average risk may continue with routine mammograms, according to Lehman.
The technology could also analyze mammograms a woman has already had, meaning the added risk information would not require another imaging exam or additional radiation, she noted.
Traditional risk assessments can consider factors such as family history and genetic mutations, while AI can look for additional clues in a woman's breast tissue, experts say. (iStock)
Lehman cautioned that an AI risk score is not a cancer diagnosis and cannot predict with certainty whether a woman will develop the disease.

"A higher score can prompt a conversation with your health care provider about additional screening and risk-reduction options," she said. "A lower score does not eliminate risk or replace regular mammography."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The NYU model remains a research tool and is not FDA-authorized for clinical use, according to Lehman.
The researchers also noted that more testing is needed. The study used mammograms from NYU Langone hospitals and imaging equipment from one manufacturer.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The team plans to test the model using data from other medical centers and different 3D mammography systems, according to NYU Langone.
Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.
Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Silent inflammation could be damaging your body — and 5 habits may help keep it in check
summary: Jim LaValle reveals how the gut-immune-brain interface drives chronic inflammation, and why stress, blood sugar and environmental toxins play key roles.
story: Clinical pharmacist Jim LaValle breaks down how diet, stress, medications, blood sugar, environmental exposures and even overtraining may contribute to inflammation — and why the gut-brain connection matters.

Inflammation is a natural immune response that helps protect the body from injury and infection, but when it becomes chronic, it can pose a health threat, according to the National Institutes of Health.
Over time, chronic inflammation can contribute to rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease and cardiovascular disease.
Keeping the condition in check can help protect healthy tissues and support overall health, experts say.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS
Jim LaValle, a clinical pharmacist and metabolic medicine expert based in Texas, told Fox News Digital that inflammation can be influenced by a variety of factors beyond injury or infection.
Inflammation is a natural immune response that helps protect the body from injury and infection, but chronic inflammation can damage healthy tissues and contribute to serious diseases. (iStock)

LaValle first pointed to the gut-immune-brain connection — the communication between gut microbes, the immune system and the central nervous system — as one pathway that can influence the body's inflammatory response.
Beyond gut health, he said several everyday lifestyle factors can play a role in preventing chronic inflammation.
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
No. 1: Manage stress
Managing stress and anxiety can help support the gut-brain connection and keep inflammation in check, according to LaValle.
He pointed to cortisol, a hormone released in response to stress, which he said can "wreak havoc on your chemistry" when levels remain elevated.
Stress can "wreak havoc on your chemistry," the expert warned. (iStock)
Chronic stress can also affect the intestinal barrier, potentially allowing substances that would normally remain inside the gut to pass through more easily, LaValle said.
This increased intestinal permeability is sometimes called "leaky gut."
ZERO SUGAR, MORE PROBLEMS? STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING GUT HEALTH EFFECTS
"So, it turns out that if I'm stressed out a lot, I can be more prone to irritable bowel," LaValle said, as stress can trigger or worsen digestive symptoms in some people.
No. 2: Watch for food triggers
Diets high in sugar, fat and ultraprocessed foods can also affect gut health.
Paying attention to which foods trigger certain symptoms may help identify potential food sensitivities or intolerances, LaValle noted.
Paying attention to what kinds of food trigger certain reactions or sensitivities may help signal what is causing inflammation in the body. (iStock)
Symptoms such as bloating, rashes or discomfort after eating certain foods may signal a food-related reaction, although they can have other causes.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Certain medications, including antibiotics, may also alter the gut microbiome, but their effects vary depending on the drug and the individual, the expert said.
No. 3: Keep blood sugar in check
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is another important factor in managing inflammation, according to LaValle.
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is another important factor in managing inflammation. (iStock)
LaValle noted that conditions such as diabetes and insulin resistance are often associated with chronic inflammation.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Research suggests that GLP-1 medications, commonly prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity, may have anti-inflammatory effects, while scientists are investigating other potential benefits beyond weight loss and blood sugar control.
No. 4: Be aware of environmental exposures
The "exposome," or the environmental exposures people experience throughout their lives, can influence inflammation and the risk of chronic disease, according to the National Institutes of Health.
Microplastics could trigger inflammation signaling, according to the expert. (iStock)

LaValle pointed to emerging research on how environmental exposures — including "forever chemicals," microplastics, metals and pesticides — may affect weight, blood sugar regulation and other aspects of health.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"A lot of us don't think about that kind of impact on our health and how that could trigger inflammation signaling," he added.
No. 5: Don’t over-train
Regular exercise supports overall health, but intense workouts without adequate recovery time can put additional stress on the body, LaValle cautioned.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"You’re not getting a good enough recovery," he said. "You’re training hard. And, in fact, you might be training hard every day to lower that cortisol, but you're not getting good recovery. And that could lead to silent inflammatory signaling as well."
Anyone who is concerned about chronic inflammation or is experiencing persistent symptoms should consult a doctor to determine the underlying cause and appropriate treatment.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Stomach-turning sexually transmitted infection is on the rise, and standard medicines are failing
summary: Shigella bacteria are becoming harder to treat as drug-resistant strains rise, and doctors warn Americans should be concerned but not panicked.
story: Speaking to Fox News Digital, Lenox Hill Hospital internist Michael Aziz discusses the increase in antibiotic-resistant shigella cases and explains why patients experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms should seek medical attention before taking over-the-counter medications.
A highly contagious gut infection that can spread during sex is becoming harder to treat as antibiotic-resistant strains become more common.

An April report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tracked nearly 17,000 shigella samples, which causes shigellosis that can bring on diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps, collected between 2011 and 2023.

In 2023, 8.5% of shigella samples with resistance data were classified as extensively drug-resistant, or XDR — resistant to all five antibiotics in the CDC’s definition — compared with none from 2011 to 2015.
The findings point to a growing resistance problem, not a surge in overall infections, noted Dr. Tyler Evans, a California-based infectious disease physician and CEO of Wellness Equity Alliance.
HIGHLY CONTAGIOUS STOMACH BUG SPREADS FAST, HITTING CERTAIN PATIENTS HARDEST
"The infection is not surging. The bacteria are changing," Evans told Fox News Digital. "Case counts can hold steady while the treatment options quietly disappear."
The percentage of Shigella isolates classified as extensively drug-resistant rose to 8.5% in 2023, according to the CDC. (Leonie Asendorpf/picture alliance via Getty Images)
There is no FDA-approved oral antibiotic for XDR shigella, he said.
Shigella bacteria can spread when tiny amounts of stool reach someone's mouth, including through contaminated food or water, unwashed hands or sexual activity.
DANGEROUS DRUG-RESISTANT FUNGUS SPREADS ACROSS US, REACHING 27 STATES
"Shigella is not considered to be a typical sexually transmitted infection," Dr. Andi Toufexis, a Texas-based family medicine physician who specializes in sexual health, told Fox News Digital.
"However, this gastrointestinal bacteria can be spread through sex when one partner comes into contact with the other's fecal matter."
Most patients with extensively drug-resistant Shigella in the CDC analysis were adult men. (iStock)
Shigella is not new, and sexual transmission has been documented since the 1970s, Toufexis said. What is changing is the growing share of tested samples classified as XDR.
MICHIGAN REPORTS 2 DEATHS IN RARE PARASITE OUTBREAK THAT HAS SICKENED MORE THAN 11,000

The CDC report found that most people with XDR shigella were adult men. Sexual exposure data were not routinely collected, so the report could not establish exactly how each infection was contracted. But previous research has found sexual contact among men who have sex with men as an important transmission route.

Eighty-six percent of XDR patients were men with a median age of 41, and of those with a known HIV status, nearly half were living with HIV, Evans noted. People experiencing homelessness and those with weakened immune systems may also face heightened risks, he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Children younger than 5 are especially likely to get shigella, according to the CDC, and many outbreaks in the U.S. have been linked to childcare and schools. Earlier U.S. outbreaks primarily affected children and involved strains that were susceptible to antibiotics.
Washing hands before preparing food can help reduce the spread of Shigella.

According to the CDC report, 37.6% of patients with hospitalization data were hospitalized for the antibiotic-resistant infection. The CDC reported no deaths among the XDR cases analyzed and said infections may be undercounted because not all positive specimens were cultured or tested for resistance. Most patients with available travel histories reported no recent international travel, though travel information was missing for many.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Evans said Americans should be "concerned, not panicked" about the infection.
Most shigella infections resolve on their own, Toufexis added, but severe illness may need treatment.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Dr. Michael Aziz, an internist at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York City and author of "The Perfect 10 Diet" and "The Ageless Revolution," urged people who suspect shigella to seek medical advice before taking antidiarrheal medicine such as Imodium.
"You want to flush out the bacteria, you want to get it out of your system," Aziz told Fox News Digital.
Experts advise people with Shigella not to take antidiarrheal medicines such as Imodium, which can slow the gut.

To reduce the chance of infection, doctors recommend washing hands, genitals and the anal area before and after sex, using condoms or dental dams and cleaning sex toys after each use. If you or a partner has diarrhea, avoid sex and wait at least two weeks after symptoms end before resuming, Toufexis said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Feeling better does not always mean that an infection is completely gone," she said.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Biden judge rejects Obama CIA chief's legal bid against Trump over one key problem
summary: John Brennan's lawsuit against Trump and senior officials was dismissed, but grand jury investigations into the former CIA director continue.
story: Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, discusses how federal authorities are advancing the investigation into former CIA Director John Brennan on ‘Hannity.’

A Biden-appointed judge dismissed former CIA Director John Brennan's lawsuit against President Donald Trump and senior administration officials, ruling that his concerns about the potential destruction of evidence needed for a future criminal defense were too "speculative."

The dismissal comes as Brennan faces two federal investigations, including a Justice Department probe into whether former intelligence officials conspired to violate Trump's civil rights through investigations into alleged ties between his 2016 presidential campaign and Russia.

A separate investigation is examining whether Brennan made false statements during 2023 congressional testimony about the Steele dossier's role in a 2017 intelligence assessment of Russian interference in the presidential election.
FORMER CIA DIRECTOR BRENNAN SUBPOENAED TO TESTIFY IN FEDERAL TRUMP CONSPIRACY CASE

Trump has repeatedly accused Brennan, President Barack Obama and other former intelligence officials of orchestrating the "Russia collusion hoax," but they have rejected those accusations, claiming that the administration is attempting to discredit legitimate intelligence findings about Russian interference in the 2016 election.

While Judge Jia Cobb called Brennan’s allegations that the Trump administration was targeting him for opposing the president "deeply concerning," she ruled that he lacked standing to sue because he had not shown that officials were likely destroying records relevant to a potential defense, and the injury he feared depended on a series of events that had not yet occurred.

Former Director of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency John Brennan testifies before the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence on Capitol Hill May 23, 2017, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"For Brennan’s constitutional injury to actually accrue, a series of dominoes must fall, and Defendants’ deletion of records is just one of those dominoes," Cobb wrote. "There is no dispute about this: Defendants describe this domino chain in their motion to dismiss...and Brennan accepts it in his response."

Brennan has been identified as a target in two federal investigations that have involved three grand jury inquiries — two in the Southern District of Florida and one in Washington, D.C. — but he has not been charged with a crime. The former CIA director was subpoenaed to testify before a federal grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida, on Oct. 15, though his scheduled appearance was postponed.

Brennan filed his lawsuit naming Trump, FBI Director Kash Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche, CIA Director John Ratcliffe, and other officials on July 1, 2026. The 46-page lawsuit, accused the Justice Department of handling its investigation into Brennan with "unprecedented, irregular conduct" that was driven by the "president’s retribution agenda."
DELETED EMAIL DETAILS ALLEGED TRUMP-TARGETING PUSH INSIDE LETITIA JAMES’ OFFICE: ‘FIND AND PURSUE CRIMES’
Former President Barack Obama and former CIA director John Brennan in the East Room at the White House Jan. 7, 2013, in Washington, D.C. (Mark Wilson/Getty Images)

Brennan argued that key evidence could disappear before he had a chance to challenge any future indictment. He pointed to deleted social-media posts, the administration’s use of Signal and other messaging tools with auto-delete features, unpreserved texts and direct messages, AI queries, Microsoft Teams chats, and alleged failures to preserve discovery in other cases, including the prosecution of Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J. He said the loss of those records could make it harder to determine whether the investigations were based on legitimate law enforcement concerns or political retaliation.

"With this lawsuit, Director Brennan has served notice that the government’s conduct and its document preservation will be carefully scrutinized in the event of any future indictment. Director Brennan will continue to vigorously defend himself against these baseless investigations, and he will challenge any attempt to use the criminal justice system for personal and political retribution," Brennan’s lawyers, Ken Wainstein and Dan Gelber told the AP.
The lawsuit also pointed to what it described as irregularities in the Justice Department’s handling of the investigation.

It cited the removal of longtime DOJ prosecutor Maria Medetis Long, who was reportedly taken off the Brennan investigation in April 2026 after expressing doubts about the strength of the case, as evidence of what it described as irregular conduct. She was replaced by Trump ally Joseph diGenova, who later resigned from his role overseeing the investigation amid reported internal disagreements over the handling of the case.
President Donald Trump speaks during a Purple Heart Day event in the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., Aug. 7, 2025 (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
TRUMP SAYS HE WILL NOMINATE ACTING AG TODD BLANCHE TO PERMANENTLY LEAD JUSTICE DEPARTMENT

Brennan’s attorneys accused the Justice Department of "judge-shopping" by trying to steer grand jury proceedings toward Trump-appointed Judge Aileen Cannon in Fort Pierce, Florida, rather than allowing the case to proceed through the court's normal assignment process. They also questioned why prosecutors were pursuing the investigation in Florida when much of the allegations occurred in Washington, D.C.

The complaint also accused DOJ and FBI leaders of improperly discussing details of the investigations publicly, raising questions about whether officials disclosed information that should have remained confidential.It cited Attorney General Todd Blanche’s statements that DOJ had issued "200 grand jury subpoenas" and was investigating a "pattern of behavior" to "destroy" Trump, as well as FBI Director Kash Patel’s public discussion of the investigations and their targets.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: ‘Buck’ stops at Walz: Flanagan ducks Minnesota fraud blame as GOP rival exposes glaring contradiction
summary: Michele Tafoya, the Republican nominee, hammered Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan over Minnesota's $9 billion fraud scandal during their debate.
story: Minnesota Republican U.S. Senate nominee Michele Tafoya, in a Fox News Digital interview, targeted Democratic rival Peggy Flanagan's record and says voters are 'angry' over fraud scandals.

Michele Tafoya, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in Minnesota and a former broadcaster, aggressively sought to put her opponent, Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, on the defensive during a debate Friday afternoon over the billion-dollar fraud schemes that drew national attention to the state earlier this year.
Early in the debate, Tafoya pressed Flanagan on her qualifications for federal office, pointing to her record as lieutenant governor.

"My opponent has been second in command in this state for eight years, drawing a taxpayer-funded paycheck. And what do we have to show for that? We have massive fraud, historic fraud. We have test scores down. We have crime spiking. We have a massive surplus turned into a deficit," Tafoya said.
TAFOYA MAKES 'COMMON SENSE' PITCH TO DISAFFECTED DEMOCRATS AS SHE VOWS TO FIGHT MINNESOTA’S ‘SOCIALIST LURCH’
Michele Tafoya says Peggy Flanagan represents a shift toward "democrat socialism" in Minnesota. (Fox News Digital ; Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)
"This election is about Peggy Flanagan."

Local and federal investigators have uncovered myriad fraud schemes involving daycare centers, food programs, health clinics and other operations accused of defrauding the state of up to $9 billion. Investigators say fraudsters either inflated the number of people they allegedly helped or fabricated their services altogether — all while receiving government dollars.
When the issue resurfaced later in the debate, the moderator asked Flanagan directly whether, in her view, she had "any ownership over the fraud."
Flanagan sought to distance herself from the issue, pointing to Walz's acknowledgment that responsibility for oversight rested with him.
"The governor has been very clear that the buck stops with him," Flanagan said.

"He was the one who had oversight here. I've led on issues like paid family and medical leave, nation-leading child tax credit, making sure that kids get breakfast and lunch at school. Those are the things and those are the areas where I took the lead."
When Flanagan then redirected the conversation to criticism of President Donald Trump, Tafoya went on the attack.
DAVID MARCUS: PEGGY FLANAGAN'S DEI RECORD AND FRAUD SCANDAL PUT MINNESOTA SENATE RACE IN THE SPOTLIGHT
Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan visited a Somali market wearing a hijab in December alongside Nimco Ahmed, who runs an autism center that is now under investigation. (Somali TV Minnesota)

"Peggy, Donald Trump isn't on the ballot. You and I are on the ballot, and only one of us let $9 billion walk out the door to fraud to suggest that we that she somehow is going to be a fraud czar all of a sudden," Tafoya said.

"My goodness, she was second in charge in this state, and she's just going to point her finger at Gov. Tim Walz when she demanded to be in the room where everything happened. But, suddenly, she has nothing to do with this. Again, sell it to someone else," she added.

Flanagan has served as Minnesota's lieutenant governor for nearly eight years, taking office in 2019. By the time Walz announced that he would not run for re-election as governor amid political scrutiny for the fraud, Flanagan had already announced her bid for U.S. Senate.
Responding to Tafoya, Flanagan doubled down on her criticism of Trump, noting that the president had recently endorsed Tafoya.
"Donald Trump doesn't just endorse anybody. In fact, he endorses against people in his own party if they dare to take him on. Michele Tafoya passed his litmus test with flying colors," Flanagan said.
Tafoya then laid out her own proposals for combating fraud, including tougher consequences for noncitizens who defraud Americans.
"No. 1, if you're a guest of this country, and you defraud Americans, you must leave. You must leave, and you should have no pathway back," she said.
FRAUD EXPERT EXPOSES HOW HIDDEN NETWORKS DROVE MINNESOTA FRAUD, OTHER MAJOR SCAMS: 'CRIMINAL ENTERPRISE'
Michele Tafoya, a Republican candidate for U.S. Senate, votes in the primary election at Shepherd of the Hills Church in Edina, Minn., Aug. 11, 2026. (Leila Navidi/The Minnesota Star Tribune)
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
"No. 2, if you're an American and you defraud your fellow Americans, we should be talking about mandatory prison minimums. Tough sentences, not an easygoing slap on the wrist.

"And No. 3, if you're a state like Minnesota who cannot keep your financial house in order, why would the federal government release billions and billions of dollars to you, only to see it go to fraud?"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
After securing their respective parties’ nominations earlier this year, Flanagan and Tafoya will face off in the state’s Nov. 3 general election.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Trump's new press secretary out of the job just days after rocky debut
summary: Katie Zacharia has been fired as White House Press Secretary.
story: President Donald Trump speaks to press about Katie Zacharia's role as White House press secretary, saying he advised her to 'reconsider' the role.
Katie Zacharia is leaving her role as White House press secretary after only seven days following a rocky first week on the job, a source familiar confirmed to Fox News Digital.

President Donald Trump told Zacharia to "reconsider" the role, revealing to members of the press on the South Lawn on Friday that he told her: "You don't have to do this if you don't want to… I think you should reconsider."
A senior White House official tells Fox News that Katie is now "transitioning out" of the role.

It comes as her one-week tenure was marked by mounting scrutiny over her legal credentials and a rocky debut before the White House press corps on Tuesday.  Critics have taken aim at Zacharia over her recent interviews attempting to recover from the bumpy start.

Zacharia was named to the role Oct. 9 and stepped behind the White House podium for her first press briefing just days later on Oct. 13. The briefing lasted 14 minutes and Zacharia took only three questions.

White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia listens to President Donald Trump talk with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House before boarding Marine One en route to Alaska on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
"Maybe it’s not for her," Trump acknowledged in his brief remarks outside the White House on Friday.
TRUMP NAMES LEAVITT SUCCESSOR AFTER WEEKS OF SPECULATION — AND SHE'S NO STRANGER TO MAGA
When pressed if this update meant that Trump fired Zacharia, the president walked back. "No no. I want her to have a good life," he said.
"She’s been brutalized by the media," Trump added.

During an appearance on "Hannity" Thursday night, Zacharia was pressed over whether she could refer to herself as an attorney. Zacharia admitted she did not pass the bar exam and never obtained a law license in the United States.

"I had already pre-registered for the bar exam, and basically during the summer, I knew I would be living in China and the result of the bar would be inconsequential. I sat for it because I didn't want to have a withdraw status," she said.
WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS WIDELY PRAISE KAROLINE LEAVITT AS SHE ANNOUNCES EXIT FROM TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks to the media in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Tuesday, October. 13, 2026 in Washington, D.C. The briefing was Zacharia's first. (Samuel Corum/Pool/FTWP)
Zacharia was also pressed on her fumbled briefing.

"What I feel is I really stepped up to the plate with very little prep time," Zacharia said. "Given the fact that I'd been on the job less than maybe eight hours and had a briefing book in the morning, I feel like I did my very best, Sean, to deliver for the American people that day."

Zacharia's debut drew scrutiny over several verbal stumbles, including a moment when she mistakenly referred to her husband as "my president" before correcting herself, as well as the briefing's brevity, during which she took questions from just three journalists in 14 minutes.

Karoline Leavitt’s first White House press briefing lasted nearly 47 minutes, while Sean Spicer’s debut ran roughly 79 minutes. While Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ first briefing as press secretary lasted about 23 minutes in 2017.
TRUMP'S NEW PRESS SECRETARY FACES FIRST MAJOR TEST AS WHITE HOUSE BRIEFING ROOM ENTERS NEW ERA

A White House official told MS NOW earlier this week that she could end up with a shorter tenure than Anthony Scaramucci, whose notoriously brief stint as President Donald Trump's White House communications director lasted just 10 days before he was ousted in July 2017.
"Getting behind the podium is tough, but she got off on the wrong foot," the unnamed White House official said. "She needs to get much better, fast, otherwise she'll break Scaramucci's record."

Zacharia clearly did not recover enough in her short media sprint this week — where she attempted to clear up confusion about her lawyer credentials — and instead was pushed out of the job on Friday without another shot at the podium.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia arrives to a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C.  (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
The White House doubled down on supporting Zacharia Wednesday when asked by Fox News Digital for comment on the Scaramucci comparison reportedly coming from the White House.

"Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team. She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary," White House Communications Director Steven Cheung told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The White House X account @PressSec, formerly run by Leavitt before switching to White House Press Office, never switched over to Zacharia, and has still not posted since Oct. 7.

Zacharia, whom Trump described as an attorney when announcing her appointment, previously served as senior communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group, which operates the president's social media platform, Truth Social.
She also served earlier this year as deputy assistant secretary for public affairs and a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security for just six weeks.
Fox News' Peter Doocy contributed to this report.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Black civic group blasts Talarico campaign over canceled event: ‘Deeply disappointed’
summary: James Talarico faces frustration from Black voter groups over a canceled event and questions about whether his $25 million outreach pledge is real.
story: President Trump and Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton are raising questions about Democratic challenger James Talarico's whereabouts after the candidate has spent nearly two weeks away from the campaign trail.

Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico is facing lingering frustration from inside his own political backyard over the cancellation of an event that was supposed to take place on Oct. 5 with a Black civic-service group.

The Central Texas African American Civic Engagement Symposium (CT-AACES) expressed deep frustration in an email, sent to the Talarico campaign and obtained by Fox News Digital, after the campaign cancelled an event – which had 325 confirmed registrants – during Talarico's two-week absence from the campaign trail due to illness.
CT-AACES said the cancellation left them with "irrecoverable financial loss," and that Talarico's campaign had not engaged in rescheduling efforts

"While we understand Representative Talarico’s health required priority, we are deeply disappointed by the campaign’s decision to issue a flat cancellation rather than committing to a rescheduled date," the email reads. "It was a missed opportunity for Representative Talarico to directly address community skepticism and demonstrate the sincerity of his commitment to Central Texas African Americans."

The cancellation is the most recent instance of the tensions that Talarico's campaign has faced with the Black community. It also casts doubt on the effectiveness of his efforts to reach Black voteBlack voters through a $25 million outreach pledge aimed at mobilizing black voters is fully reaching the ground.
TALARICO DISAPPEARANCE HAS DEM VOLUNTEERS WORRYING AND TRUMP ASKING, 'WHAT IS GOING ON?'

State Representative James Talarico poses for a portrait at his campaign headquarters after launching his campaign for the seat currently held by Senator John Cornyn in Austin, Texas on Sept. 9, 2025. (Callaghan O'Hare for The Washington Post via Getty Images)
The frustration isn’t isolated to CT-AACES.

At least one Austin-area Democratic operative who has met directly with Talarico told Fox News Digital that she remains frustrated by what she described as uneven follow-through on outreach to Black Democrats and candidates further down the ballot.

"Black voters aren't a monolith," the source cautioned, rejecting any blanket assertion that Black Texans distrust Talarico outright. "I think that there are pockets that do. There's a pocket that doesn’t. And then there's the pocket that's really unsure," she said.
The operative is particularly familiar with the nominee and the Democratic organizing landscape in the Austin region.

Asked about a $25 million investment to focus on door-knocking in Black neighborhoods, in-person community events and engagement with Black churches, the source said those investments haven’t manifested yet.

"We haven't received the money, but we're being told it's coming," she said of some accounts she has heard from the ground. "We received, you know, one or 2% of what we were told we were going to get. And then it's been silence since," she said.
DAVID MARCUS: HOW CROCKETT'S LAST STAND IN TEXAS COULD BRING DOWN TALARICO

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a press conference at the Hyatt Centric Congress Avenue in Austin, Texas, on July 22, 2026. The discussion comes as data centers have emerged as a major political issue in Texas, with Gov. Greg Abbott calling for stronger oversight of their expansion. (Getty Images)

The comments come after Talarico appeared on a Black voter coalition Zoom last week, delivering brief remarks about "put[ting] in the money … time … and effort to win" before his feed disappeared from the call reportedly without a public question-and-answer session. At the July Houston town hall where Talarico announced the $25 million pledge, nurse Kandice Webber confronted him as the event approached its scheduled end and demanded that he remain to answer questions. "Black people don’t trust you for this reason," she said, according to the Texas Tribune .
"And you cannot win without us, so you stay here and you answer our questions, or you suffer the consequences," Webber said.

During his primary, Talarico also encountered controversy over the black vote when reports surfaced the he had characterized rival candidate and former NFL linebacker Collin Allred as a "mediocre Black man." "He had the audacity to say to a Black woman that he had signed up to run against a mediocre black man," Allred said in a video response posted to X.
"We should say ‘thank you.’ Thank you for taking off the mask. Thank you for telling us who you really are and what you really think… keep my name out of your mouth while you’re at it."

Talarico, for his part, described the wording as a mischaracterization, stating that he "described Congressman Allred’s method of campaigning as mediocre" and that he would "never attack him on the basis of race."
Talarico also received criticism from Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, his primary opponent in the Senate primary, after she accused him of darkening her skin in campaign ads against her.

"And you know, I've been asked a couple of times about it. And you know, I look at this specifically as a civil rights lawyer, and I see when they're sending out ads and they're darkening my skin. And I'm just like, I know what this is, right?" Crockett said at a press conference.

The operative said she personally pressed Talarico during a June meeting to do more to endorse and support down-ballot Democrats after hearing from campaigns that donors had already exhausted their political giving on his Senate bid and were asking whether he had endorsed those candidates.
FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON
Senate candidate James Talarico waves as he approaches a gas station in Carrollton, Texas, Saturday, September 26, 2026. (Anja Schlein/The Dallas Morning News via Getty Images)

"He was very gracious. He said he understood," she told Fox News Digital. "I followed up with his staff multiple times and to this day have still not heard anything, which has been really frustrating to me."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to the Talarico campaign for a response to the characterizations and comments.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Americans back Trump's decision against livestreaming Nidal Hasan's firing squad execution
summary: Trump canceled the Nidal Hasan firing squad execution livestream, but victims' families will still be able to witness the Fort Hood shooter's scheduled death.
story: Americans are backing President Donald Trump's announcement that Nidal Hasan's execution will not be publicly livestreamed. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Americans interviewed by Fox News Digital were overwhelmingly pleased with President Donald Trump's decision to call off livestreaming the Fort Hood shooter’s planned firing squad execution after the Pentagon had announced it would be livestreamed for public viewing.

"I'm really glad that he called it off, because I feel like it's not really a deterrent, it's more like a shock effect," Sylvia from Arizona told Fox News Digital. "I don't think we really need that in this country right now."
"The only other countries that really do that are like North Korea," David from Arizona said. "We don't want to be North Korea."
AMERICANS DRAW THE LINE AT LIVESTREAMING ‘SPECTACLE’ OF FORT HOOD SHOOTER'S EXECUTION: ‘IT’S AN ABOMINATION’
President Donald Trump and North Korea's leader Kim Jong-un talk before a meeting in the Demilitarized Zone on June 30, 2019, in Panmunjom, Korea. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)
"I never approved of the idea of it being public in the first place," Nate from Virginia said. "I think it's just ridiculous to make a spectacle out of an execution, especially in 2026 of all time."
War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced earlier this month that Nidal Hasan’s execution, set for Dec. 3, would be publicly available via livestream.

Trump took to Truth Social on Thursday to announce that while livestreaming the execution could serve as a deterrent to terrorism, the execution would not be available for public viewing as he acknowledged that many Americans would rather not witness Hasan's death.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
FORT HOOD SURVIVORS PRAISE TRUMP FOR SCRAPPING HASAN EXECUTION LIVESTREAM: ‘WE’RE NOT BARBARIC’

President Donald Trump announced that the execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan would not be livestreamed, reversing an earlier Pentagon announcement that the execution would be livestreamed to the public. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images; Bell County Sheriff's Office via Getty Images)

Despite the execution not being publicly available, Trump confirmed that the family members of the victims who died in the 2009 shooting "deserve to witness JUSTICE" and will be permitted to attend in person.
"Well, maybe he has a conscience now," one person said about Trump’s reversal of the Pentagon’s decision to livestream the execution.

Some Americans who spoke with Fox News Digital argued that Trump’s decision to call off the livestreaming was to save face after criticism of the proposal was circulating, with many arguing that livestreaming the execution would turn it into a spectacle and could easily be exposed to children.
"I think it was trying to save his image," Ivy from Georgia said.
"He doesn't wanna look like a bad person, but at the end of the day, we all know who he really is — a piece of s---," Ivy said.
"I think it was just so clearly an unpopular thing to do that he realized it would probably do more harm to his public image than good," Nate said.

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist at the time of the shooting, killed 13 and injured 32 people when he shouted "Allahu Akbar" and opened fire at a military base in Texas. The mass killer is now 56 years old and uses a wheelchair after he was left partially paralyzed from being shot by police officers during his arrest almost 17 years ago.
TRUMP CLEARS WAY FOR FORT HOOD TERRORIST TO FACE ARMY FIRING SQUAD NEARLY 17 YEARS AFTER MASSACRE

Major Nidal Malik Hasan, the U.S. Army doctor identified by authorities as the mass shooter at the U.S. Army post in Fort Hood, Texas, is seen in this undated handout photo from a PDF file of the U.S. Government Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences downloaded on Nov. 6, 2009. (Reuters/Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences/Handout)
Only one person who spoke with Fox News Digital argued that livestreaming the execution would have been a good idea, even adding that he would have watched the livestream himself.
"Yeah, I would watch," Daniel from Virginia said. "Because I wouldn't want somebody to kill another person, you know what I mean? That person should be held wrong for what he's done."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Hasan was sentenced to death during his 2013 military trial after being found guilty on all 42 counts. His execution is set to be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Ilhan Omar's sister skips book tour event amid week of chaos following raid on progressive's DC home
summary: Sahra Noor skipped a scheduled book tour event in Rochester, Minnesota, after reportedly being subpoenaed in the Ilhan Omar immigration fraud probe.
story: Rep. Ilhan Omar's, D-Minn., husband, Tim Mynett, defends her immigration timeline outside their DC residence that Homeland Security Investigations raided on Monday amid a criminal fraud investigation. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

ROCHESTER, Minn. — The older sister of embattled Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., who is currently on a book tour promoting a memoir about her life as a Somali immigrant, skipped a scheduled event due to a "family emergency" amid the fallout from the raid on the congresswoman's home.

As Omar faces a federal government probe related to potential immigration fraud as well as a separate investigation into her financial disclosures, Sahra Noor was scheduled for a book tour stop at the University of Minnesota Rochester on Thursday night.

Noor, who came to the United States as a refugee alongside Omar and other family members in the 1990s, was reportedly subpoenaed in relation to the immigration investigation into her sister. She currently lives in Nairobi, Kenya, according to her LinkedIn page, but is on a worldwide book tour promoting her recently-released "Salt in the Snow: A Somali Immigrant Story."

Ilhan Omar wearing a patterned hijab and green scarf. (L) Sahra Noor, sister of Ilhan Omar, speaking at an event at the University of Minnesota in 2016. (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images; University of Minnesota)
ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION
Fox News Digital reached out to Noor for comment but did not hear back at time of publication.

According to a flyer, which was posted on Facebook by Rochester-based bookstore Garden Party Books, the event was scheduled for Thursday night at 6:30 p.m. It was set to be held at the Intercultural Student Center at the University of Minnesota Rochester.

When Fox News Digital arrived for the event, the space was completely empty. Fox News Digital had previously RSVP'd for the event via a QR code on the flyer and did not receive any communication that the event had been canceled, rescheduled or relocated.
Garden Party Books told Fox News Digital the event was canceled due to a Noor "family emergency."

The Intercultural Student Center at the University of Minnesota, Rochester, Minnesota, Thursday, October 14, 2026. Sahra Noor, sister of Rep. Ilhan  Omar, was scheduled to discuss her memoir, Salt in the Snow at this location but for an undisclosed reason the event was canceled without warning. (Obtained by Fox News Digital)

Noor's absence from the book tour stop comes amid rumors that Omar fled the United States following the raid earlier this week. While the congresswoman has not been seen in public since Monday's raid, her husband snapped when asked outside the home on Wednesday whether he had a response to the rumors that she fled the country.
The flyer said that Garden Party Books, along with the University of Minnesota Bookstores and the Rochester Public Library, were "proud supporters" of the event.
It also described Noor as a "poet, storyteller and health system leader," and said the book is a "story of migration, motherhood, grief and family."

According to Noor's website, her book was officially launched during an event in a Nairobi bookstore on Aug. 13, 2026. She appeared in early September at a festival in Cape Town, South Africa to promote her work.
OMAR RAID DRAWS OMINOUS WARNING FROM VANCE AS HE BLASTS PROGRESSIVE REP'S 'RAGE' TOWARD AMERICA

Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)

Now, she is touring in the United States. Noor held an Oct. 1 event in Minneapolis, and another five days later at the University of Minnesota. She hosted an event in St. Paul, Minnesota on Oct. 7. Her next scheduled event is at the Somali Community Cultural Innovation Hub in Seattle on Oct. 23.

Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the leading investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), executed a search warrant on Omar's home starting at around 6:00 a.m. on Monday morning.
ILHAN OMAR'S HUSBAND SNAPS OVER RUMORS SHE FLED US AFTER FEDERAL IMMIGRATION FRAUD RAID
Fox News Digital first reported Monday that the raid stems from an investigation into whether Omar or her late father, Nur Mohamed, fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork decades ago.
The investigation, two sources noted, could lead to the congresswoman's denaturalization.
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) on October 12, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Omar's phone, passport and computers were seized in the raid.
Omar has described the search as an "outrageous abuse of power" and called it an "unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Democrats call for gun control after Oregon school shooter reportedly uses shotgun purchased by his mother
summary: A 16-year-old gunman broke into Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, killing three children and a teacher before an armed bystander intervened.
story: Retired FBI agent Jason Pack breaks down the tragic school shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon. Police Chief Mike Krantz confirms that three children and one teacher were killed. Pack details how a bystander ultimately shot and killed the suspected teen gunman, preventing further loss of life inside the locked building.

Several high-profile Democratic lawmakers renewed calls for gun control after a teenager broke into an Oregon elementary school Thursday and fatally shot three children and a teacher before being killed by an armed bystander.

Sen. Ron Wyden, who has represented Oregon in the Senate since 1996, made one of the most explicit calls for tighter gun laws following the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, where the 16-year-old attacker used his mother’s shotgun, according to The Associated Press.

"The best way to honor these victims is to at long last pass common-sense gun laws that reduce the risks of more children, parents, teachers and staff forced to live in fear of similar nightmares for their schools," Wyden said in a statement.
Suzanne Bonamici, D-Ore., said Thursday night that "the epidemic of gun violence in schools across America must come to an end."
U.S. Senator Ron Wyden speaks at the rally to Say NO to Tax Breaks for Billionaires & Corporations at the U.S. Capitol on April 10, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images)
GEORGIA HIGH SCHOOL SHOOTING SUSPECT COLT GRAY CHANGES PLEA TO GUILTY, NOW FACES LIFE IN PRISON
"No parent should have to wonder if their child will come home at the end of the day," Bonamici said. "Children deserve to feel safe — and be safe — in school."

Democratic Rep. Janelle Bynum represents Oregon’s 5th Congressional District, which includes Bend. She attended a nighttime vigil for the teacher and children — aged 5, 8 and 11 — who were killed in the shooting.

"When are we going to step up and say enough of killing our babies? When are we going to say that we need safe schools, that we need to make sure that people who should not have firearms don’t have them? When are we going to stop making excuses? When are we going to practice that same bravery that that bystander had?" Bynum told KTVZ 21, a local NBC station in Bend, at the event.

Statements from Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and the state's Democratic governor, Tina Kotek, stopped short of calling for new regulation on guns, but both made it clear gun violence should have no place in American schools.

Rep. Janelle Bynum, D-Ore., seen on Nov. 15, 2024, also said more needs to be done about gun violence following the shooting at the elementary school, which is in her congressional district. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
FEDERAL APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS CONTROVERSIAL ILLINOIS BAN ON SEMIAUTOMATIC GUNS

Democrats outside of Oregon appeared a bit freer to express support for going further on gun control, especially in the early aftermath of the shooting, which also left another child, 7, and a teacher, 54, critically injured.
Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., said the gun reforms Congress passed after the Uvalde school shooting — including enhanced background checks for buyers under 21 — did not go far enough.
"Much more must be done. Not a single child should be lost to gun violence. Ever," Heinrich said in a statement posted to social media.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who supports federal red-flag laws and universal background checks, had a similar message.
"No family should ever have to suffer like this—and there have been over 50 school shootings just this year," she wrote on social media. "Congress must do much more to prevent gun violence."
People leave a family meeting area following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15, 2026, in Bend, Oregon. (AP Photo/Joe Kline)
DOJ TARGETS SPANBERGER, NEWSOM GUN LAWS WITH TWIN LAWSUITS AFTER SCOTUS AFFIRMS SECOND AMENDMENT RIGHTS
The reactions from lawmakers came as authorities in Bend continue to piece together how the deadly attack unfolded and how the teenage gunman obtained the weapon he used.
Police said they did not know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or if he had attended when he was younger.

The first emergency call came at 12:59 p.m. from a person in a vehicle who reported being shot at multiple times by someone carrying a long gun, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said Thursday. Dispatchers then received dozens of calls reporting that a shooter had entered the school.
Officers arrived within three minutes of the first emergency call. Moments later, an officer reported that a "community member" had shot the teenage suspect.
School buses are lined up outside Silver Rail Elementary School, where a shooting took place, on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 in Bend, Ore. (Joe Kline/AP Photo)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Silver Rail Elementary School, which is about 125 miles southeast of Portland, has a total of 467 students this academic year. It serves students in kindergarten through fifth grade.

After the shooting, students were bused to a nearby church that served as a family reunification center, where relieved parents embraced their children and walked them to their cars, some carrying stuffed animals and other comfort items they had brought from home, The Associated Press reported.
The Bend-La Pine school district canceled classes, sporting events and extracurricular activities Friday across all 32 of its schools.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Trump's Capitol Hill whisperer reveals secrets to president's dealmaking as he heads for exit
summary: James Braid spoke with Fox News Digital about his work the last two years on his way out of the Trump administration.
story: ‘The Five’ co-hosts discuss President Donald Trump campaigning across multiple states in the final stretch before the 2026 midterm elections.
EXCLUSIVE: There are few people in the United States who have more significantly shaped the course of American history over the last two years, while remaining as little-known as James Braid.

Millions of Americans across the country may not be familiar with the name, but in Washington, D.C., Braid is hard to miss both literally and figuratively. At 6 feet, 6 inches tall, he cast a tall shadow during his days at the White House and on Capitol Hill pushing President Donald Trump’s legislative agenda.

And that shadow has been responsible for helping push numerous legislative successes for Trump over the finish line, from rolling back Biden-era policies to passing Trump’s signature tax policy bill, until Tuesday — which marked Braid’s last day as director of the Office of Legislative Affairs. The "stock-in-trade" of the job, he told Fox News Digital in a rare interview, "is cautious optimism in the face of all odds."

From the outside, being Trump’s whisperer on Capitol Hill does not look like an easy job, particularly when the president is known to personally call out lawmakers who oppose his agenda. Recently, for example, he publicized the personal phone number of Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., over his opposition to a bill making daylight saving time permanent.
James Braid, Rep. Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and an aide stand before President Donald Trump at the White House. (White House)
TRUMP DROPS REPUBLICAN SENATOR'S PHONE NUMBER IN SOCIAL POST OVER FURY ON STALLED BILL

But Braid insisted that Trump’s people skills ultimately meant those dust-ups came out of the wash and lauded "his extraordinary capacity to have a tough conversation one day and play a round of golf the next."

"There's always a give-and-take in any relationship with a legislator, and sometimes there's a give as a result of, you know, tension," Braid said. "But you know … one errant Truth [Social post], or one critical Truth, does not a relationship make."
But some Republicans’ relationships with the president never seemed to recover, like in the case of Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., who has no love lost with Trump.
Braid said the key to working with people was always being straightforward about what the White House wants.
"We've been able to be honest brokers and deliver for a lot of these members in different ways," he said.
But Trump’s presence still looms large in Congress whether he’s there in person or not.
A senior administration official familiar with Braid’s work told Fox News Digital that ultimately, "No one speaks for President Trump except for President Trump."
The official said Trump is known to be "hands-on at every critical legislative juncture" that pushes his agenda forward.
And Braid revealed that he keeps tabs on certain votes, as well.

"He always wants to know how people are voting after every major vote. He knows where people are," Braid said, adding that Trump "ultimately knows that Republicans in Congress overwhelmingly vote with him."
But Braid admitted he has faced long odds over his last two years, particularly with the vast tax-and-policy package nicknamed the Big, Beautiful Bill.
MILLIONS TAP TRUMP TAX CUTS THIS FILING SEASON AS REFUNDS TOP $3,400

House Ways & Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., Rep. Nick Langworthy, House Energy & Commerce Committee Chairman Brett Guthrie, R-Ky., Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., James Braid and House Financial Services Committee Chairman French Hill, R-Ark., stand before President Donald Trump. (White House)

He recalled sitting in his office one day, "I looked at the quad on the TV, and every single chyron is some variation of ‘GOP megabill in trouble.’ And yeah, I mean, there's certainly, at every moment, it was tenuous. At every moment, the thread was fraying."

One specific scenario he recalled took place at Sterling Golf Club in Virginia, where he, Trump, Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought and then-deputy chief of staff James Blair were meeting with Senate Republican holdouts on the legislation.
GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US'

"We're sitting there with [Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky.], [Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.], [Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla.], me, Blair, Russ and the president, and they're bringing out these heaps of food," Braid recalled. "I think there's something like four pizzas on the table and maybe 22 hot dogs for five guys, none of them were eating. And it's just, I mean, we, I think we argued about the administration's overall funding strategy for two hours as the afternoon wore on."
Ultimately, however, the bill passed the House and Senate — for which Braid credited both administration officials and congressional leaders.
"The level of commitment that was there and present from the leadership across the Republican Party to get this thing done, basically willed it into being," he said.
James Braid stands alongside Secretary of War Pete Hegseth inside the White House. (White House)

He referenced the day Trump signed the bill when asked about his best day on the job over the last two years: "I would say July 4th in the White House with my son and the speaker of the House in the summer sunshine, watching the president sign the most significant piece of Republican domestic policy legislation."
Top congressional leaders hailed Braid as a critical champion of the GOP agenda.

"James is a total pro and one of House Republicans’ greatest teammates," House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., said. "He took the time to get to know our members and master the unique dynamics of the House Republican Conference."
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., called Braid a "tremendous partner" for his conference.
"I’m grateful for his dedicated service to our country, and I wish him and his family all the best with their next chapter," Thune said.
Vought called Braid a "lion for the president in delivering his agenda on the Hill."

And Vice President JD Vance, who hired Braid as his legislative director before both ascended to the White House, told Fox News Digital that he is "incredibly brilliant, effective and a hard worker without compare."

"He has been with me since the start of my Senate term, where he was with me for every fight and brought his talents to the president’s second term, where he has played a central role in every single policy effort since," Vance said.

James Braid, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, chief of staff Susie Wiles, and White House aide Natalie Harp look on at President Donald Trump in the Oval Office. (White House)

Now that he is departing, the senior administration official who spoke with Fox News Digital said they expect Braid to find work outside the government after years of grinding on Capitol Hill and the White House.

As for Braid, he said of his next move, "It's hard for me to even think about not doing this job, but at the end of the day, I know [Katie Bailey is] going to do great … but yeah, I'll take a little time and try to figure out what's next."
Bailey, Braid's former deputy director of the Office of Legislative Affairs, is now taking over the job.
He summed up his advice to his successor in two bullet points.

"Number one, you have to be ruthless in what you're focused on and tune out the distractions to get the issue of the day over the line and onto the president's desk," he said. "Number two, invariably, the situation feels pretty grave, but usually we muddle through, and to remain optimistic."
