The technology, he said, is intended to make troops more capable, but soldiers must remain grounded in the fundamental skills needed to fight without it.

title: Trump-appointed justice joins Sotomayor in unlikely alliance to rip DOJ's handling of illegal immigrant case
summary: Supreme Court Justices Neil Gorsuch and Sonia Sotomayor joined forces after prosecutors charged a deported man despite ordering him to stay in Oklahoma after his first conviction.
story: Supreme Court justices will begin hearing oral arguments Monday on a wide range of cases this term involving gun rights, religious freedom, immigration detention and the limits of government power.

Conservative Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch has joined forces with liberal Justice Sonia Sotomayor to question the federal government's prosecution of an illegal immigrant, marking the latest unlikely alliance between the two justices.

Gorsuch, appointed by President Donald Trump, and Sotomayor, appointed by former President Barack Obama, raised concerns about the government's decision to prosecute a Mexican national twice for being found unlawfully in the United States — even after a federal court prohibited him from leaving the Eastern District of Oklahoma following his first conviction.

The unlikely pairing emerged Tuesday when the Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal from Jesus Herrera-Salazar, who argued that his second prosecution violated the Fifth Amendment's protection against double jeopardy. Although the justices agreed the Court should not take up the case, Sotomayor issued a separate statement, joined by Gorsuch, warning of serious constitutional problems with the government's actions.
GORSUCH SAYS IDEOLOGICAL DIVIDES ON SUPREME COURT COME DOWN TO ‘HOW YOU READ LAW,’ NOT POLITICS

Supreme Court Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Neil Gorsuch issued a joint statement this week questioning the federal government's prosecution of an illegal immigrant, marking the latest in a series of unusual constitutional alliances between the two justices. (Getty Images)

"From the moment he was released from custody after serving his first term of imprisonment, Herrera-Salazar was presented with a Hobson's choice," Sotomayor wrote in the statement joined by Gorsuch. "In the Government's eyes, whether Herrera-Salazar remained in the Eastern District of Oklahoma or left the United States, he would be breaking the law."

The two justices questioned how the government could punish someone for remaining in the country after effectively prohibiting him from leaving, with the pair's joint statement describing the situation as a "constitutional absurdity."

Their agreement is particularly noteworthy given their differing judicial philosophies, but it is not the first time the pair has found common ground over constitutional protections against government action.

In November 2024, Sotomayor and Gorsuch jointly questioned whether homeowners should be compensated when police destroy private property while carrying out law enforcement operations. A few months later, they again joined forces to raise concerns about warrantless misdemeanor arrests. In both cases, as in the latest immigration dispute, the Court declined to hear the appeals, but the justices issued statements highlighting constitutional questions they believed deserved attention.
The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to continue third-country deportations while the justices consider a legal challenge to the policy. (Getty Images)

The pair's latest expression of joint public concern came after Herrera-Salazar, a Mexican national previously removed from the United States, was indicted in 2020 for being found in the country following deportation, a violation of federal immigration law.
'UNPRECEDENTED': JUDGES REVEAL BEHIND-THE-SCENES COORDINATION ON TRUMP IMMIGRATION CASES

He pleaded guilty and served a prison sentence before being placed on supervised release, during which he was expressly prohibited from leaving the Eastern District of Oklahoma without authorization under the terms of his release.

While still under those restrictions, Herrera-Salazar was stopped by police in Heavener, Oklahoma, and subsequently charged again under the same federal immigration statute prohibiting previously deported individuals from being found unlawfully in the United States. A jury subsequently convicted Herrera-Salazar, resulting in another prison sentence and additional supervised release.

The second prosecution prompted Herrera-Salazar to challenge his conviction on double-jeopardy grounds, arguing that the government had effectively punished him twice for the same continuous period of unlawful presence.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected that argument, concluding that the offense is completed when authorities discover a person's unlawful presence and that a subsequent discovery can support a separate prosecution without requiring another illegal entry.
Federal immigration agents arrest a man in the parking lot of an H-Mart grocery store on October 31, 2025, in Niles, Illinois. (Photo by Jamie Kelter Davis/Getty Images)

Sotomayor and Gorsuch questioned that reasoning, pointing to Supreme Court precedent establishing that prosecutors cannot evade double-jeopardy protections simply by dividing one continuous crime into separate periods. Their concern was not whether Herrera-Salazar had violated immigration law in the first place, but whether the government could repeatedly prosecute him for remaining in the United States without evidence of a separate unlawful reentry.

The justices also highlighted that Herrera-Salazar's supervised-release conditions restricted him from leaving Oklahoma, meaning the government was effectively preventing him from ending the conduct for which it later prosecuted him again. Sotomayor warned that, under the government's interpretation, prosecutors theoretically could have brought separate charges against Herrera-Salazar for each day he remained imprisoned following his first conviction.

The statement was issued despite the justices' agreement with the Court's decision not to review the case. Sotomayor explained that Herrera-Salazar had already been removed from the United States and expressed hope that the unusual circumstances surrounding his prosecution would not arise again.
SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE

Rather than dissenting from the Court's refusal to hear the appeal, Sotomayor and Gorsuch used what is formally known as a statement "respecting the denial of certiorari" to publicly identify constitutional concerns and urge lower courts to avoid similar problems in future cases.

Members of the Supreme Court pose for a group photo at the Supreme Court on Oct. 7, 2022. Seated from left: Associate Justice Sonia Sotomayor, Associate Justice Clarence Thomas, Chief Justice of the United States John G. Roberts Jr., Associate Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. and Associate Justice Elena Kagan. Standing behind from left: Associate Justice Amy Coney Barrett, Associate Justice Neil M. Gorsuch, Associate Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh and Associate Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
The unusual collaboration follows two earlier cases in which Sotomayor authored statements joined by Gorsuch after the Supreme Court declined review.

In November 2024, the pair raised concerns in Baker v. City of McKinney, a Texas case involving a homeowner whose property was extensively damaged during a police operation to apprehend an armed fugitive.

Police had used tear gas, explosives and an armored vehicle during the standoff, leaving the home severely damaged. Although the justices acknowledged that officers acted properly to protect public safety, they questioned whether the Constitution permits the government to impose the financial burden of such damage on an individual homeowner without compensation.

Meanwhile, in February 2025, Sotomayor and Gorsuch again joined forces, this time questioning whether the Fourth Amendment permitted police to make warrantless arrests for misdemeanors committed outside an officer's presence that they did not personally witness.

That case involved a Florida man arrested for loitering and prowling after police responding to a report of suspicious activity encountered him walking through a residential neighborhood before dawn. A subsequent search uncovered stolen mail, leading to a federal criminal charge.

title: Bill and Hillary Clinton make eleventh-hour midterm moves as party's old guard faces new reality
summary: Bill Clinton heads to Florida to campaign for David Jolly while Hillary Clinton launches "High Stakes" podcast with Kara Swisher for midterms.
story: Fox News host Greg Gutfeld and the panel discuss claims that the former first lady would have won the presidential race if she were a man.

The Clintons are back on the midterm campaign circuit — with Bill Clinton heading to Florida to stump for Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Jolly and Hillary Clinton taking to the podcast microphone as the party makes its final push toward Election Day.

The former president is scheduled to make his first public campaign appearance of the 2026 election cycle on Oct. 20 for Jolly, a former Republican congressman turned Democrat. Hillary, meanwhile, has teamed up with journalist Kara Swisher for a new midterm-focused podcast series and has been making campaign appearances of her own.

The moves bring two of the Democratic Party's most recognizable figures into the midterm fight as the party grapples with competing visions for its future, raising questions about how much influence the Clintons still wield as progressive candidates challenge the Democratic establishment.
BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and her husband, former U.S. President Bill Clinton. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
While the Clintons remain prominent in Democratic politics, one party strategist says Democrats are more focused on winning elections than revisiting the party's past.

"President Clinton remains one of the most gifted political communicators this country has ever known, particularly when it comes to connecting with working-class voters on the economic issues that matter most," said Democratic strategist Kevin Walling. "But I don’t believe that Democrats are looking for a Clinton restoration — they’re looking for a path back to winning."
Democratic strategist Mally Smith offered a more skeptical assessment of how much reach the Clintons have in the closing weeks of the election.

"Hillary and Bill are still relevant to some voters. However, they will mostly be useful in speaking to the Democratic base and those who are highly engaged in politics," said Smith. "It is a hard media environment to breakthrough and even current elected officials, let alone former office holders, will struggle to get people’s attention."

Clinton's Oct. 20 appearance will take place at an interfaith event in Hollywood, Florida, alongside Jolly, who is facing Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in the race to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis.

Jolly is campaigning on affordability, including lowering property insurance costs through a state-backed catastrophe fund, expanding Medicaid, increasing funding for public schools and protecting abortion rights.
Hillary Clinton, meanwhile, traveled to Omaha, Nebraska, on Saturday to rally support for Democratic candidates Lynne Walz and Denise Powell at a "Pumpkins, Pies, and Politics" fundraiser.
HILLARY CLINTON ISSUES ENDORSEMENT IN US MIDTERM ELECTIONS
Bill and Hillary Clinton, seen during President Donald Trump's January 2025 inauguration, are being targeted by House Republicans. (Melina Mara - Pool/Getty Images)

Asked how she would address Democrats who feel their votes no longer matter, Clinton pointed to a series of national crises that have contributed to voter frustration — including her 2016 election loss.

"And you could kind of understand that, for people who feel like they've had a series of hard times. If you look back on the last 25 years in our country, I was a senator from New York on 9/11. That was a trauma. The terrible financial crisis of 2008 was horrific for people. We had an election in 2016 that, you know, raised a lot of questions that we're still trying to find answers for about what, what kind of really went on, and then we had COVID," she said during the Nebraska event.

Clinton teamed up with journalist and podcast host Kara Swisher for a six-week limited series titled "High Stakes," which debuted Oct. 14 and will air weekly through mid-November, focusing on the 2026 midterm elections, key congressional races and issues.

The first episode, which aired Wednesday, centered on rising costs for gas, groceries and healthcare, Elon Musk's political spending and how Democrats can make affordability a winning message, while also examining key Senate races in Michigan and Maine.
HILLARY CLINTON CONCEDES INFAMOUS 9/11 NEAR-FAINTING EPISODE IN 2016 WAS A 'MISTAKE' ON HER PART
Former president Bill Clinton is pictured alongside his wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. (Kenny Holston-Pool/Getty Images)

"If the former president can help Democrats compete in a challenging state like Florida, and Secretary Clinton’s podcast can contribute to a substantive national conversation that motivates my party, that’s certainly a positive," said Walling.

The Clintons' increased visibility comes as Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates have scored primary victories against incumbent or establishment-backed Democrats in states including Colorado, New York and Michigan.
MEET THE FAR-LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT IN 2026 MIDTERMS
"The challenge for Democrats is drawing on the wisdom and experience of the party’s past without overshadowing the next generation of leaders who will define its future," he added.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Clintons and Jolly’s campaign for comment.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Somalis in Minnesota unleash fury on Trump after feds raid Ilhan Omar's DC home
summary: Minneapolis Somali community members say they feel personally attacked after federal agents raided Rep. Ilhan Omar's D.C. home in a citizenship probe.
story: Members of Minneapolis' Somali community, including a city councilman, trashed President Trump and his administration after Monday's early morning raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C. home. (Credit: Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

MINNEAPOLIS — Members of Minnesota's growing Somali community, including a city council member, tore into President Donald Trump and his administration when speaking with Fox News Digital after Monday's raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., residence.

"Somalis — we all feel attacked by President Trump," Jamal Osman, the Somali-born vice president of the Minneapolis City Council, said of the impact of the raid carried out by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents.
"Our president has broken the law many times. ICE [is] terrorizing our community ... and we're not surprised such action has taken place," Osman continued in reference to the search of Omar's home.
FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION

Minneapolis City Council member Jamal Osman speaks during a press conference to address the media following reports that the Trump administration will be targeting Somali immigrants in the Twin Cities, held at City Hall in Minneapolis, Minn., on Tuesday, Dec. 2, 2025. (Leila Navidi/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)
"We have seen the threats, the horrific language he uses against my community. It's unacceptable, and we're hoping this could stop," Osman said.

A 37-year-old social worker and Minneapolis resident named Abdi, who declined to give his last name or be interviewed on camera, had even harsher words for the president. He, like Osman, said he was born in Somalia.
"I feel like raiding a congresswoman — it feels like Donald Trump and his regime wanted to use their power to dehumanize and also humiliate someone that is part of the Congress," Abdi said.
He claimed that Trump "hates Somali people because of Ilhan Omar."
Abdi said Trump created "hate" and a "fight" with Somalis in America and claimed that they are being followed and harassed in the streets because of the president.
TRUMP RALLY CROWD CHANTS 'DEPORT' AS PRESIDENT RIPS ILHAN OMAR AFTER FEDERAL RAID
"It's personal," he said. "And Ilhan Omar — he doesn't treat her as a congressmember — he treats her as someone who's below him."

"If they take the citizenship away from her, then I will say, ‘Are we in a dictatorship?’ That's using power to use against an American citizen, then maybe the thinking we have for the United States is completely different."
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on October 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
Osman said the raid is proof of what the Trump administration is willing to do.

"We live in the United States, which is the land of the laws. I don't expect Trump or anyone in this matter to break the U.S. Constitution," he continued. "There's laws. He can, of course, threaten, but there's a court process, there's due process. He can't say he's gonna deport her, he's gonna deport me, thousands of Somalis."
OMAR RAID OUTRAGE GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE WHEN INTERNET NOTICES HER PAST 6-WORD CLAIM: 'COULDN'T AGREE MORE'
Osman's message to the president was simple: "Stop it."
"We're American citizens like everyone else," he said.
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on October 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
A third person, a 22-year-old Somali American woman who declined to be named or filmed, told Fox News Digital that she wasn't surprised about the raid on Omar's home.

"I thought it was bound to happen soon enough," she said. "They've been talking about her in a negative manner. The government [has been] constantly questioning her immigration status and her naturalization in the country. So it was bound to happen for them to investigate her soon enough."
When reached about the comments from the Minneapolis Somali community, the White House pointed Fox News Digital to the president's public reaction to the raid on Monday.

"I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me," Trump brushed off. "I think she’s a terrible person. Just a complainer. She comes from a country that is a non-country, and then she comes over here, and she complains about our Constitution."
"I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ. I have nothing to do with it."

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., attends a field hearing at the Minnesota Senate Building on Jan. 16, 2026, in St. Paul, Minn. The hearing, titled "Kidnapped and Disappeared: Trump's Deadly Assault on Minnesota," featured local citizens and politicians discussing Immigration Operation "Metro Surge." (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images)
ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION

HSI, the principal investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), executed a search warrant at Omar's home in the nation's capital early Monday morning, as first reported by Fox News Digital.

Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that the raid stems from an investigation into whether Omar or her late father, Nur Mohamed, fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork decades ago. The investigation, the sources note, could lead to the congresswoman's denaturalization.
The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Omar's phone, passport and computers were seized in the raid — it is not clear which other items or materials were taken from her residence, if any.
Omar has not been seen since the raid, but offered her reaction to the unfolding investigation on social media Monday afternoon.

"This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies. For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," she said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: FBI probes suspicious white powder letters sent to Schumer, Dem senators as threat spreads nationwide
summary: Senior Capitol Hill staff were warned about suspicious letters containing unknown substances mailed to multiple congressional offices and election offices nationwide.
story: Federal officials investigate '86 47' vandalized on the National Mall grass, a message threatening President Donald Trump.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and two other Senate Democrats were the intended recipients of mail that federal investigators say contained "suspicious substances," Fox News Digital has learned. A source familiar confirmed to Fox News Digital that Schumer's office was the intended target, among other congressional offices, of a mysterious envelope containing an unknown substance.
He wasn't the only Senate Democrat targeted.

Sens. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., and Alex Padilla, D-Calif., were both informed by the FBI that their respective offices were sent a suspicious letter on Thursday, following warnings in both chambers of Congress that federal investigators were "investigating multiple letters containing suspicious substances that were mailed to various addresses nationwide, including multiple Congressional offices."
Josh Sorbe, a spokesperson for Murphy, told Fox News Digital that the senator’s office "was sent a letter with a suspicious substance."
ARMED MAN ARRESTED AT US CAPITOL BARRICADE AS POLICE PROBE WHY HE DROVE ONTO RESTRICTED GROUNDS
A U.S. Capitol Police officer at the Capitol in Washington, D.C. (Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)

"Our office was promptly informed of the letter by FBI, SAA, and Capitol Police, and we continue to work closely with them and federal law enforcement," Sorbe said. "Due to those efforts and various safety protocols, the Senator and staff were not in immediate danger. Our office is grateful for the investigators involved in this incident, and we intend to continue close coordination as the investigation continues."

A spokesperson for Padilla told Fox News Digital, "We received the notification from the FBI that one of our offices was mailed a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted by USPS."

The two incidents follow warnings sent out to top-ranking staff on the Hill earlier Thursday by both the Senate and House sergeants at arms that the FBI, U.S. Postal Inspection Service, and U.S. Capitol Police were actively investigating the matter, per notices obtained by Fox News Digital.
DEPROGRAMMED: FORMER DSA INSIDER REVEALS ‘FRIGHTENING’ SOCIALIST AGENDA DROVE HIM FROM ‘EXTREME’ IDEOLOGY

"Law enforcement officials are working to intercept any additional letters before they are delivered, however, it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations," the notice from the Senate Sergeant at Arms read.
The exact nature of the suspicious substances, and just how many congressional offices are intended recipients, remains unclear.

Top staff in the House were warned by the House Sergeant at Arms that the office had "been made aware of reports of letters containing suspicious white powder substances received by public officials throughout the United States."

"Although no House Members have been identified as intended recipients at this time, the SAA continues to monitor the situation and coordinate with law enforcement partners," the notice read. "All offices are reminded to remain vigilant and follow safe mail handling procedures to help protect staff from potentially harmful materials."

An FBI spokesperson declined to confirm specific instances or letters, but said in a statement that, "The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices."

"Some of the letters contained an unknown substance, and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," the spokesperson said. "We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters. This FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens."
MASSIVE TROVE OF REPUBLICAN VOTER AND DONOR INFO BREACHED IN BIDEN DOJ PROBE: SENATE CHAIRMAN
Signs from the Metro DC Democratic Socialists of America. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

Included in the Senate Sergeant at Arms' notice was an image of one of the envelopes that included a return address in the top-left corner for the Democratic Socialists of America’s (DSA) headquarters in New York City.

It is unclear whether the DSA had any involvement in sending the letters. Fox News Digital reached out to the DSA for comment but has not heard back.A representative for the organization told the New York Post that the DSA "has not occupied this office address since 2013."
"We are also no longer headquartered at 75 Maiden Lane," the rep said.
The notice warned that "all suspicious letters, packages, or substances should be treated as potentially hazardous."

Suspicious letters were also sent to state elections offices around the country. The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said in a joint statement that, "Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties."

"Election officials take these matters seriously and work closely with law enforcement and security partners to protect their personnel and facilities," the organizations said. "We have security measures and contingency plans in place to respond to potential threats and emergencies while maintaining essential election operations."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
It comes on the 25-year anniversary after an anthrax-laced letter was opened by a staffer in then-Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle’s office on Oct. 15, 2001.

Since then, Congress has drastically overhauled how it accepts mail. Packages and mail no longer come directly to the Hill, and instead are processed in facilities where they are screened and irradiated before making their way to a congressional office.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: ‘Big Condiment’ warning gets Warren roasted online over progressive's economic priorities
summary: Elizabeth Warren's warning about the $45 billion McCormick-Unilever merger sparked online mockery, with users joking about "Big Condiment" prices.
story: 'The Big Money Show' panelists analyze this high-profile feud between Treasury Secratry Scott Bessent and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Ma., as they spar over economic policy and his response regarding the senator's letters.

A post made by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., this week quickly became a punchline online after she warned that a proposed $45 billion deal bringing some of America’s best-known condiment and food brands under one roof could drive up grocery prices even further.

The merger would combine McCormick brands such as Cholula and Frank’s RedHot with Unilever Foods products including Hellmann’s and Knorr. Warren argues the deal could weaken competition and leave shoppers with fewer choices.
Users online joked about Warren cautioning against "Big Condiment."
DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT
"One company could soon control them all," Warren said of four popular condiments. "I have concerns that McCormick and Unilever's $45 billion merger could increase YOUR grocery prices."
The post drew jokes from users who argued that housing, infrastructure and the national debt are bigger concerns than a potential rise in the prices of condiments.
"Yes, a simultaneous increase in the prices of (checks notes) mayo and (checks notes again) hot sauce could bring the country to its knees," one user on X wrote.
"The only thing raising my grocery prices is federal deficit and the resulting inflation you all seem to be ok with," another added.

Venture capitalist Hank Medina sarcastically posted to his X account with 1.7 million followers, "The United States will crumble if big mayo merges with big hot sauce. SOUND THE ALARM FOLKS!!! We have no other condiment alternatives if this happens."
But the real impact of a food merger is no laughing matter.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., urged federal regulators to scrutinize McCormick’s proposed $45 billion deal with Unilever Foods, warning it could reduce competition and raise grocery prices. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, accelerating from 3.4% in August, according to the latest Bureau of Labor Statistics report. Prices climbed 0.6% in September alone, underscoring the persistent affordability pressures facing American households just weeks before the midterm elections.
Narrowing in on grocery prices, they rose 1.8% from a year ago but dipped 0.1% in September, while overall food prices were up 2.5% annually.
With an affordability crisis plaguing the U.S. heading into the midterms, any threat of further impacts on Americans' pocketbooks is worth noting ahead of Election Day.
Meanwhile, Warren has launched a broader campaign to challenge food-industry consolidation — not just against the recent condiment merger proposal.
ECONOMIST CALLS OUT AMERICA’S SOCIALIST ELITE, SAYS THEY GOT RICH BASHING CAPITALISM
McCormick’s proposed $45 billion deal with Unilever Foods would bring brands including Frank’s RedHot, Cholula, Hellmann’s and Knorr under one company. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
In an Oct. 6 letter to the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission, she urged regulators to scrutinize the McCormick–Unilever deal alongside two other proposed food-industry mergers.

The Massachusetts progressive argued the multibillion-dollar deal could reduce competition for shoppers' grocery dollars and retailers’ shelf space across overlapping pantry staples, leaving consumers with fewer choices and higher prices.

If the deal announced in March were approved, it would combine McCormick with Unilever’s foods business in a transaction valued at about $45 billion.
The combined company would bring together brands such as Cholula, Frank’s RedHot, Hellmann’s and Knorr. It is expected to close by mid-2027, subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Fox News AI Newsletter: AI engineer accused of bugging conference room
summary: The Fox News AI Newsletter covers the latest artificial intelligence technology advancements, including the challenges and opportunities AI presents now and for the future.
story: A man described as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national formerly employed as an OpenAI engineer, looks behind a television where a recording device had been placed at a conference room in OpenAI offices, in a still image from surveillance video. (Reuters)
IN TODAY'S NEWSLETTER:
- Ex-OpenAI engineer charged with planting recording device had one-way flight booked to Saudi Arabia, DOJ says
- Anthropic warns self-replicating AI could spread across household devices within months
- One state is ground zero as Trump's multibillion-dollar tech ambitions face a midterm test

INSIDE JOB: The former OpenAI engineer charged with planting a recording device inside a conference room at the AI giant's San Francisco office had a one-way flight booked to Saudi Arabia days before he was taken into federal custody, the Justice Department said.

FRIDGE TAKEOVER: Artificial intelligence models could soon be capable of copying themselves across everyday household devices, potentially creating networks that are difficult to shut down, according to new research from AI company Anthropic.

title: Amazon About You may know you a little too well
summary: Amazon's About You feature includes personality details from your shopping history, and some shoppers are finding hilariously awkward results.
story: Amazon's 'About You' page sparks concern as the 'Outnumbered' panel reacts to the retail giant's data tracking. Kayleigh McEnany, Kat Timpf, Adam Carolla, Harris Faulkner and Kennedy discuss a viral post regarding the discovery.

Amazon knows what you buy, what you search for and even what you tell its shopping assistant. Now, the company is giving you a look at the personality profile it has built from all that information. When I checked my own Amazon About You profile, I found 81 results, including a reference to my mother that caught me off guard. The feature brings together details about your shopping habits and preferences. Some are helpful. Others might make you wonder how Amazon reached those conclusions in the first place.

Shoppers are now sharing screenshots of descriptions that range from funny to completely inaccurate. Amazon says the feature helps improve shopping recommendations. However, it also raises an interesting privacy question. How much should a retailer know about you, and how much control do you really have over that information?
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE
Amazon's About You feature reveals the personal preferences and shopping habits the company uses to recommend products. (Amazon)

Amazon introduced About You in May 2026, although the feature has recently attracted widespread attention as shoppers share their profiles on social media. Amazon has personalized shopping recommendations for years. If you bought a coffee maker, you probably noticed suggestions for filters or other accessories soon afterward. That kind of recommendation has become familiar to anyone who shops online. Now, Amazon is taking personalization further with About You, a section that shows shoppers what the company believes about their interests and preferences.

According to Amazon's announcement, the feature draws on information from several sources, including your purchase history, product reviews and items saved to Lists. Searches and conversations with Alexa for Shopping can also influence what Amazon learns.

For example, someone who regularly buys dairy-free milk might receive recommendations for other dairy-free products. A shopper researching gardening supplies could start seeing suggestions for fertilizer or companion plants. That sounds useful enough. However, Amazon can also develop assumptions about your personal preferences from individual purchases or short-lived interests. That's where things can get awkward.
Amazon's About You feature is already amusing shoppers

Some shoppers have started sharing screenshots of their Amazon profiles on social media. The results range from remarkably accurate to unintentionally hilarious. One Threads user discovered that Amazon had included the description "flat buttocks" in her profile. "I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I'm literally speechless," she wrote.

She even acknowledged that the assessment wasn't entirely wrong. Still, it's hard to imagine anyone asking an online retailer for that particular evaluation. Meanwhile, another shopper shared a profile describing an obsession with minimalist, one-bag travel and a preference for Anker charging products. The shopper confirmed that Amazon had accurately identified those interests. A different user discovered that Amazon had recorded a "one-time specialty cheese exploration." The response was simple: "guilty."

Other shoppers have shared descriptions such as "has no friends" and "cannot keep real plants alive." One woman even reported that Amazon had described her as a "fifty-year-old man." These are the kinds of assumptions that can leave you wondering whether Amazon knows you at all.

My own profile included some remarkably specific observations. Amazon said I "do not like scary movies," "value professional grade audio equipment," "prefer dark chocolate treats" and "enjoy swimming." It even noted my regular fresh flower purchases. But one entry really surprised me. Amazon claimed my mother had stayed at a hotel with another person, whom it identified by name, and had a negative experience. I certainly didn't expect to find that kind of information about a family member in my shopping profile.

These examples show how an algorithm can turn shopping activity into surprisingly specific personal descriptions. Of course, Amazon's conclusions may be incomplete or inaccurate. Buying something for a friend, for example, doesn't necessarily mean you have any personal interest in that product.
YOUR PHONE MAY REVEAL DOCTOR, CHURCH AND PHARMACY VISITS
Amazon organizes what it knows about shoppers into categories, including diet, hobbies and family, which users can review and update. (Megan Montgomery/Threads)
Why Amazon knows so much about your shopping habits

Every time you interact with Amazon, you potentially give the company another clue about your preferences. A product search can suggest an interest, while a purchase provides a stronger signal about something you wanted at that moment. Amazon also uses information from its AI shopping assistant. If you tell Alexa for Shopping that your cat prefers a particular flavor of food, Amazon can use that detail to recommend similar products later.

According to the company, these interactions help make recommendations more relevant. However, a single purchase might reflect a temporary need rather than a lasting preference. Think about buying an unusual gift for a relative. You might suddenly find Amazon treating that purchase as evidence of a personal hobby. That raises another concern. Some purchases can indicate sensitive interests involving health, relationships or other aspects of your private life. Even when Amazon draws an incorrect conclusion, you may still want to remove it from your shopping profile.
How to see what Amazon knows about you
Amazon makes About You available through its Shopping app, mobile website and desktop website. You can review the information the company has associated with your profile and make changes.

If you don't see About You using those steps, try this alternate route in the Amazon Shopping app:
Tap You or the person icon at the bottom of the app.Select Account.Under Account Settings, look for Shopping preferences.Tap About You.Select Manage your information if that option appears.

How to remove personal information from Amazon About You

Here's where I would spend a few minutes if you use Amazon regularly. The company says About You lets you correct preferences, provide feedback and remove information you don't want used for personalization.

Open About You using the steps above.Select a category to review the details Amazon has recorded or inferred about you.Find an entry you want to delete.Select Remove for that entry.When the confirmation prompt appears, select Remove again. You don't need to provide a reason.Repeat these steps for other unwanted entries.

Select a category to review the details Amazon has recorded or inferred about you.
Find an entry you want to delete.
Select Remove for that entry.
When the confirmation prompt appears, select Remove again. You don't need to provide a reason.
Repeat these steps for other unwanted entries.

If you want to correct a detail instead of removing it, open the entry and look for an edit or feedback option. Make your changes and follow the prompts to save them. Amazon hasn't established that every account will show identical editing controls. The available options may depend on the information displayed. Removing a detail from About You changes how Amazon uses that preference for personalization. It does not necessarily erase the original purchase, search or conversation from every Amazon system.
How to reduce what Amazon uses for recommendations
Editing your About You profile is a useful starting point. However, you should also review the activity that influences Amazon's suggestions.
Amazon provides browsing history controls that can help reduce recommendations based on products you've viewed.

Sign in to Amazon.com.Open Browsing History from your account or browsing history controls.Review recently viewed products.Choose Remove from view for items you don't want included in your visible browsing history, when that option appears.Look for Manage history if you want to adjust additional browsing history settings.

Look for Manage history if you want to adjust additional browsing history settings.
Removing a product from the browsing history display should not be treated as confirmation that Amazon has deleted every record of the interaction.
Amazon also provides controls for managing recommendations associated with past purchases.

Sign in to your Amazon account.Visit Amazon's recommendation preferences help page.Follow the available links to your recommendation settings.Review purchases or other activity that may influence your recommendations.Exclude eligible items from recommendations when Amazon provides that option.
Sign in to your Amazon account.
Visit Amazon's recommendation preferences help page.
Follow the available links to your recommendation settings.
Review purchases or other activity that may influence your recommendations.
Exclude eligible items from recommendations when Amazon provides that option.
This can be particularly helpful when you've purchased gifts or products that have nothing to do with your interests.
Review Alexa shopping interactions

If you regularly use Alexa for Shopping, consider what you share during those conversations. Amazon says the assistant can remember details you provide and use them to improve future shopping experiences. Ask "What do you know about me?" to review the preferences Alexa can describe. Then use About You to correct or remove unwanted details. For additional privacy controls, review your Alexa privacy settings and voice history in the Alexa app or your Amazon account. Deleting voice recordings and removing shopping preferences are separate actions, so check both.
Can you completely delete your Amazon shopping profile?

Amazon provides ways to edit preferences and manage certain recommendation signals. However, the company hasn't established that removing everything displayed in About You permanently deletes all underlying information. Your purchase history, for example, can remain associated with your account even after you exclude an item from recommendations. Amazon may retain certain transaction records for operational or legal reasons. Also, About You is only one part of Amazon's broader personalization system. Correcting an assumption doesn't necessarily stop Amazon from generating new recommendations based on future shopping activity. If privacy is your priority, review your browsing history, recommendation settings and Alexa privacy controls rather than relying exclusively on the new profile page.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've always found Amazon's recommendations fascinating, but seeing 81 personal details in my own profile was an eye-opener. Some were surprisingly accurate. Others, including information about my mother, left me wondering how Amazon reached those conclusions. I appreciate being able to review and remove these details, but I'd like more transparency about what happens to that information afterward. My advice? Take a few minutes to check your own Amazon About You profile. You might be surprised by what the company thinks it knows about you.

Would you be comfortable with Amazon building a personality profile from everything you buy and search for, or has online shopping personalization gone too far? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Was your identity stolen? What to do in the first 24 hours
summary: Identity theft recovery starts with securing bank accounts, freezing credit and enabling two-factor authentication within the first 24 hours.
story: Cybercrime losses reached nearly $21 billion last year, prompting Kurt Knutsson to warn of increasingly sophisticated AI scams. He joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to break down the FBI data, highlighting that investment fraud alone cost victims $8.65 billion. Knutsson hosts a free live class to teach families how to protect their money and secure accounts.

Discovering that your identity has been stolen can leave you feeling angry, frightened and unsure where to begin. Maybe someone drained your bank account, opened a credit card in your name or filed a fraudulent tax return using your Social Security number. Whatever happened, your next steps can help limit the damage.

The first 24 hours are especially important because identity thieves may continue using your information until you secure your accounts. Fortunately, you can take several steps right away to protect yourself and begin recovering.
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT
Reviewing your credit reports and documenting suspicious activity are important steps toward recovering from identity theft. (Sara Diggins/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)
Why the first day is so important

Identity theft can quickly spread beyond the account where you first discovered the problem. Someone who gains access to your email, for example, might use it to reset passwords for your banking, shopping or other accounts. That's why acting quickly can make a difference.

However, you don't have to solve everything in one day. Identity theft recovery can take weeks or even months, depending on the circumstances. Your immediate goal is to stop additional fraud, protect your information and create a record of what happened.
What to do in the first 24 hours after identity theft
The following checklist breaks the process into manageable steps. The time frames are guidelines, so prioritize active fraud and compromised accounts rather than waiting for a particular hour.
Start with the accounts most likely to expose your money or personal information.

Contact your bank or credit card company. If someone accessed your account or made unauthorized transactions, call the number on your card or the institution's official website. Report the fraud and ask whether the account should be locked, frozen or replaced. Also ask about disputing unauthorized transactions.Change compromised passwords. Start with the affected account and your primary email address if it may have been exposed. Use strong, unique passwords and a trusted device.Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Protect your email, financial accounts and other important services. Use an authenticator app or passkey when supported.Check for unauthorized account changes. Review recovery email addresses, phone numbers, forwarding rules and active sessions. Sign out of unfamiliar devices.

Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA). Protect your email, financial accounts and other important services. Use an authenticator app or passkey when supported.
Check for unauthorized account changes. Review recovery email addresses, phone numbers, forwarding rules and active sessions. Sign out of unfamiliar devices.
Important: If money has been stolen, report it to your financial institution immediately. Federal protections and reporting deadlines vary by account and transaction type.
Next, make it harder for criminals to open additional accounts using your personal information.

Place a fraud alert on your credit file. Contact Equifax, Experian or TransUnion. The bureau you contact must notify the other two. An initial fraud alert is free and generally lasts one year.Freeze your credit with all three bureaus. A credit freeze is free and restricts access to your credit reports, making it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name. You must contact each bureau separately.Review your credit reports. Visit AnnualCreditReport.com to check reports from all three bureaus. You can freeze your credit even if you expect to apply for a loan or credit card soon. Simply lift the freeze temporarily when necessary.
Creating an official record can help you dispute fraudulent accounts and recover your identity.

An FTC identity theft report can help you exercise certain rights under federal law, including requesting that credit bureaus block fraudulent information. However, you generally do not need to file an FTC report before notifying a bank about unauthorized transactions.
A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?
Acting quickly after identity theft can help protect your bank accounts, credit cards and personal information from further fraud. (Nastasic/Getty Images)
Identity thieves sometimes try to use stolen information across multiple services.

Review other important accounts. Check email, banking, retirement, shopping and payment accounts for suspicious activity. Replace any reused passwords.Contact your mobile carrier. You can also request an Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) at IRS.gov to help prevent fraudulent federal tax returns using your information.
Hours 16 to 24: Document everything
Once you've addressed the most urgent threats, organize your recovery efforts.

Create a fraud recovery record. Write down dates, times, account numbers or case references, representatives' names and the steps you've taken. Store sensitive details securely.Make a follow-up checklist. Identify remaining accounts, disputes and organizations you still need to contact.Schedule additional credit checks. Keep correspondence, dispute letters and identity theft reports in a secure location.

Common identity theft recovery mistakes to avoid
Even when you're moving quickly, certain mistakes can create additional problems.

Trying to handle everything at once. Focus on active fraud and the most sensitive accounts first. Other tasks can follow.Assuming a credit freeze fixes existing fraud. Always contact institutions through independently verified phone numbers or official websites.Failing to document conversations. Keep records of who you contacted, what they said and any deadlines they provided.Stopping after securing one account. Review other accounts that may share passwords or recovery information.

9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE
Helping a family member organize financial records and contact the right institutions can make identity theft recovery less overwhelming. (John Carl D'Annibale /Albany Times Union via Getty Images)
What can wait beyond the first day

Some recovery tasks will continue beyond the first day, including disputing fraudulent accounts, correcting credit reports and following up with creditors. However, report unauthorized financial transactions immediately. Federal protections and reporting deadlines vary depending on the type of account and transaction. Your initial priority is to stop additional fraud and secure your information.
How identity theft protection can add another layer of security

Recovering from identity theft often involves contacting multiple financial institutions, disputing fraudulent charges and keeping track of important paperwork. An identity theft protection service may help simplify the process by offering recovery assistance, ongoing monitoring and guidance when suspicious activity appears.

Identity recovery support: Some services provide dedicated restoration specialists who can help guide you through disputes, paperwork and communication with affected institutions.Financial protection: Depending on the plan, certain services offer reimbursement for eligible stolen funds, recovery expenses and legal assistance. Coverage limits and exclusions vary.Ongoing monitoring: Alerts can help identify suspicious activity involving your personal information, financial accounts or credit reports.Recovery guidance: Some services offer access to identity theft specialists who can explain next steps and help you navigate the recovery process.

Ongoing monitoring: Alerts can help identify suspicious activity involving your personal information, financial accounts or credit reports.
Recovery guidance: Some services offer access to identity theft specialists who can explain next steps and help you navigate the recovery process.

Keep in mind that no identity theft protection service can prevent every type of fraud or guarantee that stolen money will be recovered. You can also take important steps for free, including freezing your credit, placing fraud alerts and reporting identity theft at IdentityTheft.gov.
See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.
If you're helping someone else through this

Many people go through this first-24-hours checklist not for themselves, but for an aging parent, a spouse or another family member. If you're the one helping, the same steps apply. Start by securing compromised accounts, freezing credit, reporting fraud and documenting what happened. Keep in mind that you may need permission or legal authorization to speak with financial institutions on someone else's behalf.

Patience is important, too. Identity theft can be frightening, especially for someone who isn't comfortable managing financial accounts online. Helping them make phone calls, organize paperwork and track important deadlines can make the recovery process easier.
In the days that follow

Once the first 24 hours are behind you, continue working through your checklist. Dispute fraudulent charges and accounts, follow up on your identity theft report and request that fraudulent information be removed from your credit reports. Keep monitoring your financial accounts for suspicious activity, since criminals may attempt additional fraud using stolen information.
Recovery timelines vary depending on the type and extent of the theft. Some problems can be resolved quickly, while more complicated cases may take months.

Consider asking a trusted family member or close friend to help you stay organized. Having someone review documents, take notes or track deadlines can help prevent important details from slipping through the cracks.

The most important thing is to stay focused on what you can control. Secure your accounts, report suspicious activity promptly and follow through on unresolved disputes. You may not fix everything in the first 24 hours, but taking these steps can help limit further damage and put you on the path to recovery.
Kurt's key takeaways

When someone steals your identity, it's easy to feel like you've lost control of your financial life. I've seen how quickly one compromised account can lead to bigger problems, especially when criminals get access to email or other personal information. My advice is to focus on what you can control right away. Contact your bank, secure your most important accounts and freeze your credit with all three bureaus. Then report the theft and keep a record of every conversation. You don't need to pay a company to take these initial steps. I also recommend keeping an eye on your accounts long after the first day. Identity thieves may try to use stolen information again, even after you've addressed the original problem. A little extra attention now can help you catch suspicious activity before it causes more damage.

title: Apple wants to move into your home. Should you let it?
summary: Apple's $299 HomeView smart display uses facial recognition to personalize screens for up to six household members and show live security camera feeds.
story: Apple announced its new HomeView smart home product at an event Tuesday. (Reuters)

Your kitchen counter probably has enough gadgets already. Apple would like to put one more there, and this one recognizes your face. At its "Welcome Home" event on Oct. 13, Apple introduced a $299 smart display called HomeView that promises to make running your home as easy as having a conversation.

And Apple has bigger plans for Siri. The company also unveiled a new HomePod mini, an upgraded Apple TV 4K and a collection of smart home accessories. Together, they could change how you interact with everything from your front door to your television. But there's a catch. Some of the most interesting AI features require compatible Apple devices, and buying into Apple's connected home could get expensive.
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.
IOS 27 IS HERE: 10 IPHONE FEATURES YOU’LL WANT TO TRY NOW
Apple's $299 HomeView lets you adjust your thermostat, control lights and manage connected devices from one touchscreen. (Apple)
Apple's $299 HomeView recognizes who's standing in front of it

The biggest announcement from Apple's "Welcome Home" event is HomeView, a new 7-inch touchscreen that doubles as a smart home control center. It sits on a rounded speaker base and comes in four colors. Apple also offers a wall-mounted version for people who would rather keep their countertops clear. Here's where things get interesting. HomeView can recognize up to six household members by their faces. Walk up to the screen, and it can switch to your personalized home screen with your calendar and reminders. Another family member can approach and see their own information instead. Initial setup and support for multiple household members require a compatible iPhone or iPad running the latest software, although general Siri AI conversations don't require that device to support Apple Intelligence.

Apple says personal information stays protected through facial recognition and checks involving a paired iPhone or iPad. To display sensitive content, the system requires the recognized person's paired device to be nearby and recently unlocked. That adds an important layer of security, especially in homes where several people share the same screen. Beyond the personalized experience, HomeView handles FaceTime video calls with Center Stage, which keeps you in the frame as you move around. It can display recipes while you're cooking or help locate a missing iPhone using Find My. You can also control compatible smart home equipment without opening another app.

One feature caught my attention. HomeView can display up to nine live security camera feeds simultaneously. You could check a package delivery or see what's happening in the backyard without pulling out your phone. Both HomeView models cost $299. Preorders opened Oct. 13, with availability beginning Nov. 13. However, the wall-mounted version requires a separate mounting accessory, starting at $59.95.
Siri AI wants to become the assistant you've been waiting for

For years, Siri has been useful for simple requests, but longer conversations haven't always gone smoothly. Apple's new Siri AI is designed to change that. It can handle more natural conversations, understand what's displayed on a screen and answer broader questions using information from the web. For example, you could ask Siri to find a recipe someone emailed you or locate a song a friend recommended in a message. With the right device connected, Siri can search relevant personal information and help complete those requests. Apple also says conversations started on HomeView can continue in the Siri app on other compatible Apple devices.

However, there's an important compatibility requirement. HomeView can provide general Siri AI conversations without an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. More personalized features require a paired, compatible device running current software with Siri AI enabled. Siri AI on HomeView is also launching in beta. In addition, Apple says certain AI features that use server-based models will have daily usage limits. The company plans to offer expanded access for a fee in the future.
HomePod mini 2 gets better sound, but Siri AI comes later

Apple's HomePod mini 2 is getting its first major refresh. The compact speaker now costs $149 and comes in five colors, including pink and green. Inside, Apple added an S10 chip that processes audio in real time to improve sound performance. There's also a new feature called Sound Glow. The speaker's illuminated top responds to music, changing colors and pulsing along with what you're playing.

The bigger story is what happens when Siri AI arrives. Apple says the speaker will eventually support more natural conversations and personalized requests when paired with a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone. It can also recognize different household members by their voices. However, Siri AI won't be available when HomePod mini 2 first ships. Apple says it will arrive through a future software update. That's a pretty important detail if the smarter assistant is your main reason for upgrading. HomePod mini 2 is available for preorder now and goes on sale October 30.
ASKED SIRI TO CALL YOUR BANK? A SCAM COULD COST THOUSANDS
The new $149 HomePod mini 2 comes in five colors with upgraded sound and Siri AI features planned for a future software update. (Hollie Adams/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Apple TV 4K finally lets you talk without grabbing the remote

Apple also introduced a new Apple TV 4K, and one of its most useful features has nothing to do with picture quality. The fourth-generation streaming box includes three microphones that can hear Siri requests from across the room. That means you can search for a show or ask a question about what you're watching without reaching for the remote. Siri AI can also handle follow-up questions, such as asking where a program was filmed.

The new Apple TV 4K runs on Apple's A19 chip, which the company says delivers up to 50% faster CPU performance than the previous generation. It also supports a four-speaker surround sound setup using compatible HomePod speakers arranged in matching front and rear pairs. And there's one improvement I think plenty of people will appreciate. The newest Siri Remote can play a sound to help you locate it. It also supports Precision Finding with certain compatible iPhones. That's helpful when the remote disappears somewhere in the couch.

The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and arrives November 13. However, you may not need to buy one to try Siri AI. Apple says the assistant is also available in beta on second-generation Apple TV 4K models and later. To use it, you or the person managing your Apple Home will need a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad running the latest software with Siri AI turned on.
Apple's new smart home collection could make life easier

Apple is also making a bigger push into the connected home with Apple Home Collection. The company worked with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric to develop cameras, smart locks and thermostats that connect directly through Apple's Home app. The LG Smart Deadbolt Lock is particularly interesting. It uses Ultra Wideband technology to recognize when someone approaches with a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch carrying a home key. The door can then unlock automatically without requiring a tap. You can also use a PIN or backup key. The lock starts at $349.95.

Apple also introduced an LG video doorbell with two cameras. One captures visitors while the other helps monitor packages left near the doorstep. It starts at $249.95. Meanwhile, an indoor camera starting at $199.95 can automatically tilt down to stop monitoring when a household member returns home. For temperature control, LG and Schneider Electric are offering smart thermostats starting at $199.95. Using Apple's Home app, supported systems can adjust heating and cooling based on whether someone is home. In eligible locations, they can also respond to electricity rates to help manage energy costs. One convenience I like is that these accessories work directly through Apple's Home app. You don't need to create separate manufacturer accounts or download additional apps to manage them. Apple says the collection will start arriving in December, with certain products following in early 2027.

People view the Apple HomeView, an iPad-like device meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops that will showcase its AI-upgraded Siri virtual assistant, during a smart home product launch in New York City on Oct. 13, 2026. (REUTERS)
What happens to your privacy when Siri moves into your house?

This is the part of Apple's announcement that deserves a closer look. A screen that recognizes your face can be convenient, especially when several people share a home. But what happens when that same system connects to your security cameras and personal information? Apple says HomeView uses protected processing environments called Secure Exclaves to isolate camera and microphone data from the rest of the system. Separately, HomeView checks that it recognizes the user's face and that their paired iPhone or iPad is present and has been recently unlocked before displaying personal information. Siri requests can run directly on the device or use Apple's Private Cloud Compute technology. Apple says data processed through Private Cloud Compute is neither stored nor accessible to the company.

For compatible security cameras, Apple also supports end-to-end encrypted HomeKit Secure Video storage. Certain AI video summaries and recording features require an eligible iCloud+ subscription. Those safeguards are encouraging. Still, I would want to understand exactly which household members can access the system before setting everything up. I'd also review camera placement and sharing permissions, particularly for devices inside the home. For additional privacy guidance, see our CyberGuy article, Are Apple devices spying?
APPLE'S $250M SIRI SETTLEMENT: HOW TO CLAIM UP TO $95
Apple's new smart home collection includes connected cameras, a video doorbell, smart locks and thermostats designed to work through the Apple Home app. (iStock)
What this means to you

Apple's latest announcements could make managing a connected home easier, especially for households that already rely on iPhones. HomeView gives you a shared control center, while the upgraded Siri could make everyday requests feel more natural. However, the cost adds up quickly. HomeView starts at $299, and the new Apple TV 4K costs another $299. Add compatible cameras or a smart lock, and you're spending considerably more. Some camera features also require an iCloud+ subscription.

There's also the question of how much of this technology you actually need. If you already have a smart speaker that controls your lights and a television that streams your favorite shows, Apple's latest hardware may offer more convenience than you need. I'd start by checking which Apple devices you already own and whether they'll support the new Siri features. Then think about which upgrades would actually make your day easier. After all, spending hundreds of dollars to save a few taps on your phone deserves a little consideration.
Kurt's key takeaways

Apple wants a bigger role in our homes, and I can see the appeal. I like the idea of asking Siri a question without having to repeat myself or reaching for my phone every time I want to control something. And for families juggling different schedules, a smart display that recognizes who's using it could be genuinely helpful. But I'm still not convinced everyone needs another screen in the house. Will Siri AI finally be as smart and helpful as Apple promises? And how comfortable should we feel giving an AI assistant access to our personal information and home security cameras? Apple has outlined some strong privacy protections, but I'd want to know exactly what information these devices collect and who can access it. For now, I'd be selective. If your current devices work well, there's no reason to rush out and replace them. HomeView has some interesting possibilities, but at $299, I'd want it to make my day easier in a meaningful way. The real test will be how well all these products work together once they're in our homes.
Would you feel comfortable having an AI-powered screen that recognizes your face and connects to your home's security cameras? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Man posing as NFL player accused of conning women out of $1.3M
summary: Domonique DuBose spotted red flags when a man on Hinge with 85,000 followers and a blue checkmark claimed to be a San Francisco 49ers player.
story: A man claiming to play for the San Francisco 49ers matched with a woman on a dating app, but Domonique DuBose had her doubts. When DuBose joined The CyberGuy Report podcast, she explained how she became suspicious of a man who allegedly used a fake NFL identity to pursue women and promote fraudulent investments.

A man claiming to play for the San Francisco 49ers matches with you on a dating app. His Instagram has 85,000 followers and a blue checkmark. There are videos showing what appears to be his football lifestyle. He drives luxury cars and seems to have plenty of money. So, would you believe him?

Domonique DuBose had her doubts. When she joined me on The CyberGuy Report podcast, she explained how she became suspicious of a man who allegedly used a fake NFL identity to pursue women and promote fraudulent investments. Federal prosecutors say Daejon Labrayae Love and an alleged accomplice received approximately $1.3 million from at least 26 women.

Love pleaded not guilty Tuesday to a felony charge of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and a public defender representing him did not reply to a request for comment. Magistrate Judge Jolie A. Russo ordered Love detained as a flight risk.

DuBose recognized warning signs and avoided losing any money herself. "Basically, I caught on right away," DuBose told me. What she uncovered raises serious questions about how easily someone can fake an identity online and how you can spot the warning signs before it's too late.
